title: Decoding All 14 Uniswap v4 Hook Permission Bits & Verifying CREATE2 Salts Offline (Zero Dependencies)
summary: When deploying or auditing a Uniswap v4 Hook , the PoolManager does not inspect your contract ABI to decide which callbacks to invoke — it reads the lowest 14 bits of the deployed contract address ( uint160(address) & 0x3FFF ). Even more importantly, many tutorials still cite older draft bit positions. Under official Uniswap/v4-core Hooks.sol , the exact bit layout is: Bit Mask Constant Risk Class 13 0x2000 BEFORE_INITIALIZE_FLAG Lifecycle 12 0x1000 AFTER_INITIALIZE_FLAG Lifecycle 11 0x0800 BEFORE_ADD_LIQUIDITY_FLAG Lifecycle 10 0x0400 AFTER_ADD_LIQUIDITY_FLAG Lifecycle 9 0x0200 BEFORE_REMOVE_LIQUIDITY_FLAG Lifecycle 8 0x0100 AFTER_REMOVE_LIQUIDITY_FLAG Lifecycle 7 0x0080 BEFORE_SWAP_FLAG Lifecycle 6 0x0040 AFTER_SWAP_FLAG Lifecycle 5 0x0020 BEFORE_DONATE_FLAG Lifecycle 4 0x0010 AFTER_DONATE_FLAG Lifecycle 3 0x0008 BEFORE_SWAP_RETURNS_DELTA_FLAG Custody / Delta 2 0x0004 AFTER_SWAP_RETURNS_DELTA_FLAG Custody / Delta 1 0x0002 AFTER_ADD_LIQUIDITY_RETURNS_DELTA_FLAG Custody / Delta 0 0x0001 AFTER_REMOVE_LIQUIDITY_RETURNS_DELTA_FLAG Custody / Delta Notice bits 0..3 : any hook with a RETURN_DELTA bit set can directly modify swap or liquidity settlement balances (custom fees, custom AMM curves, or value extraction), so decoding uint160(addr) & 0x3FFF is step one of every hook security review. Minimal Offline Decoder (JavaScript) const mask = parseInt ( address . slice ( - 4 ) , 16 ) & 0x3fff ; const beforeSwap = Boolean ( mask & ( 1 << 7 ) ) ; const afterSwap = Boolean ( mask & ( 1 << 6 ) ) ; const hasDelta = Boolean ( mask & 0x000f ) ; Combining 14-Bit Hook Flags with Leading-Zero Calldata Gas Savings Because every zero byte ( 0x00 ) in EVM calldata costs 4 gas instead of 16 gas , mining 3–5 leading zero bytes alongside your 14-bit hook mask saves 36–60 gas permanently on every transaction . On a single-threaded CPU ( HookMiner.sol , ~400 KH/s), finding 0x000000 + 14-bit flags (38 bits) takes ~8 days. On a single NVIDIA L4 running single-block CUDA Keccak-256 ( 1.36 GH/s ), the same 38-bit search finishes in ~3.4 minutes . Free Browser Tools & Open-Source CLI We published free 100% client-side developer utilities (zero private keys, pure JS / Python Keccak-256) so you can decode addresses and verify EIP-1014 salts offline: Browser Uniswap v4 Hook 14-Bit Decoder & Offline CREATE2 Verifier : trxvanity.xyz/tools/uniswap-v4-hook-decoder Zero-Trust GPU CREATE2 & v4 Hook Salt Miner (1.36 GH/s L4) : trxvanity.xyz/create2 Free Client-Side EVM (ETH / BSC / Base) Vanity & Nonce-0 Generator : trxvanity.xyz/tools/evm-vanity-generator Open-Source Zero-Dependency Python CLI (MIT) : github.com/a5768549/uniswap-v4-hook-verifier

title: Temporal Cloud vs Self-Hosted Temporal on EKS: The 69 Million Action Break-Even and the 59 GB History Threshold
summary: Two teams run the same workflow engine and receive invoices that disagree with their volume. The first runs one million durable workflows a month at thirty actions each on Temporal Cloud Business and pays $9,206.22. The second runs twenty million workflows at eight actions each, twenty times the executions and 160 million actions a month, and pays $5,430.58. The gap is not a discount. The first team's workflow is a dunning sequence that waits seventy-five days for a customer to pay. The second team's workflow fans out notifications and finishes in minutes, and both pay the published rate card. Temporal Cloud bills two meters and a plan fee, and they respond to different things. Actions follow how much work a workflow performs, while history storage follows how long an execution stays open and how much it remembers while it waits. At list prices read on 27 November 2026, the smaller workload on long-lived workflows costs 69 percent more than a workload carrying five times its actions. Self-hosting the Temporal Service on EKS replaces both meters with an infrastructure bill that barely moves between 30 million and 160 million actions. That bill is $3,002.26 a month in the reference footprint used here, and the decision is really about which workload crosses it. Figure: stacked bar chart of the monthly Temporal Cloud bill for three workload shapes (A: 160M short actions $5,430.58, B: 40M actions $2,084.82, C: 30M long actions $9,206.22). Dev.to does not render inline SVG, so view the figure in the original post . Assumption Box Prices are US East (N. Virginia) list prices in USD on a 730-hour month, read on 27 November 2026. Temporal Cloud rates come from the vendor's pricing page and documentation of 8 October 2026: actions at $50, $45, $40, $35, $30 and $25 per million across the published tiers, active history at $0.042 per GB-hour, retained history at $0.00105 per GB-hour, Business plan fee of the greater of $500 or 10 percent of consumption, Developer plan at $50 per million with 10 percent support and no base fee. Step Functions Standard is $0.000025 per state transition with 4,000 free each month. AWS infrastructure comes from the EC2 on-demand feed published 24 November 2026, the RDS price list published 27 November 2026, the ELB price list published 25 November 2026, the EKS pricing page at $0.10 per cluster-hour and the EBS pricing page at $0.08 per GB-month for gp3. Used here: m7g.xlarge $0.1632 per hour, m7g.2xlarge $0.3264, db.m7g.xlarge Multi-AZ $0.674, db.r7g.xlarge Multi-AZ $0.956, RDS gp3 Multi-AZ $0.23 per GB-month, Network Load Balancer $0.0225 per hour. Engineering time is carried at $95 per hour fully loaded [assumption]. Executions per month, actions per execution, history kilobytes, open days and retention are [modeled] and are not measurements; no vendor benchmark is reproduced. Excluded on every side: worker and compute charges for the business logic itself, object storage for relocated payloads, data transfer, taxes, commitment discounts and paid support upgrades. Two meters that move apart Actions are the compute meter. A workflow start, an activity start or retry, a timer, a signal, an update and a query each count, and workflow replay does not. The action price steps down with monthly volume on Business and above. It is $50 per million for the first five million, $45 to ten million, $40 to twenty, $35 to fifty, $30 to a hundred and $25 to two hundred. Then the plan fee applies on top: the greater of $500 or 10 percent of consumption. At five million actions the $500 minimum is 80 percent of the bill , which turns a $50 rate into $125 per million in effective terms. History is billed by the gigabyte-hour. Active history is $0.042, retained history $0.00105, so a gigabyte costs $30.66 a month while its workflow is open and $0.77 once it closes. Set that against the same bytes in the database a self-hosted deployment would run. RDS for PostgreSQL with gp3 storage in Multi-AZ is $0.23 per GB-month. Open workflow history costs 133 times as much per gigabyte as the storage that would hold the same events on RDS. Meter Published rate Monthly equivalent Self-hosted comparison Difference Actions, first tier $50.00 per million $50.00 per million Node hours, fixed Twice the Step Functions step price Actions, 100M to 200M $25.00 per million $25.00 per million Node hours, fixed Level with Step Functions Active history $0.042 per GB-hour $30.66 per GB-month $0.23 per GB-month on RDS gp3 133 times Retained history $0.00105 per GB-hour $0.77 per GB-month $0.23 per GB-month on RDS gp3 3.3 times Plan fee $500 or 10 percent $500 at low volume None 80 percent of a 5M bill Step Functions transition $0.000025 each $25.00 per million Node hours, fixed No storage charge Quick Decision Matrix The matrix is a set of metering questions, because the three engines do not sell the same quantity. Decision vector Temporal Cloud Step Functions Standard Self-hosted Temporal on EKS Billing unit Action, plus GB-hours of history State transition, each step and retry Instance hours, database storage, labor Cost while a workflow waits History at $0.042 per GB-hour, no action Nothing until the next step runs Nodes stay up regardless Cost of a retry One action One transition per retry Absorbed in capacity Replay Not billed Not a billing concept, retries are transitions Your CPU time History limit Retention 30 to 90 days, per-run history bounded History dropped 90 days after completion Unlimited, your storage Multi-tenant controls Up to 100 namespaces, RBAC and audit logs included IAM and CloudWatch, no tenant model Not built in, you build RBAC and audit Operational surface Namespace policy, quotas, cost review State machine definitions and IAM Upgrades every two weeks, shard sizing, on-call Temporal Cloud charges nothing for replay and charges for the time a workflow waits, through its history. Step Functions charges nothing while it waits and everything for each step it executes, retries included. Self-hosted Temporal charges for nodes whether anyone uses them or not. What one execution costs on each meter Take a single execution of a twenty-action workflow. At the first tier it costs $0.001 in actions. The same execution holding 100 KB of history costs $0.0000042 for every hour it stays open. Divide one by the other and the meters cross where the workflow has been open long enough. A 100 KB history turns storage-heavy after 10.4 days, 50 KB after 20.8 days, 25 KB after 41.6 days and 10 KB after 104 days. That crossover is the most useful number here because both inputs are engineering decisions: what the workflow writes into events, and how long it waits. Figure: bar chart of the days a workflow can stay open before its history storage cost equals its action cost at 20 actions per execution (10 KB: 104 days, 25 KB: 41.6, 50 KB: 20.8, 100 KB: 10.4). Dev.to does not render inline SVG, so view the figure in the original post . Closed workflows are not the problem: retention costs $0.77 per gigabyte a month, forty times cheaper than active storage. The bill is made while workflows are open, and a team that measures only its action volume is measuring the cheaper half of its invoice. Three shapes and their totals The scenarios below use the same published rates and differ only in shape: executions per month, actions per execution, history size and how long an execution stays open. A is a notification fan-out that finishes in minutes, B is an order settlement that waits three days, and C is a dunning and approval process that waits 75 days. Every volume is a model, and the self-hosted footprint is sized by availability zones rather than by throughput. Monthly cost line A: short jobs B: settlements C: long waits Executions 20,000,000 2,000,000 1,000,000 Actions 160,000,000 40,000,000 30,000,000 History per execution, open days 10 KB, minutes 30 KB, 3 days 100 KB, 75 days Active history, GB 0.06 5.72 238.42 Retained history, GB 190.73 57.22 95.37 Temporal actions $4,862.50 $1,487.50 $1,137.50 Temporal active history $0.00 $97.32 $7,231.79 Temporal retained history $68.08 $0.00 $0.00 Temporal plan fee $500.00 $500.00 $836.93 Temporal Cloud total $5,430.58 $2,084.82 $9,206.22 Temporal Developer plan $8,962.96 $2,441.23 $9,771.31 Step Functions Standard $3,999.90 $999.90 $749.90 Self-hosted infrastructure $4,087.57 $1,482.26 $1,482.26 Self-hosted engineering $2,280.00 $1,520.00 $1,520.00 Self-hosted total $6,367.57 $3,002.26 $3,002.26 Step Functions is the cheapest column in all three rows and the only one that does not move when history grows. The other two trade places depending on how long workflows stay open. Scenario A: twenty million short executions Twenty million executions at eight actions each is 160 million actions, and actions are almost the whole Temporal bill at $4,862.50 of $5,430.58. Storage contributes $68.08 for 191 GB of closed history, because 10 KB histories that close in minutes never accumulate as open bytes. Step Functions prices the same shape at 160 million transitions, $3,999.90, twenty-six percent below Temporal Cloud and with no plan fee to add. The self-hosted footprint for this volume is twelve m7g.2xlarge nodes and a larger Multi-AZ database: $4,087.57 of infrastructure and $2,280 of engineering time, or $6,367.57. At this volume self-hosting costs 17 percent more than Temporal Cloud , and the premium buys nothing the team cannot already buy from the managed service. Scenario B: two million order settlements Two million executions at twenty actions each is 40 million actions and $1,487.50 of action charges. Active history is only 5.72 GB because a settlement waits three days, so storage adds $97.32 and the total reaches $2,084.82. Step Functions charges $999.90 for the same 40 million transitions, less than half the cloud bill. The reference footprint costs $3,002.26, 44 percent above Temporal Cloud and three times the Step Functions price. This is the shape where a managed service is easiest to defend: moderate volume, short waits, and no platform rotation on call. Scenario C: 238 GB of open history One million executions at thirty actions each is 30 million actions, the smallest action count of the three scenarios. Each execution carries 100 KB of history and waits 75 days, so 238.42 GB is open at any moment. Active history alone is $7,231.79 a month and 79 percent of the $9,206.22 bill. The action charge for the same workload is $1,137.50. The team pays more than six times as much to remember what each workflow is doing as to do it. Nothing here is a pricing error. The same history on RDS gp3 Multi-AZ would cost $54.84 a month, and on Temporal Cloud it costs $7,231.79 because the meter multiplies duration by size at a managed-service rate. Step Functions would charge $749.90 for 30 million transitions and Standard workflows can run for up to a year, so the shape is not out of reach for it. What it does not sell is the same durable programming model, and its execution history is deleted 90 days after completion rather than billed. Where the two bills cross Against the $3,002.26 reference footprint with light history, Temporal Cloud costs less until about 69 million actions a month and more above it. The second crossover is storage. At 20 million actions a month, 59 GB of open history is where the cloud bill meets that footprint, and every gigabyte beyond it is priced at $30.66 instead of $0.23. Two numbers decide the architecture: 69 million actions a month, or 59 GB of open history, whichever the workload reaches first. Labor moves both numbers. The table below holds the infrastructure fixed and changes only the engineering hours carried against it. Engineering hours per month Footprint cost at $95 per hour Action break-even What that assumes 8 $2,242.26 45.1M Upgrades are routine and nobody is paged 16 $3,002.26 69.2M Two hours a week on patching, upgrades, on-call 24 $3,762.26 94.6M A release every two weeks with real testing 40 $5,282.26 153.8M A part-time platform engineer and incident work Capacity moves the numbers in the direction nobody wants. That footprint is sized by three availability zones and paired service replicas, not by throughput, so whether it carries 69 million actions is a load test question rather than a rate-card question. Temporal fixes the shard count at build time, and the documentation is explicit that adding shards later requires a rebuild and a migration. That single constraint is the most expensive part of self-hosting, and it arrives before the first invoice. Levers that move both lines The largest lever is what a workflow writes into its history. Activity inputs and results are recorded as events, so a 100 KB history that carries a generated invoice becomes 8 KB once the file is parked in object storage and the event holds a key. That change is not cosmetic. At 20 actions per execution it moves the storage crossover from 10.4 days to 130 days , and it shrinks the bytes every replica has to store and every restore has to read. Continue-As-New is the structural version of the same idea. It closes the current run, starts a fresh one with a small history, and moves the accumulated bytes to retained storage at the cheaper rate, all for the price of one action. Retention is a policy rather than a rate. Cloud caps it between 30 and 90 days, and anything longer is meant to leave through the Export feature, which generates billable actions of its own. Scheduled workflows and batch jobs are easy to miss: each one contributes actions and storage for its inputs, outputs and failures. Task queue fairness adds 0.1 of an action per action for every hour it is enabled on a namespace, whether or not any workflow uses a fairness key. On 30 million actions that is three million extra actions, about $105 at the tier that applies. Plan choice is the last lever, and it is not obvious. The Developer plan has no base fee and a flat $50 per million, so below about 23 million actions a month it is cheaper than the Business plan , whose $500 minimum dominates until its volume tiers close the gap. Migration checkpoint: Terraform and Go If the numbers point to self-hosting, provision the pieces that make a later exit cheap. The database is the part that cannot be replaced casually, so it gets Multi-AZ and the larger instance before the nodes do. resource "aws_eks_cluster" "temporal" { name = "temporal-prod" role_arn = aws_iam_role . cluster . arn version = "1.36" vpc_config { subnet_ids = var . private_subnets endpoint_private_access = true endpoint_public_access = false } } resource "aws_eks_node_group" "temporal" { cluster_name = aws_eks_cluster . temporal . name node_group_name = "temporal-systems" node_role_arn = aws_iam_role . node . arn subnet_ids = var . private_subnets instance_types = [ "m7g.xlarge" ] capacity_type = "ON_DEMAND" scaling_config { desired_size = 6 min_size = 6 max_size = 12 } update_config { max_unavailable = 1 } } resource "aws_db_instance" "temporal" { engine = "postgres" engine_version = "17.4" instance_class = "db.m7g.xlarge" allocated_storage = 600 max_allocated_storage = 2000 storage_type = "gp3" multi_az = true backup_retention_period = 7 deletion_protection = true auto_minor_version_upgrade = false } The database version is pinned deliberately. Temporal upgrades the server one minor version at a time, and an unattended database upgrade is how a self-hosted service loses a weekend. Before any cutover, measure the thing the pricing model cares about: open history bytes. A short Go program over the Temporal client sums the history size of open executions and prices it with the same rate the vendor charges. package main import ( "context" "fmt" "time" "go.temporal.io/api/enums/v1" "go.temporal.io/api/workflowservice/v1" "go.temporal.io/sdk/client" ) const activeGBHour = 0.042 // Temporal Cloud active history, USD per GB-hour func main ( ) { c , err := client . Dial ( client . Options { HostPort : "temporal-frontend:7233" , Namespace : "default" } ) if err != nil { panic ( err ) } defer c . Close ( ) ctx , cancel := context . WithTimeout ( context . Background ( ) , time . Minute ) defer cancel ( ) var tokens [ ] byte var openBytes int64 var open int for { resp , err := c . ListWorkflow ( ctx , & workflowservice . ListWorkflowExecutionsRequest { Query : "ExecutionStatus = 'Running'" , NextPageToken : tokens , PageSize : 1000 , } ) if err != nil { panic ( err ) } for _ , info := range resp . GetExecutions ( ) { if info . GetStatus ( ) != enums . WORKFLOW_EXECUTION_STATUS_RUNNING { continue } d , err := c . DescribeWorkflowExecution ( ctx , info . GetExecution ( ) . GetWorkflowId ( ) , info . GetExecution ( ) . GetRunId ( ) ) if err != nil { continue } openBytes += d . GetWorkflowExecutionInfo ( ) . GetHistorySizeBytes ( ) open ++ } tokens = resp . GetNextPageToken ( ) if len ( tokens ) == 0 { break } } gb := float64 ( openBytes ) / ( 1024 * 1024 * 1024 ) fmt . Printf ( "open executions: %d, open history: %.2f GB\n" , open , gb ) fmt . Printf ( "active history if held one month: $%.2f\n" , gb * 730 * activeGBHour ) } Two parts are deliberately rough: the listing paginates without a stable snapshot, and history size is read from the server. What is worth keeping is the shape of the measurement: open executions multiplied by their history bytes, priced at the active rate. That product is the line that decides Scenario C, and no action dashboard shows it. Five practical questions Does Temporal Cloud bill workflow replay? It does not. The pricing page states that actions generated during workflow replay are not counted, because replay happens on the worker and produces no new server-side operations. That is one of the few places where the managed service is strictly cheaper than running the same code yourself. Is the Business plan always the right plan? No. Developer has no base fee but a flat $50 per million with 10 percent support, so it wins below roughly 23 million actions a month. Business wins once its tiered rates and $500 minimum fall below the flat rate, which is where most production workloads end up. Why does open history cost 133 times as much as database storage? Because the product is different. RDS bills for bytes on a volume you operate, while Temporal Cloud bills for a replicated, queryable history service and meters the hours it is held. What reduces the storage line fastest? Smaller payloads and shorter open lifetimes. Moving blobs out of events with a claim-check pattern and closing long-running workflows with Continue-As-New both attack the product of size and duration, which is the only thing the meter measures. When does self-hosting actually win? Above roughly 69 million actions a month or 59 GB of open history against a 16-hour engineering month, and only if the footprint carries that volume in a load test. Below those numbers the cloud bill is smaller, and above them the platform work becomes the product team's problem. Sources and scope Temporal rates and plan mechanics come from the Temporal Cloud pricing page and its documentation of 8 October 2026, and the self-hosted constraints from the production readiness checklist updated 16 November 2026. Step Functions rates and limits come from its pricing page and workflow-type documentation. AWS rates come from the EC2 on-demand feed published 24 November 2026, the RDS price list published 27 November 2026, the ELB price list published 25 November 2026, and the EKS and EBS pricing pages. The same method applied to the database layer is in Serverless Postgres versus AWS RDS PostgreSQL , and the meter-mismatch argument for observability is in Datadog versus OpenTelemetry with ClickHouse and Grafana . Every volume here is modeled and no capacity is claimed: the footprints are sized by topology, and a load test is the only thing that turns them into a throughput statement. Originally published at SaaS Cost Lab .

title: Go AI Agent Framework With Retries, Budgets and Human Approval
summary: One of my team's main projects has an AI-heavy backend written in Go. I work mostly in Python, where agent frameworks are mature, so I know what the Go side was missing: an agent that's a normal value inside the service, not a Python process reached over a queue. The loop itself takes an afternoon. Deciding what happens at each place it can break is what became Golem , an open-source Go AI agent framework. This post is about that second part: bad tool calls, provider errors, loops, cost and human sign-off, and where each one lands in a run. It also covers how Golem compares with the other Go options and when you should pick something else. It describes v1.2.0, released on 16 November 2026. What breaks once the agent loop is running? The loop is short. The model reads a conversation, asks for a tool, you run it, you feed the result back and repeat until the model answers. Each step then fails in its own way: The provider returns a 429 or a 503 halfway through a run. The model calls a tool with arguments that don't match your schema. The model returns JSON that is almost the shape you asked for. The model asks for the same tool call again and again. A tool needs a person to approve it before anything irreversible happens. A run dies on turn six and you lose the first five turns. Python has good answers to several of these. Pydantic AI showed that an agent can have typed dependencies and validated output, and I used it as a reference. But copying Python mechanisms into Go would have given me something un-Go-like: decorators are awkward, runtime validation hides what the compiler could check, and exceptions as control flow don't suit a language that returns errors. So the question I started from was what an agent should look like if you begin with Go's strengths. What is Golem? Golem is an open-source Go library for building agents. The repository started on 16 August 2026, and v1.0.0 on 25 October 2026 froze the API under a rule written down in ADR 0041 : semantic versioning, additive changes only below v2, checked by an API diff against the previous tag. The short version: Agents are generic: Agent[Deps, Output] . Dependencies and the final output are real types. The module has no dependencies outside the standard library, and needs Go 1.26 or newer. Adapters cover OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, and local models through Ollama or LM Studio. An MCP client works over stdio and streamable HTTP, and an MCP server exposes one agent as a tool. Retries, fallback models, self-correction, usage limits, loop detection, streaming and run events are built in. A deterministic fake model lets you test agents offline. It ships with 39 guides, every example runs offline, and statement coverage is 81.6%. go get github.com/abubakarsiddik31/golem The layering is plain. Your service owns the dependencies, the core owns the run, and everything that touches the outside world sits behind a small interface. Why build agents in Go at all? Agent work is mostly waiting on a network, so it's fair to ask whether the language matters. I think it does once the agent leaves the notebook. An agent service holds many conversations at once, calls tools concurrently, streams tokens to clients and has to shut down cleanly. Goroutines, context.Context and a single static binary fit that shape. A deployed agent can be one small container image with no interpreter, no virtualenv and no dependency tree to audit. The compiler is the second reason. When a tool depends on a database handle and a tenant ID, I want the compiler to tell me if I pass the wrong one. In Golem that's a type parameter, not a convention. What does a first agent look like? This is the smallest working agent, from the README: client , err := openai . New ( openai . Config { APIKey : os . Getenv ( "OPENAI_API_KEY" ) , Model : "gpt-4o-mini" , } ) if err != nil { panic ( err ) } agent , err := golem . New [ struct { } , string ] ( client , golem . DecodeFunc [ string ] ( func ( _ context . Context , r model . Response ) ( string , error ) { return r . Message . Content , nil } ) , ) if err != nil { panic ( err ) } result , err := agent . Run ( context . Background ( ) , golem . RunContext [ struct { } ] { } , "Why is Go ideal for AI agents?" ) fmt . Println ( result . Output ) fmt . Printf ( "Tokens: %d input, %d output\n" , result . Usage . InputTokens , result . Usage . OutputTokens ) You build the agent once with golem.New and run it many times. It needs a model and an output decoder, and the decoder is the line where untrusted model text becomes a value your program is willing to use. Everything else is an option function. The result carries the typed output, the full normalized conversation and cumulative token usage. How do typed tools and dependencies work? Most agent bugs I've seen live in tools. A tool needs a database, an HTTP client or a user identity, and frameworks often solve that with globals or closures, which makes tools hard to test. In Golem a tool is a typed value, and its Exec function receives the run's dependency value directly: type Database struct { Users map [ int ] string } getUser := tool . MustNew ( tool . Tool [ Database ] { Name : "get_user" , Description : "Look up a user name by their ID." , Schema : json . RawMessage ( `{ "type": "object", "properties": {"id": {"type": "integer"}}, "required": ["id"] }` ) , Exec : func ( ctx context . Context , db Database , args json . RawMessage ) ( tool . Result , error ) { var input struct { ID int `json:"id"` } if err := json . Unmarshal ( args , & input ) ; err != nil { return tool . Result { } , err } name , ok := db . Users [ input . ID ] if ! ok { return tool . Text ( "User not found" ) , nil } return tool . Text ( name ) , nil } , } ) agent , err := golem . New [ Database , string ] ( client , decoder , golem . WithTools [ Database , string ] ( getUser ) , ) result , err := agent . Run ( ctx , golem . RunContext [ Database ] { Deps : Database { Users : map [ int ] string { 42 : "Alice" } } } , "Who is user 42?" ) The schema is written by hand and the arguments arrive as raw JSON. That's deliberate. Arguments are untrusted model output, and I'd rather you see the validation than have reflection do it somewhere you can't read. It costs a few more lines per tool, and in return a tool's behavior is visible in the file where it's defined. What happens when a run goes wrong? A Golem run is a transparent loop, and each failure has a named place to land. How does an agent correct bad output? When the model returns bad output or bad tool arguments, the cheapest fix is often to say what was wrong and ask again. A decoder or tool does that by returning an error that wraps *model.ModelRetry : if input . N <= 0 { return "" , & model . ModelRetry { Err : fmt . Errorf ( "n must be positive, got %d" , input . N ) } } The run feeds that message back to the model. Self-correction is opt-in, with separate budgets from WithOutputRetries and WithToolRetries , so a model can't argue with your validator forever. With no budget, the same error fails the run at a named stage with its cause intact. A failure the model should simply see, like a missing file, is &tool.Failed{Reason} : the model gets the reason as a tool result and no retry budget is spent. How do you survive provider errors? Transient provider errors (408, 429, 5xx and transport faults) are retried with WithMaxAttempts . The default is one attempt, so retries are opt-in. Backoff starts at 500 ms, doubles and caps at 30 seconds unless you supply your own. Tool and decode failures are never retried by this mechanism, since they aren't transport problems. When retrying isn't enough, model.NewFallback(primary, backup) tries models in order. For streams there's one rule: a fallback only happens before the first fragment is forwarded, because after the caller has seen output, switching models would replay it. How do you stop a runaway agent? Two limits cover it. golem.UsageLimit bounds input, output and total tokens, model requests and tool calls, and a dollar cost if you supply a price table with WithPrice . Token counts come from the provider's reported usage, so a token limit only trips when the provider reports usage, while requests and tool calls are counted by the run itself. Pricing is yours to supply, because I don't want to ship a table that goes stale between releases, and the library says plainly that the cost estimate is only as good as your rates and isn't a billing guarantee. The second limit is loop detection, added in v1.2.0 ( ADR 0051 ). WithLoopDetection(maxRepeats) counts calls to the same tool with canonically equal arguments across the whole run, and fails the run before the offending call executes. That ordering is the point: a model that polls a tool can't repeat a side effect while you wait for the check. WithLoopPolicy adds checks for repeated results, alternating A-B calls and repeated final text, with a choice between stopping the run and nudging the model. Oversized tool output is the quieter cost. WithToolOutputLimit caps a tool result before it enters the conversation, keeps the head and tail, and appends a marker with the original size ( ADR 0050 ). What do you keep when a run fails? When a run fails on turn six, you still want turns one to five. Golem attaches them to the error as RunError.Partial : the conversation through the last completed turn, the usage so far and the counts of requests and tool executions. Pass Partial.Messages to RunWithHistory to resume instead of starting over, which matters when the run has already spent real money. How does an agent wait for a person? Some tools shouldn't run without sign-off: deleting files, moving money, sending email. A tool defers by returning an error wrapping *tool.Deferred , of kind tool.DeferApproval or tool.DeferExternal . The other tool calls in that batch execute, and Run returns successfully with Result.Pending listing what's waiting. No further model call happens. You resume with RunWithDeferredResults , passing the paused conversation and a decision for each pending call. Approved calls run, denied calls tell the model it was denied, and external results are inserted as given. Because a pause is a returned value, you can store it, show it in a UI and resume it hours later from another process. The reasoning behind that boundary is in the case for keeping meaningful actions with people . Can a Go agent use MCP? The Model Context Protocol is now the usual way to expose tools to agents, so Golem includes a client. mcp.NewStdio starts a server as a subprocess, mcp.NewHTTP connects to a remote endpoint, and mcp.AsTools turns the server's tool list into ordinary tool.Tool values with the server's own schema. A server error flagged as isError comes back as a correctable ModelRetry , and protocol or transport failures fail the run instead of being quietly corrected. The guide says one thing I agree with: don't reach for MCP when a typed Go tool is one function away. A subprocess speaking JSON-RPC has more moving parts than a function call. How do you test an agent without a model? Agent tests are usually flaky (a real provider) or meaningless (mocked HTTP). Golem ships testmodel , a scripted in-memory model that plays back the responses you queue and records the exact request the agent sent: client := testmodel . New ( ) . Respond ( model . Response { Message : model . Message { Role : model . RoleAssistant , Content : "pong" } } , ) agent , _ := golem . New [ struct { } , string ] ( client , decoder ) result , err := agent . Run ( context . Background ( ) , golem . RunContext [ struct { } ] { } , "ping" ) You can assert on the normalized request, the ordered messages in Result.Messages and which stage failed, with no network, keys or sleeps. The repository's CI runs its suite with the race detector, plus a fuzz target on the message JSON format. How does it compare with other Go agent frameworks? I compared Golem with the three other Go options I'd look at: langchaingo , Eino and Genkit for Go. I read each repository's source tree and go.mod on 27 November 2026. Dependency counts are the non-indirect lines in the require block, so they're approximate, and frameworks move fast, so check upstream before you depend on a detail. Golem langchaingo Eino Genkit (Go) Direct dependencies 0 About 60 About 10 About 40 License MIT MIT Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 MCP client In the core module Not in the repository Separate eino-ext module Plugin in the repository, client and server Pause for human approval tool.Deferred , resumable Not found Interrupt and resume in adk Tool approval middleware Retry and model fallback Built into the run Not found Retry and failover in adk Retry and fallback middleware Design centre One explicit agent loop with typed dependencies LangChain-style chains and agents Graph and workflow composition Flows with OpenTelemetry tracing Two things stand out. Golem is the only one with no dependencies outside the standard library, and the only one where a tool receives a typed dependency value for the run. I haven't found an equivalent of RunContext[Deps] in the others, but I haven't audited every API, so read that as what I found, not a proof. The other half is that Golem is not alone on the guardrails. Genkit's Go module ships MCP, retry, fallback and tool approval as plugins and middleware, and Eino's adk package has retry, failover and interrupt-and-resume. Only langchaingo lacks them in the repositories I read. The Golem README understated Genkit on this. The others are ahead in other places. Eino's graph model is more expressive than Golem's linear loop for branching, parallel and multi-agent pipelines, and it has more community components. langchaingo covers more providers and vector stores. Genkit has first-party Google tooling and tight Gemini integration. What Golem offers is a smaller surface: one runtime for a single agent inside a service, with the controls in the core module instead of in add-on packages. When should you pick something else? Pick Golem if you want agents inside a Go service, typed dependencies, a module with nothing else to audit and tests that run offline. Pick something else if your agent is mostly prompt experimentation, if you need a graph engine for complicated multi-agent pipelines, or if you need a large catalog of prebuilt integrations today. Python is still ahead on that last one, and I won't pretend otherwise. Golem also has no evaluation harness and no durable workflow engine, and v1.0.0 lists both as non-goals. Herbie, a self-hosted chat and workflow app I built, runs its Go backend on Golem. I don't have production numbers to publish yet, so everything above is design reasoning plus what the repository's tests and examples show. The documentation site has a guide for each feature, and examples/ has runnable programs for nearly all of them, several with no API key. Project page: the Golem overview and capability matrix Repository: github.com/abubakarsiddik31/golem Docs: abubakarsiddik31.github.io/golem API reference: pkg.go.dev/github.com/abubakarsiddik31/golem Issues and pull requests are welcome. If you try it and something feels un-Go-like, I want to hear about it. Frequently asked questions What is Golem? Golem is an open-source AI agent framework for Go. It provides typed agents, tools with dependency injection, structured output, MCP support, and controls like retries, usage limits, loop detection and human approval. Does Golem have external dependencies? No. It uses only the Go standard library. Which LLM providers does it support? OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, and local models through Ollama, LM Studio or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Can I test agents without calling an API? Yes. The testmodel package gives you a deterministic fake model, and the examples run offline. Does it support MCP? Yes. The mcp package is a client for stdio and streamable HTTP servers, and mcpserver exposes an agent as an MCP tool. Originally published at abubakar-siddik.com .

title: Five Sectors, One Break Point
summary: The five sectors picked this week are a long way apart, their public rules say nothing to each other, but inside they all break in the same place. A translation firm has two books. Assignment is one, terminology is the other. The glossary is scattered across the folders of individual projects, and the same word comes out one way in this project and another way in the next; the translator is dispatched, and what gets used is last year's wording from some project's folder. An exhibition stand builder has two books. Drawings are one, the schedule is the other. The drawing was revised while the site keeps building to the old one, because the revision went out in a group chat and which version the crew holds depends entirely on who forwarded the last message. A film production company has two books. Scheduling is one, footage is the other. Schedule, location, cast and call sheets are four tables that each mind their own business; the footage sits on several external drives, and whether the copy finished all comes down to somebody remembering. A tea wholesaler has two books. Batches are one, warehousing is the other. The temperature and humidity record that should exist often turns out to hold nothing but the time the machine was switched on and off; which shelf a given lot is on comes down to a handwritten label stuck on the day it came in. A pet funeral service has two books. Bookings are one, workflow is the other. This line does not run on footfall, it runs on one phone call; booking, collection, cremation and handover run in four steps, and no step can do the work of another. Put the five side by side and they are not five sectors' problems. They are one break point. Every job has to pass through two steps, and both steps are recorded, and neither record is wrong; but nobody records the handover between them. So nobody can say how far along that job actually is. And the job machines take on in these five sectors is the same one: carry it over to the next step. Join the output of one stage to the input of the next - the translator who was picked to the wording the team has actually settled on, the schedule for move-in day to the drawing the site is really working from, the footage of that scene to that call sheet, this lot to the batch it was received as, this job to the certificates it is supposed to have. Every handover that does not line up gets flagged. ​ What stays human is the same too ​: which wording finally settles for this term, which drawing is the valid one, which take to keep and which to cut, whether this lot may leave the warehouse, and what is said to the family, each sector has its own people. Machines join the handover, people decide the exceptions. Quick Reference Five sectors, one action: carry the output of one stage over to the input of the next. settles, whether a senior translator steps in (the project manager decides) Exhibition stand builders Drawing versions and move-in scheduling The version in the last group message, the schedule asked for one by one Schedule joined to the drawing version, flagging which version goes up that day Which version counts, whether to rebuild, whether to add people (the builder's project manager decides) Film production Shooting schedule and footage The schedule on four tables, the footage on several drives Call sheet joined to where the footage landed, flagging which job it belongs to and what is missing Whether to move the schedule, which take to keep, how footage is licensed (the producer decides) Tea wholesalers Batches and ageing in the warehouse The batch on the intake note, the state on a handwritten label Shelf and temperature joined to the intake batch, flagging which shelf this lot is on Whether this lot may leave, how it is handled, what it is priced at (the wholesaler decides) Pet funeral services Bookings and workflow compliance The booking in the switchboard operator's hands, the certificates along the four steps Workflow step joined to the certificates per job, flagging how far the job has got and what is missing How the family is comforted, how paperwork is completed, what is said outside (the service decides) And the external requirements in these five sectors get more specific all the time: ​ The 2026 China Translation Industry Development Report, released on the association's website on 28 April 2026, and GB/T 19363.1-2022, Translation Services - Part 1: Requirements for Translation Services (effective 1 July 2023, identical adoption of ISO 17100:2015) ​: the total annual output value of China's translation industry in 2025 was about 70.12 billion yuan, and 14,393 enterprises run translation as their main business; senior talent remains in short supply, human-machine collaboration has become a basic consensus across the industry, and the requirements for written translation services already have a written national standard to follow ​ The China Council for the Promotion of International Trade's China Exhibition Economy Development Report 2025, and T/CAWS0002-2022, Safety Management Specification for the Exhibition Industry (effective 1 May 2022) ​: 4,095 trade and economic exhibitions were held nationwide in 2025 with a total exhibition area of 159 million square metres, up 6.53 percent and 2.5 percent year on year respectively; the standard has a chapter on the timing of construction (move-in) and dismantling (move-out), and Chapter 14 requires the sector to build an information system for exhibition safety management and an information platform for recording safety data ​ Figures published by the National Film Administration on 5 January 2026, with Articles 13, 17 and 19 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Promoting the Film Industry and Article 16 of the Regulations on Commercial Performances ​: national box office in 2025 was 51.832 billion yuan, up 21.95 percent year on year, with domestic films taking 79.67 percent; filing a script synopsis and obtaining a filing certificate, submitting the finished film for examination and issuing a public screening permit, re-submitting changed content for examination, and re-approving changed performance materials ​ The 2025 Statistical Communique on National Economic and Social Development of the People's Republic of China, published by the National Bureau of Statistics on 28 February 2026, and the 2025 China Tea Production and Sales Situation Analysis Report from the China Tea Marketing Association ​: tea output in 2025 was 3.92 million tonnes, up 4.8 percent year on year; total output of finished and semi-finished tea was 3.6403 million tonnes with an output value of 333.194 billion yuan, with a digitalised primary tea trading platform granting traceability labels and state-owned public tea warehouses GB/T 30375-2013 on storage of tea, GB/T 14456.1-2017 on green tea - Part 1: General requirements, and GB/T 30766-2014 on the classification of tea (public standards in force): the classification, requirements, inspection rules and storage of green tea all have written basis ​ The 2025 China Pet Industry White Paper (Consumer Report), and Articles 25 and Chapter 6 of the Animal Epidemic Prevention Law of the People's Republic of China ​: the consumer market for dogs and cats in urban China reached 300.2 billion yuan in 2024, up 7.5 percent on the year, with 124.11 million urban dogs and cats; a venue opening animal and animal product harmless treatment has to obtain an Animal Epidemic Prevention Conditions Certificate, and a local government reply document made public on 12 June 2025 states that the harmless treatment of pet bodies must comply with the relevant provisions of the Animal Epidemic Prevention Law In other words: which stage is supposed to leave a record, and in what order, is already written down in all five sectors. Whether the next stage picks up the same thing the last stage produced is still left to each company. Assignment list Drawing versions Call sheet Intake batch Collection slot | | | | | Terminology Move-in schedule Footage landing Shelf, temp and Four workflow | | ageing steps | | | | | machines carry the output of one stage over to the input of the next, and flag every handover that does not line up | | | | | Project manager Builder's PM Producer Wholesaler Service Dispatch, wording Version, schedule Cut and licence Handling, price Comfort, paperwork Below we follow that one line. 1. Translation firms: the person goes out, the wording comes from last year's folder The size of the industry sits in a public report. The 2026 China Translation Industry Development Report puts the total annual output value of China's translation industry in 2025 at about 70.12 billion yuan with 14,393 enterprises running translation as their main business; artificial intelligence has a clear substitution effect on junior translators, senior talent remains in short supply, and human-machine collaboration has become a basic consensus across the industry. And the requirements for written translation already have a written national standard. GB/T 19363.1-2022, Translation Services - Part 1: Requirements for Translation Services, took effect on 1 July 2023 with identical adoption of ISO 17100:2015. But assignment and terminology are two books. Which translator is good at which field, and which job this order should go to, all sit in the project manager's head; when a client asks for a new version at short notice, the translator reaches for last year's glossary, and what comes back does not match the other projects. The glossary was always the most valuable thing the company had, and now every new project means copying it out from scratch. How many pages of glossary one project runs through, how many trips a revision takes - not on the public page. ​ What the machine takes is the handover ​: it drafts a candidate list by language pair, subject field and delivery record, then joins the wording in force on that project to the list, and flags which terms the dispatched person is not using the wording the team has currently settled on. ​ What stays human is the dispatch and the wording ​: who takes the job, which wording finally settles for the term, whether a senior translator has to step in, the project manager decides. The machine does not speak for the company. Two books were always supposed to be joined. What this saves is the project manager's time choosing people and digging through glossaries, landing on project delivery labour; what it protects is not letting one word come out two ways across two projects. 2. Exhibition stand builders: the schedule is drawn up on one version, the site builds to another The market is still growing. The China Council for the Promotion of International Trade's China Exhibition Economy Development Report 2025 puts the number of trade and economic exhibitions held nationwide in 2025 at 4,095 with a total exhibition area of 159 million square metres, up 6.53 percent and 2.5 percent year on year respectively, and 224 exhibition centres actually in operation; the report also notes that artificial intelligence and digital twin technologies are iterating quickly and are adding momentum to the digital upgrade of the exhibition sector. And the timing of move-in is written into a standard. T/CAWS0002-2022, Safety Management Specification for the Exhibition Industry, has a chapter on the timing of construction (move-in) and dismantling (move-out), and in Chapter 14 requires the sector to build an information system for exhibition safety management and an information platform for recording safety data. But drawings and schedule are two books. The builder takes on one stand, yet the build runs in four stages - drawings, construction, move-in, move-out - and each stage has its own deadline. The worst case is a drawing that was revised while the site keeps building to the old one: the revision went out in a group chat, which version the crew is holding depends entirely on who forwarded the last message; the move-in schedule also travels by group chat, asked for one by one, with no reliable answer and dates that can only wait for someone to reply. How many drawing revisions one stand goes through, how many trips to site - not on the public page. ​ What the machine takes is the handover ​: it first lays out a table of what happens on which day from the drawing versions, the four deadlines and the order of move-in, then joins each drawing version to the version actually in use on site on that same day, flags the line where they differ and writes down what changed - so it is visible at a glance which version is going up that day. ​ What stays human is the version and the schedule ​: whether to revise, which version counts, whether to tear down and rebuild, whether to add people to finish on time, the builder's project manager decides. Drawings and schedule were always supposed to be joined. What this saves is the time spent on versions and running to site, landing on build and project management labour; what it protects is not finding out that the stand was built to the old drawing only after it is finished. 3. Film production: the footage of one scene on the call sheet lands on another drive The market is moving up. Figures published by the National Film Administration on 5 January 2026: national box office in 2025 was 51.832 billion yuan, up 21.95 percent year on year, with 1.238 billion cinema admissions, domestic films taking 41.293 billion yuan or 79.67 percent. And filing a project and its versions is a publicly checkable step. The National Film Administration website carries a filing and approval lookup for films and a public notice of public screening permits being issued; Articles 13, 17 and 19 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Promoting the Film Industry require the legal person or other organisation intending to produce a film to file a synopsis of the script and obtain a filing certificate, require the finished film to be submitted for examination with a public screening permit issued for approval, and require a film that needs its content changed to be re-submitted for examination in accordance with the law; Article 16 of the Regulations on Commercial Performances requires the application materials for a commercial performance to include the time, place, number of sessions, the programme and the audiovisual material, and any change to those materials requires the application to be re-approved. But schedule and footage are two books. Schedule, location, cast and call sheets are four tables that each mind their own business, and none of them reads the others; when the schedule changes, all four move, the call sheet alone has to be sent out again. The footage sits on several external drives, and who it was copied to, where it is, and whether the copy finished all come down to somebody remembering; backups are copied by hand, whether a copy that stopped halfway was noticed depends entirely on who happened to remember that day, and once the drive is brought back nobody asks again. How many call sheet versions one project goes through, how many rounds of copying the footage needs, how many times a scene has to be shot again - not on the public page. ​ What the machine takes is the handover ​: it first lays out what changed and who has to be told from the call sheet and the availability of locations and cast, then joins the footage on each drive back to the scene it belongs to, line by line onto one sheet - which job on the call sheet this scene's footage belongs to, and which copy is still missing. ​ What stays human is the schedule and what is kept ​: whether to move the schedule, which take to keep and which to cut, how the footage is licensed, the producer decides. The machine does not edit for people. Schedule and footage were always supposed to be joined. What this saves is the time spent sending call sheets and chasing footage, landing on production and coordination labour; what it protects is not letting four tables each go their own way. 4. Tea wholesalers: which shelf this lot is on, labelled on the day it came in Output is a matter of public statistics. The 2025 Statistical Communique on National Economic and Social Development of the People's Republic of China, published by the National Bureau of Statistics on 28 February 2026: tea output in 2025 was 3.92 million tonnes, up 4.8 percent year on year. And where batches and warehousing are heading is in the association's report. The 2025 China Tea Production and Sales Situation Analysis Report from the China Tea Marketing Association records total output of finished and semi-finished tea in 2025 of 3.6403 million tonnes with an output value of 333.194 billion yuan, green tea taking 59.03 percent of output across the six major tea categories, and China's tea exports breaking through 400,000 tonnes for the first time; the report also records that 110 pesticide residue limit standards for tea products have been drawn up, that Hainan has launched a digitalised primary tea trading platform that grants traceability labels on the basis of circulation records, and that Fujian and Yunnan have set up state-owned public tea warehouses to keep the quality information of incoming tea trustworthy. (The tea output figure of the national statistics bureau and the finished tea output figure of the association are two different measures and are not mixed here.) Storage has its own standards in force. GB/T 30375-2013 on storage of tea, GB/T 14456.1-2017 on green tea - Part 1: General requirements, which sets out the classification, requirements, inspection rules, labelling, packaging, transport and storage of green tea, and GB/T 30766-2014 on the classification of tea, are the written basis for product classification. But batches and warehousing are two books. The strangest thing about tea is that it comes in as green leaf and turns into a different product while it sits, and the wording has to change when it is sold. Batches, warehousing, moisture and ageing each have their own rules, and none of those rules landed on any sheet at all, they all live in somebody's memory. The temperature and humidity record in the warehouse should exist, and what comes out of it often holds nothing but the time the machine was switched on and off, with the stretch in between empty; which shelf a given lot is on and how far along the ageing is comes down to a handwritten label stuck on the day it came in. How long a batch takes to age, how long stock sits before it turns - not on the public page. ​ What the machine takes is the handover ​: it first lays out a table of what state each lot should be in now, from the intake batch, the shelf and the ageing progress, then connects the temperature and humidity record to it, bringing which lot is on which shelf and when it was last moved onto one sheet line by line - which shelf this lot is on now, and whether it is still the batch that came in. ​ What stays human is the handling and the price ​: whether this lot may leave the warehouse, how it is handled and what it is priced at, the wholesaler decides. The machine does not judge quality for them. Batches and warehousing were always supposed to be joined. What this saves is the time spent tracking batches and watching the warehouse temperature, landing on warehousing and sales labour; what it protects is not letting a warehouse of stock sit until nobody can say what is in it. 5. Pet funeral services: when the phone rings, nobody can say how far that job has got This line is carved out of the pet consumer market. The 2025 China Pet Industry White Paper (Consumer Report) puts the consumer market for dogs and cats in urban China at 300.2 billion yuan in 2024, up 7.5 percent on the year, with 124.11 million urban dogs and cats; the KPMG China 2025 China Pet Industry Market Report states that the urban pet (dog and cat) market in China exceeded 300 billion yuan in 2024. And where this step lands is written in a public reply document. Article 25 of the Animal Epidemic Prevention Law of the People's Republic of China requires a venue opening animal and animal product harmless treatment to apply for an Animal Epidemic Prevention Conditions Certificate, and Chapter 6 sets the requirements for harmless treatment of diseased and dead animals; a local government reply document made public on 12 June 2025 states that pet end-of-life services not including the harmless treatment of the body have no dedicated administrative regulations, and that the harmless treatment of pet bodies must comply with the relevant provisions of the Animal Epidemic Prevention Law and follow the centralised harmless treatment mechanism for diseased and dead livestock and poultry. But bookings and workflow are two books. This line does not run on footfall, it runs on one phone call: the family pet has died, when can you come, nobody can say; the family is distressed and the timing is unpredictable, so the booking does not connect, or connects late, and the whole workflow slides back. Booking, collection, cremation and handover run in four steps, and no step can do the work of another, and they cannot be run out of order; the certificates each step should have are not all there, and afterwards nobody can tell which step was not finished, so the job has to be redone. How many jobs a year are taken, what share of certificates can be completed - not on the public page. ​ What the machine takes is the handover ​: it first lays out a day sheet for the day's jobs from the collection slots, the cremation slots and the order of handover, then joins the certificates each job should have and the one that is still missing to the workflow step it belongs to, line by line - how far this job has got now. ​ What stays human is the family and the paperwork ​: how the family is comforted, how the paperwork is completed, whether the handling method is changed, what is said outside, the service decides. The machine does not speak for people. Bookings and workflow were always supposed to be joined. What this saves is the switchboard operator's time taking calls, chasing certificates and running out, landing on service delivery labour; what it protects is not letting a job half done turn out not to add up. Five Sectors, One Gap Sector What already exists The break visible only at the handover Translation firms Candidate translator lists, per-project glossaries Whether the person dispatched is using the wording the team has settled on Exhibition stand builders Drawing versions, four move-in deadlines Which version of the drawing is going up that day Film production Call sheets, location and cast availability, footage drives Which job on the call sheet this scene's footage belongs to Tea wholesalers Intake batches, shelves, ageing progress Which shelf this lot is on, and whether it is still the batch that came in Pet funeral services Collection slots, cremation slots, certificates per job Which step this job is at, and which certificate is still missing The break looks the same in all five: nobody is missing a sheet. Both stages are recorded, and the handover between them is not, so nobody can say how far along the job is. This Sector's Throughline: the most expensive thing is not that the work goes undone, it is that two stages each keep their own record and nobody records the handover Walking all five, this round's conclusion differs again: Earlier cross-industry rounds: property, government, eyewear, baby retail, parcel returns, one thing done wrong W44's cross-industry: five sectors, one sentence - "I'll decide" W45's cross-industry: five sectors, one notebook that says four words W47's cross-industry: five sectors, one thing recorded in several places This round: five sectors, one break point - two stages each keep their own record and nobody records the handover And an unrecorded handover is not a carelessness problem. Every dispatch record really dispatched a person; every glossary in every project folder was really settled at the time; every drawing version really was drawn; every call sheet really was sent; every intake note really does carry a batch; every certificate really does exist. They are each right, and the handover in between is not recorded, so nobody can say how far along the job is, or which version it picked up. What machines take on here is one class of work: carry it over to the next step, then flag the handover that does not line up. In all five the boundary looks nearly identical: machines join the handover, people decide the exceptions. The Quick Reference table above already lists the handover the machine joins and the sentence that stays human for each sector: the machine only carries the output of one stage over to the next and flags the handover that does not line up, while who to dispatch, which version counts, which take to keep, what a lot is priced at and what is said outside each belong to their own people in each sector. If these five jobs sat inside one company and had to be ordered, the sequence is fairly clear: Translation firms come first, because the handover sits right next to delivery. GB/T 19363.1-2022 has already written the requirements for written translation services into a national standard, and the association's report records that human-machine collaboration is a basic consensus. The reality is ​ the dispatch is all in the project manager's head, the glossary is scattered across project folders, and one word comes out two ways across two projects ​. Machines join the candidate list to the glossary in force, flagging the dispatch that is not using the wording the team has settled on - while which wording finally settles is the project manager's judgement. Pet funeral services come second, because the break is in a service promise. Articles 25 and Chapter 6 of the Animal Epidemic Prevention Law fix the permit for harmless treatment venues and the handling requirements, and the public reply document sets out where pet end-of-life service ends and harmless treatment begins. The reality is ​ the booking does not connect and the certificates are not all there, and afterwards nobody can tell which step was not finished ​. Machines join the four workflow steps to the certificates per job, flagging how far the job has got and which certificate is missing - while how the family is comforted and what is said outside is the service's judgement. Film production comes third, because the other end of the handover is money. Articles 13, 17 and 19 of the Law on Promoting the Film Industry fix filing, examination and re-examination, and the public filing and permit notices show that keeping a record of projects was always publicly checkable. The reality is ​ the call sheet goes out, the footage sits on several drives, and whether the copy finished comes down to somebody remembering ​. Machines join the call sheet to where the footage landed, flagging which job this scene's footage belongs to and what is still missing - while whether to move the schedule and which take to keep is the producer's judgement. Exhibition stand builders come fourth, because both ends of the handover are hard deadlines. T/CAWS0002-2022 has already written construction and dismantling times into a group standard, and Chapter 14 requires safety data to be recorded in information systems. The reality is ​ the drawing was revised, the site keeps building to the old one, and the move-in schedule was asked for one by one ​. Machines join the schedule to the drawing version on the same day, flagging which version goes up that day - while which version counts and whether to rebuild is the builder's project manager's judgement. Tea wholesalers come last, not because it matters less, but because the handover lands on price rather than on delivery. GB/T 30375-2013 and GB/T 14456.1-2017 have already written storage and the general requirements for green tea into standards in force, and the association's report puts a digital trading platform and traceability labels in the direction of travel. The reality is ​ the temperature and humidity record holds nothing but the machine's switch-on and switch-off time, and a warehouse of stock is held together by handwritten labels ​. Machines join the shelf, the temperature and the intake batch, flagging which shelf this lot is on and whether it is still the batch that came in - while whether this lot may leave and what it is priced at is the wholesaler's own judgement. What We Can't See These can only be answered inside each business: How many people one project screens down to for a dispatch, how many entries the glossary has accumulated, how many trips a revision takes How many drawing revisions one stand goes through, how many times the move-in schedule is asked for, how many days a missed window slips by How many call sheet versions one project goes through, how many rounds of copying the footage needs, how many times a scene is shot again How long one batch takes to age, how long stock sits before it turns, how many lots a year get mixed up How many jobs a year are taken, what share of certificates can be completed, how many runs one job takes on average These aren't shortcomings - they are part of the deliverable. The unknowns are themselves part of the deliverable. The Takeaway These five sectors are a long way apart, but the most expensive thing they share every day is one way of breaking: a translation firm records who to dispatch in the project manager's head and how to word it in each project folder; an exhibition stand builder records the drawing in the last message forwarded in the chat and the move-in schedule as something asked for one question at a time; a film production company records the schedule on four tables that each mind their own business and the footage on several drives; a tea wholesaler records the batch on the intake note and the goods in the warehouse on a handwritten label; a pet funeral service records the booking in the switchboard operator's hands and the certificates along the four workflow steps. Every stage is recorded and no stage is wrong, but ​ the handover in between is not recorded ​, so nobody can say how far along that job is, or which version it picked up. ​ And which stage is supposed to leave a record, and in what order, is already written down ​: GB/T 19363.1-2022 writes the requirements for written translation services into a standard, T/CAWS0002-2022 writes construction and dismantling times into a group standard, Articles 13, 17 and 19 of the Law on Promoting the Film Industry fix filing, examination and re-examination, GB/T 30375-2013 and GB/T 14456.1-2017 write storage and the general requirements for green tea into standards in force, and Articles 25 and Chapter 6 of the Animal Epidemic Prevention Law fix the permit and handling requirements for harmless treatment venues. Machines are not taking anyone's job; they are taking the work of carrying the output of one stage over to the input of the next. What stays is five sentences: which wording finally settles, which drawing is the valid one, which take to keep, whether a lot may leave the warehouse, and what is said to the family. Translations still go out order by order, stands still go up one by one, films are still shot shot by shot, tea still comes in lot by lot, jobs still come in one at a time - but when nobody records the handover between two stages, nobody can say how far along the job is. This assessment is based on publicly available information, is exploratory in nature, is not an internal audit, and does not represent the official position of the company in question. Which step should we break down next? Drop it in the comments. Export manufacturing, cross-border e-commerce warehousing, event ticketing, moving and cleaning, or whichever one finds "two stages each keep their own record and nobody records the handover" most expensive.

title: Three free email tiers, three different bets: what systeme.io, MailerLite and Kit actually give a solo builder in 2026
summary: Disclosure: this post contains affiliate links. If you sign up through them, this site may earn a commission at no extra cost to you, and it is how the site pays for itself. Prices and plan limits below were checked against each provider's own pricing page in November 2026; every number is a published list price, not an estimate. Details are on the about page . A solo builder's email stack is usually assembled the same way: a static site or a blog, one signup form pasted into the footer, and whatever tool was fastest to wire up on a Saturday. Six months later the question is no longer which editor looks nicest — it is which free tier still holds the list, what the first paid step costs per thousand contacts, and how much of the plumbing you have to maintain alone. I compared the three free plans that solo builders actually land on in November 2026 — systeme.io, MailerLite and Kit — by their published limits, their first paid tier, and the cost per 1,000 contacts at that tier. Every number below comes from each provider's own pricing page this month, not from a review roundup. Free stopped being the trial tier Two years ago a "free plan" in email marketing meant a demo: a few hundred contacts, a watermark, and an upgrade wall the moment you tried to send anything real. That is no longer where the market is. In late 2026 all three of the tools in this comparison run permanent free plans that take no card and expire on no schedule, and the largest of them covers ten thousand subscribers. Which makes the choice harder, not easier. Three tools, three free plans, three completely different ideas about what a free user is allowed to do. systeme.io gives away a whole funnel and one automation. MailerLite gives away the best editor in the group and three automations, but only for 250 subscribers. Kit gives away the biggest list in the industry and then withholds the one feature that makes a list useful. This guide is what each free plan actually includes in November 2026, what the first paid step costs, the arithmetic of that first paid step per thousand contacts, and the stack I would run as a solo creator with no budget. It is written from the position of someone who publishes weekly, needs a capture page and a welcome sequence, and does not want to pay for either until the list exists. The three free plans side by side Read this table as a description of permissions, not of features. The question is not "does it have automations" but "how many, and for how many subscribers, before I have to pay". Tool What the free plan includes Automations on free Pages on free First paid step systeme.io 2,000 contacts, unlimited emails, 3 funnels 1 workflow automation Included in the 3 funnels $17/mo Startup MailerLite 250 subscribers, 2,500 emails a month 3 automations 1 landing page $12/mo Comfort (500 subs) $19/mo (1,000 subs) Kit (formerly ConvertKit) Up to 10,000 subscribers, unlimited broadcasts None Unlimited landing pages and forms $39/mo Creator (1,000 subs) $390/yr billed annually Now the same numbers expressed as cost per thousand contacts at the first paid tier, which is the only comparison that matters once you outgrow free: Tool First paid tier Contacts covered Cost per 1,000 contacts systeme.io Startup $17/mo 5,000 about $3.40 MailerLite Comfort $19/mo 1,000 $19.00 Kit Creator $39/mo (or $32.50/mo yearly) 1,000 $39.00 That table is the whole argument in one place. systeme.io is roughly a fifth of MailerLite's cost per contact and a tenth of Kit's at the entry tier, and it is the only one of the three that includes a funnel builder, a checkout, and a course area in the same account. What you give up for that is polish, and we will get to that. Tool one: systeme.io, the funnel and the list in one login systeme.io started as a cheaper answer to ClickFunnels and grew into an all-in-one: landing pages, funnels, email campaigns, automations, a course area, and order forms. The free plan is unusually generous for a tool with a paid tier behind it: 2,000 contacts, unlimited email sends, three funnels, and one workflow automation , with no card required and no expiry date. For a one-person site, the important part of that sentence is not 2,000 contacts. It is three funnels . A funnel in this context is a page plus the sequence behind it, and having three means you can run a lead magnet, a product launch, and an evergreen signup side by side without upgrading. Most free tiers in this market give you one page and call it a day. The limit to plan around is the single automation. One workflow on the free plan is enough for exactly one welcome sequence — three or four emails that send in order after someone subscribes — and nothing else. If you want a second automation, such as a rule that tags buyers separately from leads, you have to either fold it into that one workflow or move to Startup at $17 a month. Startup is worth understanding before you need it: 5,000 contacts and ten funnels for $17. That is the tier most solo sites sit on for years, and it costs less than the two paid tiers of the other tools in this comparison while covering five times the list. Create a free systeme.io account here — the free plan is permanent, needs no payment details, and includes the funnel builder, so the cost of testing the whole loop is zero. Where it is weak The editor is functional, not delightful, and the template library looks dated next to MailerLite's. Deliverability is fine but not class-leading, which matters more than any feature once your list is real: if forty percent of your sends land in promotions, the funnel is decoration. And the all-in-one promise means the email side is a good email tool inside a bigger product, not the best email tool you can get for the money. Tool two: MailerLite, the best editor and the smallest free list MailerLite is the tool most people recommend when someone asks for a clean, fast email platform, and the reason is the editor. Drag a block, drop a block, and the result looks like a designed email rather than a form letter. Its deliverability reputation is strong, its automation builder is the easiest of the three to understand, and its free plan includes 3 automations and 1 landing page . The catch is the size of the free list: 250 subscribers and 2,500 emails a month . At 250 subscribers that is ten full-list sends a month, which is fine for a weekly newsletter and impossible for anything more frequent. A solo site that publishes weekly and sends a monthly roundup will never notice. A site running a five-email welcome sequence plus weekly broadcasts will hit both ceilings within a few weeks. The paid steps are the cheapest in this comparison at the low end: Comfort at $12 a month for 500 subscribers, $19 for 1,000 . That is the right shape of pricing for someone with a small, engaged list — you pay for what you actually have, in small increments, rather than jumping to a five-thousand-contact plan you cannot fill. The trade-off appears when you compare the second table above. At 1,000 subscribers MailerLite costs $19 a month for 1,000 contacts; systeme.io costs $17 for 5,000. You are paying for polish, editor quality, and automation ease, and that is a legitimate thing to pay for — but call it what it is rather than pretending it is the cheap option. The free plan, precisely 250 subscribers. 2,500 sends a month. Three automations. One landing page. No card, no time limit. For a newsletter that is still finding its first hundred readers, this is a complete product, and the upgrade only becomes urgent when the list outgrows the number, not when the features run out. Tool three: Kit, the biggest free list and no automation Kit, still widely known by its old name ConvertKit, made a decision in 2023 that nobody else in the market has matched: its free plan covers up to 10,000 subscribers , with unlimited landing pages, unlimited forms, and unlimited broadcasts . Ten thousand people, for nothing, forever. What it does not include is any automation or sequence. On the free plan you can build a landing page, collect addresses, and send an email to the whole list when you feel like it — and that is the end of it. No welcome sequence, no delivery of the lead magnet you promised, no rule that sends a different email to people who clicked. For a creator whose whole model is "publish an article, send a broadcast, sell a course", that is survivable. For anyone whose model depends on what happens in the first hour after a signup, it is not, and the fix is Creator at $39 a month (or $390 a year, which works out to about $32.50 a month) for up to 1,000 subscribers . So the honest reading of Kit's free plan is this: it is the best free list in the industry and the weakest free automation in this comparison. If your first asset is a list and your marketing is personality-driven broadcasting, ten thousand free subscribers is a genuinely large runway.
