If your first asset is a funnel, you are one signup page away from a $39 bill. The stack I would actually run, at each stage None of these three is the right answer in every situation, and the difference between them is mostly about what you are building first. This is the decision I would make from a standing start. Starting from zero, with a blog and no list: systeme.io free, alone. The site needs a capture page and a welcome sequence more than it needs a beautiful editor, and both are in the free plan. Cost: $0. When the list reaches 2,000, upgrade to Startup at $17 rather than migrating. Already writing a newsletter with 50–200 readers who open it: MailerLite free, then Comfort at $12 when you pass 250. The editor and the three automations are the reason, and at this size the list limit is not yet the binding constraint. Building toward a paid product, and the list is the business: Kit free to collect the first thousands, with the plan to move to Creator at $39 on the day you need a sequence to sell. Until then, do the sequence manually: send the welcome email by hand for the first hundred subscribers, and you will learn more about what the sequence should say than any automation builder will teach you. The mistake to avoid is running two of them as "the list". A list split across two platforms has worse deliverability, worse reporting, and two dashboards that disagree. One email home, one funnel page, and if you insist on a second tool, give it a single narrow job — a quiz page, a waitlist, one form — and pipe the addresses into the main list. The setup, in five steps Name the thing the subscriber gets. "The 12-tool stack I actually run" beats "subscribe to my newsletter", and the page should deliver it in the first email, not the third. Build one capture page, not a site. One headline, one paragraph, one field, one button. On systeme.io or Kit this is twenty minutes; on MailerLite it is the single free landing page. Write a three-email welcome sequence and stop. Email one delivers the file. Email two answers the question the file raises. Email three offers the one tool the reader most likely needs next, which is where an affiliate link lives honestly, because the reader asked for the material it sits in. Put one link at the end of every article. Not a popup, not a slide-in. One line: the asset, what is inside it, and a link. It converts less on any given visit and it does not make readers hate the site. Look at two numbers a week: visits and subscribers. Rising visits with flat subscribers means the page or the offer is wrong. Rising subscribers with flat visits means a distribution problem no email tool can fix. What this costs, and what pays for it At the start, nothing. All three free plans take no card. The first real bill in this comparison is $12 a month on MailerLite Comfort, $17 on systeme.io Startup, or $39 on Kit Creator, and the arithmetic above makes it clear which of those three buys the most list. The affiliate side is what makes the free arithmetic interesting. systeme.io pays 60% of every subscription for as long as the referral stays subscribed , which on the $17 Startup tier is about $10.20 a month per referral, with a $30 minimum payout. Two people who sign up on the cheapest paid plan cover the cost of the whole stack and then some, and unlike a one-time bounty the payment continues until they cancel. That is a modest business, and it should be described as one. Two referrals is a coffee a week. The point is not the quantity; it is that the funnel you built for your own list is the same funnel that produces referrals, so the marginal work is an honest recommendation at the end of an article you were writing anyway. If your site also publishes audio editions or short video narration, the same logic applies to the voice side of the stack — that is the two-tool loop in the previous post in this series , which pairs an email platform with ElevenLabs and walks through the arithmetic in the same way. What free plans will not do They will not fix deliverability. A brand-new domain that sends to a scraped list lands in spam on every platform in this article, and the free tier makes it worse, not because the tools are bad but because reputation is earned by one thing: people who chose to receive your mail and open it. They will not bring traffic. A funnel converts the visitors you already have. At forty visits a day, a good capture page produces a handful of subscribers a week, and that is the correct result rather than a failure. They will not make migration free. Moving 2,000 contacts from one platform to another sounds like a CSV export and is really a week of re-testing forms, re-creating automations, and re-warming a sending domain. Pick the platform whose next tier you can afford, not just the one whose free tier is largest, and you will not have to do it twice. FAQ Which of the three is really free forever? All three are permanent plans, not trials, and none requires a card. Read the limits before you commit: systeme.io's free plan is limited by contacts and automations, MailerLite's by subscribers and monthly sends, and Kit's by automations rather than by list size. Is Kit's free plan genuinely 10,000 subscribers? Yes — up to 10,000 subscribers with unlimited landing pages, forms, and broadcasts. The restriction is automation: no automations or sequences on the free plan, so the welcome email you promised has to be sent by hand, or you pay for Creator at $39 a month. Can I use systeme.io and MailerLite at the same time? You can, and many people do, but decide which one owns the list. Running both as the primary list splits your audience, doubles the work of every send, and makes your open rates meaningless. A common arrangement is one platform for the list and the other for a single narrow job, such as a quiz or a sales page. What happens when I outgrow the free plan? You pay, and the first step is small: $12 at MailerLite for 500 subscribers, $17 at systeme.io for 5,000 contacts, $39 at Kit for 1,000. The one to watch is MailerLite, where the free ceiling of 250 subscribers is the lowest of the three and the per-contact cost at 1,000 is $19. Which one should a blog with almost no traffic start with? systeme.io. The missing piece for a site at forty visits a day is not a prettier email, it is a page and a sequence that stop the reader from leaving with nothing. That is the free plan, and it costs nothing to leave in place while the traffic grows. Bottom line In 2026 the free tiers are good enough to run a real funnel, and they are not interchangeable. systeme.io gives you the funnel and one automation for 2,000 contacts. MailerLite gives you the best editor and three automations for 250. Kit gives you ten thousand subscribers and no automation at all. Pick by what you are building first: a funnel, a newsletter, or an audience you intend to sell to. Then build the one page and the three emails, and let the two numbers — visits and subscribers — tell you when to pay. Starting free is not a compromise this year; it is the correct order of operations. Prices and plan limits in this article were checked against each provider's pricing page in November 2026 and will change. If you spot something out of date, please tell us through the contact page .

title: Chasing down why Ansible stalled on a fresh Ubuntu 26.04 box
summary: I keep a couple of disposable Ubuntu containers around for trying out playbooks before I point them at anything that matters, and this week Lobsters was carrying a report from Jeff Geerling: Ansible's privilege escalation hangs against Ubuntu 26.04. The cause was Ubuntu's new default sudo implementation, a Rust rewrite called sudo-rs , printing a password prompt that Ansible doesn't recognise. The report named a fix and a couple of workarounds. I wanted to know exactly how long the hang is, whether the fix is actually in the Ansible release most people would reach for, and whether the workarounds hold up against a real box. Reproducing it I built a plain Ubuntu 26.04 container with openssh-server and sudo-rs installed (the minimal base image doesn't ship it, but it's Ubuntu 26.04's own default once installed, not a custom build), added a user called deploy whose sudo access needs a password, and pointed a one-task playbook at it with become: yes . With ansible-core 2.17.6, a version released well before any of the fixes mentioned in the report, three runs looked like this: run 1: 12.82s, exit code 2 run 2: 12.76s, exit code 2 run 3: 12.80s, exit code 2 Every run fails the same way, on the very first task, before a single real command runs: TASK [Gathering Facts] ********************************** fatal: [127.0.0.1]: FAILED! => {"msg": "Timeout (12s) waiting for privilege escalation prompt: "} Twelve to thirteen seconds of nothing, three times running, then a hard failure. The right password was sitting in the inventory the whole time. Ansible never got as far as sending it. Why: the prompt itself Ansible tells sudo exactly what prompt text to print, so it knows what to wait for on the wire. I captured the raw bytes of both sudo implementations answering that same request: # traditional sudo, asked for a custom prompt [sudo via ansible, key=test] password: sudo: no password was provided # sudo-rs, asked for the identical prompt [sudo: [sudo via ansible, key=test] password:] Password: Traditional sudo prints the prompt Ansible asked for, verbatim. sudo-rs wraps it inside its own fixed template and appends a capitalised "Password:" of its own. Ansible is matching for the exact string it supplied, so the extra wrapping is enough to miss it. I went looking at the actual fix rather than guessing at it. Diffing the sudo become plugin between ansible-core 2.17.6 and a version that passes, the fix is a second regex, added specifically for this: def check_password_prompt ( self , b_output : bytes ) -> bool : matched = super ( ) . check_password_prompt ( b_output ) if not matched : # try sudo-rs, which is not backwards compatible and does i18n sudo_rs = re . compile ( rf "\[sudo:\s+{re.escape(self.prompt)}\]\s+\S.+\Z" . encode ( ) ) matched = any ( sudo_rs . match ( l ) for l in b_output . splitlines ( ) ) return matched That is a comment in Ansible's own source calling sudo-rs "not backwards compatible", which tells you the project doesn't see this as a wording quirk they're working around quietly. Does the backport claim actually hold today The report said the fix landed in ansible-core 2.22.0 and was backported to the 2.16, 2.18, 2.19, 2.20 and "possibly" 2.21 branches. I installed the latest released patch of each branch from PyPI as of today and ran the same playbook against the same container: ansible-core Python needed Result 2.16.20 3.10+ fails, 12s timeout 2.17.6 3.10+ fails, 12s timeout 2.18.20 3.11+ fails, 12s timeout 2.19.15 3.11+ fails, 12s timeout 2.20.11 3.12+ passes, ~2.1s 2.21.6 3.12+ passes, ~2.1s 2.22.0 3.13+ passes, ~2.1s So the fix is real, but as of today it has not shipped in any released patch of the 2.16, 2.18 or 2.19 branches, only in 2.20 and above. Anyone pinned to one of those older branches gets nothing from upgrading within that branch, and those branches exist specifically to support older Python versions, which is exactly the situation where this matters most. The only way to actually fix this right now is to move to ansible-core 2.20 or newer, which also means moving the control node to Python 3.12. That's a bigger ask than "pip install --upgrade ansible" and it's not what the backport list implies. A control node still on Ubuntu 24.04's system Python, which ships 3.12, is fine. One stuck on Python 3.11, which is what Debian 12 ships, is not: I installed the plain ansible package (the meta-package, not ansible-core directly) into a clean Python 3.11 virtualenv, and pip resolved it to ansible-core 2.19.15, the exact version I'd already confirmed still fails. On a control node like that, pip install -U ansible doesn't get you the fix, because 2.19.15 is the newest ansible-core release pip can satisfy under 3.11. The part that doesn't trigger it at all In my experience, a lot of cloud images set up their default user with passwordless sudo via cloud-init rather than a sudo password, and that's the case this bug can't reach. I added a second user, cloud-user , with NOPASSWD: ALL and no ansible_become_pass set, and ran the same unpatched ansible-core 2.17.6 against it three times: run 1: 1.98s, exit code 0 run 2: 1.76s, exit code 0 run 3: 1.73s, exit code 0 No password prompt is ever generated, so there's nothing for the mismatch to break. If your playbooks only touch hosts with passwordless sudo, this bug doesn't reach you at all; it only bites once become_pass is actually set, which in my case means any host where I deliberately locked sudo down behind a password. The documented workaround, tested The report's other suggestion was to keep the traditional sudo binary around under its side-by-side name and point Ansible at it with ansible_become_exe=sudo.ws , instead of upgrading anything. I installed the regular sudo package alongside sudo-rs (Ubuntu's packaging keeps both, with update-alternatives choosing which one answers to /usr/bin/sudo ), and reran the unpatched 2.17.6 with ansible_become_exe=sudo.ws set for that host: run 1: 1.96s, exit code 0 run 2: 1.84s, exit code 0 run 3: 1.90s, exit code 0 It works, and it's roughly as fast as the fixed version. It needs the sudo package actually installed next to sudo-rs , though, which a minimal image (including the official Docker one I started from) doesn't have by default. What it costs once you have more than one host A single stuck host costs about 13 seconds. I wanted to know whether that's the whole bill or just the entry fee. Against three affected containers with Ansible's default of 5 forks, three repeated runs landed at 13.2s, 12.8s and 12.8s: the whole play fails in about the same time as a single host, because the per-host timers run in parallel and a batch that fits inside your fork count pays the cost once. With --forks 1 , forcing it serial, the same three hosts took 37.0s, 37.1s and 37.0s across three runs, almost exactly three times the single-host cost, because each timeout now blocks the next connection instead of overlapping it. For anyone running a serial rolling deploy or --forks 1 for safety against a fleet of affected hosts, the 12-second figure quoted everywhere is per batch, not per run. What I got wrong on the way My first attempt at testing three hosts gave a play recap with one line, 127.0.0.1 , where I'd expected three. I'd written the inventory with 127.0.0.1:2222 , 127.0.0.1:2223 and 127.0.0.1:2224 as the hostnames, on the assumption that the port after the colon would just become ansible_port . What I'd actually done was declare the same host, 127.0.0.1 , three times with three different variable sets, and Ansible's inventory parser kept only the last one. It never ran against three hosts at all; it ran once, against whichever port I'd listed last. Naming the hosts target1 , target2 and target3 , with ansible_host set separately on each line, was what actually got three distinct connections going. Run it yourself # target container cat > Dockerfile << 'EOF' FROM ubuntu:26.04 RUN apt-get update -qq && DEBIAN_FRONTEND = noninteractive apt-get install -y -qq \ openssh-server sudo-rs python3 && mkdir -p /run/sshd RUN useradd -m -s /bin/bash deploy && echo 'deploy:deploypass' | chpasswd RUN echo 'deploy ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL' > /etc/sudoers.d/deploy && chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/deploy RUN sed -i 's/#PasswordAuthentication yes/PasswordAuthentication yes/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config EXPOSE 22 CMD [ "/usr/sbin/sshd" , "-D" ] EOF docker build -t ansible-sudo-rs-test . && docker run -d -p 2222:22 ansible-sudo-rs-test # inventory.ini cat > inventory.ini << 'EOF' [ target ] 127.0.0.1 ansible_port = 2222 ansible_user = deploy ansible_ssh_pass = deploypass ansible_become_pass = deploypass ansible_python_interpreter = /usr/bin/python3 EOF # test.yml cat > test.yml << 'EOF' - hosts: target become: yes tasks: - command: whoami register: out - debug: { var: out.stdout } EOF python3 -m venv venv-old && venv-old/bin/pip install ansible-core==2.17.6 venv-old/bin/ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini test.yml # hangs 12s, fails Where I land on this I'd pin ansible-core to something from the 2.20 line or newer on any control node that talks to Ubuntu 26.04 with password-based sudo. I wouldn't trust a patch release of 2.16, 2.18 or 2.19 to pick the fix up quietly, because right now none of them have it, and I only found that out by actually installing each one and watching it fail the same way. Where bumping the control node's Python isn't realistic yet, ansible_become_exe=sudo.ws got me to a working playbook in under two seconds, but somebody still has to go and apt-get install sudo on the target first, because the image I started from doesn't carry it. Before doing any of that, though, I'd check what the account Ansible logs in as actually needs: mine only broke once I gave it a password to type.

title: Trimming silence from backing tracks and stems with pydub
summary: Backing tracks and stems often come with a few seconds of silence at the start and a long fade or dead air at the end. For a karaoke set or a practice playlist that wastes time and makes the count-in unpredictable. Here is a small Python script that trims leading and trailing silence from a folder of audio files with pydub , while keeping a short, consistent lead-in. Install pip install pydub pydub uses ffmpeg for anything other than WAV, so install ffmpeg as well and make sure it is on your PATH. The script import sys from pathlib import Path from pydub import AudioSegment from pydub . silence import detect_leading_silence KEEP_HEAD_MS = 300 # keep a short lead-in so the first beat is not clipped KEEP_TAIL_MS = 800 # keep a little room after the last note THRESH_OFFSET_DB = 30 # silence = quieter than (track loudness - 30 dB) def trim ( seg : AudioSegment ) -> AudioSegment : thresh = seg . dBFS - THRESH_OFFSET_DB head = detect_leading_silence ( seg , silence_threshold = thresh ) tail = detect_leading_silence ( seg . reverse ( ) , silence_threshold = thresh ) start = max ( 0 , head - KEEP_HEAD_MS ) end = min ( len ( seg ) , len ( seg ) - tail + KEEP_TAIL_MS ) return seg [ start : end ] def main ( folder ) : folder = Path ( folder ) out = folder / "trimmed" out . mkdir ( exist_ok = True ) for f in sorted ( folder . iterdir ( ) ) : if f . suffix . lower ( ) not in ( ".wav" , ".flac" , ".mp3" , ".m4a" ) : continue seg = AudioSegment . from_file ( f ) t = trim ( seg ) t . export ( out / ( f . stem + ".wav" ) , format = "wav" ) print ( f "{f.name}: {len(seg)/1000:.1f}s -> {len(t)/1000:.1f}s" ) if __name__ == "__main__" : main ( sys . argv [ 1 ] if len ( sys . argv ) > 1 else "." ) Why a relative threshold A fixed threshold such as -50 dBFS works for loud, mastered tracks but cuts into quiet acoustic intros. Setting the threshold relative to the track's average loudness ( seg.dBFS - 30 ) adapts to each file: a loud pop instrumental and a soft piano backing both get trimmed at a sensible point. Things to watch Fade-outs. A long fade will be kept until it drops below the threshold. If you want the fade shorter, add t = t.fade_out(2000) after trimming. Count-ins. If a track starts with a drummer's stick clicks, they are loud enough to be kept, which is usually what singers want. Lossy input. The script always writes WAV, so you do not stack another round of MP3 encoding on top of the original. Where this fits I run this after separating the vocal from a song, because separated instrumentals often keep the original's silent padding. The separation step itself I do in the browser with Video Vocal Remover , then trim and level the whole folder before a session. pydub silence helpers: https://github.com/jiaaro/pydub/blob/master/pydub/silence.py

title: I built a free PredatorSense alternative for Acer Predator Orion desktops
summary: My Acer Predator Orion 3000 (PO3-655) had two modes: too loud or too hot . PredatorSense, Acer's own tool, didn't give me a fan curve I could actually live with. So I wrote my own app. BaronFan is a free, open-source fan and RGB control app for Acer Predator Orion desktops on Windows 10/11. 👉 Download: https://github.com/BaronLabsDev/BaronFan/releases/latest 👉 Source: https://github.com/BaronLabsDev/BaronFan What it does 📈 Real fan curves for the CPU, front and rear fan – just drag the points, or use a fixed speed or BIOS automatic 🔇 Quiet, Balanced and Cool profiles , plus a quiet mode that ignores short temperature spikes, so the fans don't ramp up every time a browser tab loads 🌈 RGB lighting – whole case or single zones, colours, effects, brightness, profiles, live preview, or simply off 🎮 NVIDIA GPU fan curve (experimental, off by default) 📊 Monitor with temperature and RPM history 🛡️ Safety first – fans go back to the BIOS on exit, sleep, sign-out or crash No account, no ads, no telemetry. English and German. The interesting part: talking to the fan controller The Orion's fans are driven by an ITE Super I/O chip. There's no official API, so BaronFan talks to it through the PawnIO driver. Things I learned along the way: The BIOS doesn't hold a fixed target. Write a fan value and the firmware dithers around it and slowly drifts down. A fan curve has to keep re-asserting its value instead of writing it once. Handing control back is harder than taking it. If you return the fans to the BIOS at a very low value, the case fans start and stop in a loop after the app exits. BaronFan now hands back at a safe minimum (50 % CPU, 20 % case). Unsynchronised port access is dangerous. The BIOS and the app share the same I/O ports. Without proper locking, a register write can land in the wrong place, and I once watched the tachometer-enable bits get clobbered, so the RPM readings froze. The app now detects and repairs that. Lighting goes through Acer's WMI interface. Global colour writes have to be sent to every zone individually, and some effects simply don't exist on every model. The app itself is deliberately boring tech: C# WinForms on .NET Framework 4.8, compiled with the csc.exe that ships with Windows – no SDK needed to build it. NVIDIA GPU fans go through NVML. Honest status Fan control is verified on the PO3-655 . Other Orion models (Orion 3000/5000/7000/X) can unlock fan control after a short, careful fan test in the app: small steps, capped, and the fans are handed back to the BIOS afterwards. Unknown fan chips are never written to. Fan control needs the free PawnIO driver ( winget install namazso.PawnIO ). Lighting, monitor and GPU fan work without it. Help wanted: other Orion models If you own a different Predator Orion, the built-in device check shows (read-only) what BaronFan detects. Report result opens a pre-filled GitHub issue without any personal data – you see the text and submit it yourself. Every report helps me support another model. If BaronFan saves your ears, a ⭐ on GitHub helps other Orion owners find it, and you can support development on Ko-fi . I'm the developer of BaronFan. It is an unofficial project and not affiliated with Acer. Acer, Predator, Orion and PredatorSense are trademarks of Acer Inc.

title: Prices are per storefront: modeling localized in-app purchase lists (and catching item churn) in an app catalog
summary: We run Best IPTV Player , a catalog that tells people which IPTV player apps their devices can run. Players only: no channels, no playlists, no content subscriptions. Every fact needs a publisher or store source and a check date, and anything we cannot source stays unknown . Today (27 November 2026) we localized our IPTVX page into French: IPTVX prix, appareils et licence . The English page already had a US price table. The obvious shortcut would have been to convert the dollars to euros. We didn't, and this post explains why, plus the small amount of code that keeps per-country prices honest. We did not install or run IPTVX for this. Everything below comes from public store listings and the publisher's FAQ. 1. Store prices are set per storefront, not converted Here is the IPTVX FULL subscription on two App Store storefronts, read on the same day: Item App Store France App Store US FULL – 1 month 3,49 € $3.99 FULL – 3 months 8,99 € $10.49 FULL – 6 months 16,99 € $18.99 FULL – yearly 24,99 € $28.99 FULL – yearly, Family Sharing 48,99 € $56.00 PRO - TV (legacy, per the FAQ) 49,99 € $44.99 Look at the last row. Every subscription row is a smaller number in euros than in dollars, but the legacy PRO - TV item is a bigger one (49,99 vs 44.99). No single exchange rate turns one column into the other. If you show a French reader "$28.99 ≈ 26,70 €", you've just made up a price that nobody charges. So the rule in our data is: a price is a tuple (storefront, currency, amount, item, checked_at, source_url) , never a bare number. from dataclasses import dataclass from datetime import date @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class PricePoint : app : str store : str # "apple" | "google_play" storefront : str # ISO country, e.g. "fr", "us" item : str # store item name, verbatim amount : str | None # keep the store's string; None = not published currency : str kind : str # "exact" | "range" checked_at : date source_url : str amount stays a string on purpose. "3,49 €" and "$3.99" are what the stores print. We parse them to decimals for sorting, but the page shows the store's own text. 2. Use the lookup API for what it covers Apple's public iTunes Search API has a lookup endpoint that takes a country parameter: for c in us fr ; do curl -s "https://itunes.apple.com/lookup?id=1451470024&country=$c" \ | jq -c '.results[0] | {country: "' $c '", formattedPrice, currency, version, currentVersionReleaseDate, sellerName}' done On 27 November 2026 that returned "Free" / USD and "Gratuit" / EUR , version 25.1.3 , released 2026-11-22T00:05:28Z , seller Bending X - FZE . It also returns releaseNotes in the storefront's language, which is how we picked up a change: the current notes describe a free tier with ads for live TV, films and series, where watching a video ad unlocks more viewing time and subscribers stay ad-free. What lookup does not give you is the in-app purchase list. That list is only on the public product page, so we save one snapshot of each storefront page per check. We don't crawl it. It's a handful of pages per app, by hand, on the day we edit. 3. Google Play gives you a range, so store a range Google Play's listing for the same app doesn't break prices down by plan. It shows one string per storefront: US: $3.99 - $54.99 per item France: 3,49 € - 48,99 € si facturé via Play That's a different kind of fact, so it gets kind="range" and two amounts. It is not an "unknown" price, and it is not a plan price either. On the page we say exactly that: the exact price of each Android plan is unknown to us, and the range is what the store publishes. 4. Diff snapshots, because item lists churn Subscription prices are not the only thing that moves. We checked the same US listing on 21 November and on 27 November. The subscriptions were identical, but the optional cosmetic items changed. On the 21st there were two themes at $12.99 each. On the 27th there was one "Midnight Skin + Icon" at $6.99. The French storefront lists a different one, "Gold Skin + Icon" at 7,99 €. A tiny diff catches this before it becomes a stale row: def diff ( old : list [ PricePoint ] , new : list [ PricePoint ] ) : key = lambda p : ( p . store , p . storefront , p . item ) o = { key ( p ) : p . amount for p in old } n = { key ( p ) : p . amount for p in new } for k in sorted ( o . keys ( ) | n . keys ( ) ) : if o . get ( k ) != n . get ( k ) : yield k , o . get ( k ) , n . get ( k ) # added, removed or repriced Two details matter here: Item names repeat. The App Store page lists "PRO - TV" twice with the same price. Deduplicate on (item, amount) before diffing, or you'll get phantom changes. Names are localized. "FULL - 1 Month" vs "FULL - 1 Mois". We map storefront names to one canonical item ID by hand, once per app. String matching across languages isn't worth automating for a few dozen apps. 5. Entitlement rules belong next to the price A price without its scope is misleading. The IPTVX FAQ says Apple purchases don't unlock Android or Google TV, Google Play purchases don't unlock Apple devices, and the Fire OS build (a sideloaded APK, not an Amazon Appstore listing) uses a Google Play subscription. So a household with an iPhone and a Fire TV Stick pays twice. We store that as an entitlement_scope on the item, not as prose: ENTITLEMENT = { ( "iptvx" , "apple" ) : { "covers" : [ "ios" , "ipados" , "tvos" , "macos" , "visionos" ] , "family_sharing" : True } , ( "iptvx" , "google_play" ) : { "covers" : [ "android" , "android_tv" , "google_tv" , "fire_os" ] , "family_sharing" : False , "concurrent_streams" : "1; up to 3 on the same verified home network" } , } Anything the publisher doesn't state stays out of the dict. Concurrent streams for Apple subscriptions, the length of the free-with-ads viewing window, and whether a lifetime item is still sold are all unknown on our page. Takeaways Store the storefront, currency and check date with every price. Never convert. Use the official lookup API for version, base price and release notes. Snapshot the product page for in-app items. Model "range" separately from "exact" and from "unknown". Diff snapshots. Item lists change even when the headline price doesn't. The French page with both price columns, the facts table, the FAQ and all sources is here: IPTVX prix (FR) . If you're picking a player rather than building a catalog, the selector on our home page filters apps by what each publisher actually states. Sources, checked 27 November 2026: App Store France , App Store US , Google Play , IPTVX FAQ .

title: Treat printed QR destinations as a web release contract
summary: A QR code on a card can outlive the landing page it points to. Once the card is printed, changing a route in the CMS does not update the destination in anyone’s pocket. Treat that encoded URL as a small public interface, not incidental artwork. Record the contract before printing For each print run, record the exact decoded URL, its intended final destination, a named owner and the point at which the link can be retired. Use an HTTPS URL a team can maintain. Keep the encoded path independent of campaign copy or a CMS slug likely to change. Print a short human-readable address too, so the journey is not scan-only. For example, a synthetic stall might print https://example.com/card and send it to /collections/weekend . Before changing the collection’s slug, test the printed URL itself. Opening the new route directly does not verify the original journey. Check the chain, then the task Use a GET request to see how the redirect behaves, rather than assuming the server handles HEAD identically: curl -sS -L --max-redirs 5 -o /dev/null \ -w '%{http_code} %{url_effective}\n' https://example.com/card Replace the example with a URL you control. Check the final host, path and response. Then scan from a real printed or test-sized proof on a phone and complete the expected task. Test the typed fallback too. A successful status does not establish that the intended form, product or collection is present. Keep the check in the release Place the known printed URLs in a small launch checklist. If a deploy changes their destination, agree the expected final result, test it after release and retain the prior routing so a bad change can be reversed. Check retiring links against the oldest material still in use, not just this month’s artwork. AI was used to draft this guide and generate the conceptual cover. The example is synthetic.

title: AWS Shared Responsibility & IAM Policy Evaluation Explained
summary: Two concepts show up in almost every AWS certification exam (CLF-C02, SAA-C03, SCS-C03) and cloud security interview: the Shared Responsibility Model and IAM policy evaluation order . Here is a practical breakdown from our interactive lesson on BytePatterns : 1. Security of the Cloud vs. Security in the Cloud AWS secures the cloud itself: physical facilities, hardware, networking, and the virtualization layer. You secure what you put in it: your data, guest OS patches, security group / firewall rules, encryption settings, and IAM (who can call which API). 2. IAM Policy Evaluation: Deny Beats Everything When a principal makes an API request in AWS, IAM evaluates every applicable policy in a strict order: Default Deny: Everything is denied unless explicitly allowed. Explicit Allow: At least one policy must explicitly allow the action and resource. Explicit Deny: If any applicable policy contains an explicit Deny , it overrides every Allow — no exceptions. 3. Use IAM Roles Instead of Static Access Keys Never embed long-lived AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY pairs in config files on EC2. Instead, attach an IAM Role via an instance profile: Credentials are temporary and rotated automatically by AWS. Permissions stay scoped to the exact bucket or resource (e.g., s3:GetObject on one bucket): { "Version" : "2012-10-17" , "Statement" : [ { "Effect" : "Allow" , "Action" : "s3:GetObject" , "Resource" : "arn:aws:s3:::photos-bucket/*" } ] } Tip: Least privilege feels slower at first, so use IAM Access Analyzer to generate tight policies from actual CloudTrail activity. Want to test yourself with the interactive ordering exercise and mini quiz? Read the interactive lesson on BytePatterns Try the free 65-question SAA-C03 Practice Exam

title: Testing Python SMS OTP Login Risks for GDPR, PSD2, NIST Compliance (Replays)
summary: Don't treat SMS OTP as enough for GDPR or PSD2 compliance: test login risks before trusting delivery success. For fintech signup, choose the integration by its replay behavior, with a verification link confirming a contact and a separate policy governing account access. A successful send is too weak a database fact to carry both responsibilities. Start with the replay contract, because every ambiguous retry otherwise becomes another integration decision hidden in application code. TL;DR: SMS OTP alone does not establish GDPR or PSD2 compliance, and NIST treats telephone-network authentication as restricted rather than phishing resistant. For a fintech account signup, deliver the verification link through a replaceable transport, then test what happens when delivery repeats or confirmation arrives twice. The useful integration boundary is the smallest durable state transition whose meaning survives those failures. A pharmacy refill alert raises the same underlying question: does reaching a phone prove enough to authorize access to an account? No. A reminder, a contact-verification event, and an authenticated session represent different claims. This decision record uses fintech signup as the concrete implementation and integration effort as the deciding constraint; it does not assume that pharmacy obligations and payment-service obligations are interchangeable. Can SMS OTP retries prove enough for GDPR and PSD2 compliance? The decision is to make contact confirmation a transaction with a replayable outcome. Assume a confirmation commits, but the browser never receives the response. The next request must discover that the same challenge has already completed its narrow job; it must not turn a retry into another authorization event, create another delivery job, or silently verify a different contact. This is a proposed application contract, not a timeout or schema prescribed by a regulator. Keep three invariants. The challenge identifies one contact version and one purpose. An eligible challenge can change from pending to consumed only once. Contact verification alone never grants account access. Those rules allow the delivery adapter to remain small because it does not have to decide what a duplicate means for the account. Retries expose semantics. A storage-oriented review should ask where these rules are enforced. If a worker records success in an object log and another process eventually updates the contact, there is an interval in which the application has two competing answers about completion. Keep eligibility, consumption, and the contact update inside one transaction; use an asynchronous audit copy for evidence under a defined retention policy, rather than as the authority for the current decision. The trade-off is a synchronous database dependency on confirmation, with a correspondingly smaller set of intermediate states to reconcile. This also places a limit on what the evidence means. A bearer link establishes possession of its secret at redemption. Without additional binding, it cannot establish that the browser redeeming the link is the browser that started signup. Binding to the initiating session adds integration and recovery work; that work is justified only if the selected threat model requires that relationship. Durability isn't identity. Compare the work left after the happy path The comparison below concerns application designs, not messaging products. Integration effort is assessed qualitatively by the state and failure handling the team must own; these are design judgments, not measured implementation times. Design under review Additional application work Failure that remains Decision for this signup Contact link with an atomic confirmation result Challenge state, restricted delivery job, expiry, contact version, replay outcome Stolen or forwarded bearer link can confirm a contact Accept for contact verification with a separate access policy SMS OTP used as the entire login decision Attempt limits, telephone lifecycle, recovery, assurance assessment SIM swap and phishing can invalidate assumptions about the recipient Reject as a complete compliance claim Contact confirmation plus a phishing-resistant authenticator Authenticator registration and recovery in addition to delivery Recovery can undermine the stronger ceremony Evaluate for the account-access assurance requirement The apparent shortcut in the second row comes from omitting work, not from eliminating its necessity. A digits-only screen still needs an answer for number reassignment and a user who relays a code to a phishing site. Replacing the digits with a URL does not repair the telephone channel. NIST SP 800-63B-4 describes public telephone network authentication as restricted and discusses SIM changes and number porting as risk indicators. It also distinguishes manually entered OTPs from phishing-resistant authentication and requires an offered phishing-resistant option at AAL2. Those are concrete boundaries when claiming alignment with that assurance level; they do not establish which US legal obligations apply to an arbitrary commercial service. Count recovery too. For integration planning, the important comparison is therefore between the responsibilities retained by each design. Message delivery, contact confirmation, authenticator enrollment, and account recovery each require an owner. Putting them behind one callback does not make their failure meanings identical. Execute the transition before trusting the receipt The following Python is an executable model of the confirmation contract. It deliberately uses an in-memory record so the replay behavior is visible; it provides no concurrent or durable storage guarantee. A production repository must perform the corresponding checks and update in a transaction, with the eligibility check protected against concurrent confirmation. The caller obtains the current contact version from authoritative account state. from dataclasses import dataclass from datetime import datetime , timedelta , timezone from enum import Enum class Outcome ( Enum ) : CONFIRMED = "confirmed" ALREADY_CONFIRMED = "already_confirmed" REJECTED = "rejected" @dataclass class Challenge : contact_version : int expires_at : datetime purpose : str = "signup-contact" consumed_at : datetime | None = None def confirm ( challenge , current_contact_version , now ) : if challenge . purpose != "signup-contact" : return Outcome . REJECTED if challenge . contact_version != current_contact_version : return Outcome . REJECTED if challenge . consumed_at is not None : return Outcome . ALREADY_CONFIRMED if now >= challenge . expires_at : return Outcome . REJECTED challenge . consumed_at = now return Outcome . CONFIRMED # Illustrative test time and lifetime, not a compliance threshold. now = datetime ( 2026 , 1 , 1 , tzinfo = timezone . utc ) challenge = Challenge ( contact_version = 2 , expires_at = now + timedelta ( minutes = 10 ) ) assert confirm ( challenge , 2 , now ) is Outcome . CONFIRMED # The response was lost; the browser retries the same confirmation. assert confirm ( challenge , 2 , now ) is Outcome . ALREADY_CONFIRMED # A superseded contact must not inherit a previous confirmation. assert confirm ( challenge , 3 , now ) is Outcome . REJECTED Notice the order: an already consumed challenge can return its historical outcome after expiry, provided its contact version and purpose still match. That response must convey an earlier completion, never fresh authorization. An unused expired challenge is rejected. A team may choose a less revealing public response for privacy, while preserving these distinctions internally. This is only the state transition. Token validation must precede it. Generate the bearer secret with a cryptographically strong source such as Python's secrets module, associate its digest with the challenge, and limit access to the delivery payload, which necessarily contains or can obtain the usable link. Neither a digest in one table nor an encrypted audit bucket protects a token copied into an unrestricted worker log. Require explicit confirmation before mutation. HTTP defines GET as safe, and security scanners or previews can fetch a link before a person acts; allowing that fetch to consume the challenge couples contact state to automated inspection. An explicit confirmation action adds interaction work but gives the mutation an intentional boundary. Session binding and CSRF protection must follow the surrounding application's threat model. The integration test should cross the real persistence boundary. Race two confirmations and verify that only one performs the contact update. Then lose the response after commit, retry, and inspect both the outcome and account permissions. Also test expiry before first redemption and a contact change before redemption. The small model above cannot verify database isolation, so passing its assertions is insufficient evidence for those concurrency claims. Reject the shortcut, preserve its legitimate role The rejected option is accepting a delivery receipt or an SMS OTP as the entire compliance decision. The valid role is narrower: transport evidence supports delivery operations; contact verification supports signup; telephone-based authentication may participate where the applicable assurance policy permits it and its restrictions have been assessed. None of those labels grants a blanket EU or US compliance result. GDPR Article 32 requires security appropriate to risk, while Article 5 addresses purpose limitation, data minimization, and storage limitation. Collecting every message body indefinitely can increase the retained personal data without resolving the authentication question. Retain evidence that answers a defined review question, with an explicit retention decision for each category. PSD2 Article 97 applies strong customer authentication to specified payment-service activities, including online payment-account access and electronic payment initiation. The associated technical standards address independent authentication elements and dynamic linking for remote electronic payments. A signup link does not supply that transaction-specific assessment. Even a password-plus-SMS screen needs review against the actual requirements rather than an assumption that two interface steps establish compliance. That boundary matters in the pharmacy framing too: successful refill-alert delivery cannot stand in for a patient-account access decision. Establish the obligations for that service separately. Release only after the ambiguous cases are observable Deploy the confirmation schema and its delivery handoff as one reviewed change. An outbox or equivalent durable handoff can record the delivery job in the same transaction as the challenge, allowing the worker to retry transport without issuing a fresh verification event. Resends need a specified policy for existing challenges; otherwise support and engineering may interpret an older valid link differently. Watch queue age, expired challenges, replay outcomes, and contact-version rejections separately from transport acceptance. Correlation identifiers let support trace a signup without retaining raw tokens, full verification URLs, or message bodies in routine logs. Test the worker's retry behavior independently of the confirmation transaction, because a second delivery and a second state mutation are different failure modes. Message volume and retries matter operationally, but transient unit prices do not settle this integration decision. Email and SMS also carry delivery controls outside the account database. RFC 7208 defines SPF checks on authorized sending hosts; it does not authenticate the human recipient. CTIA messaging guidance concerns another operational layer. Use those sources for the questions they actually address. The release criterion is concrete: demonstrate that duplicate delivery, lost responses, and changed contacts preserve the meaning of the stored verification result, then review account access against its separate assurance policy. That is the integration effort to budget. A successful send alone cannot answer whether SMS OTP is enough. References NIST SP 800-63B-4, Authentication and Authenticator Management: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html GDPR, especially Articles 5 and 32: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj PSD2, especially Article 97: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2015/2366/oj Strong customer authentication regulatory technical standards: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2018/389/oj RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics, safe methods: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.1 Python secrets documentation: https://docs.python.org/3/library/secrets.html RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208 CTIA messaging interoperability and compliance guidance: https://www.ctia.org/the-wireless-industry/industry-commitments/messaging-interoperability-sms-mms

title: How I built my own OS
summary: I run my own operating system now. Not a fork with a new wallpaper and a different logo in the about screen. A whole desktop, with its own settings app, its own CLI, its own theme engine, its own bar plugins, its own boot animation, its own project manager and its own editor. It's called CLOUDWERX OS, I use it all day every day, and it's the most fun I've had with a computer since I was a kid. This is how I got here. It's a long one, so grab a coffee. Or something stronger, it's your life. It started with a BBS I was 12 when I ran my own BBS in DOS. It was called Burning in Hell BBS, because I was 12 and that was the most metal name I could think of. It ran on Oblivion/2 (OBV/2 if you're cool), and yes, people actually dialed in. A phone line, a modem screaming at another modem, and some kid's cursed ANSI art. That was my first taste of running something that other people used, and I was hooked immediately. After DOS came Windows 3.1, and I stayed on Windows basically forever. I got into computers right away and I've been obsessed ever since. I started working professionally at 19 as a bench tech, and then I worked my way through pretty much every corner of the industry. Refresh and imaging, support as an IT Analyst, field services, cloud migrations for a large financial firm, O365 support, and a pile of smaller, weirder roles that don't fit on a resume without a footnote. Somewhere in there I tried Linux. Many, many times. I'd learn a little bash here, a little something there, get excited, and then hit the wall. Hardware wouldn't work, wifi wouldn't connect, some driver wanted a ritual sacrifice. Eventually I'd pull my hair out and run straight back to the sweet, sickly embrace of Bill Gates and Steve Ballmer. The funny part is I always knew I was in a prison of my own choosing. A pretty limited one. I just had no idea how free the people on the other side actually were. Three years ago, something changed About 3 years ago I realized I could use ChatGPT to get through the growing pains. That was the missing piece. All the stuff that used to make me quit (the 2am "why is there a black screen" problems) suddenly had a patient teacher sitting next to me. Here's the part I don't talk about much. I have severe ADD, and it did me no favors when it came to learning Linux. Or coding. Coding always felt like it was on another planet, because I could never get through a damn book. I'd read the same page four times and nothing would stick. I bought the books, I really did. They made nice shelf decorations. What changed was having something I could just talk to. I could ask the dumb question, ask it again in a different way, get an answer that fit the exact thing I was staring at, and keep moving. That's how I learn, it turns out. In the last 3 years I've learned more than in the 20 before it, and I'm not exaggerating even a little. The moment I knew it was working was when I updated my kernel and then couldn't log into my computer. Old me would've reinstalled Windows by sunrise. New me got dropped into a tty with ChatGPT in my ear and fixed the whole thing. I didn't quit. I never went back after that. I landed on Linux Mint and loved it for the first few years. Then Claude Code came out and something clicked that I'm still thinking about. I could run agents in my terminal. The terminal is really the key to this whole story, so let me explain why. You can do everything from it. Want to move your mouse cursor? Done. Edit a file? sed . Compare and combine files? Easy. Shell scripting, cron jobs, systemd timers? Now you're cooking with gas. It came slowly, and then one day it was just there: I'm free to tear things apart and rebuild them. The source is open and sitting out in the world. I can mix and match, redesign, and make things exactly how I want them. Niri broke my brain (in a good way) A few months ago I installed CachyOS and gave Niri a shot. Niri BLEW MY MIND. If you haven't seen it, it's a scrolling tiling Wayland compositor, and it was like someone read my mind about everything I hated in floating window managers and fixed all of it. Windows live on an infinite strip. You scroll. That's it. I've never wanted to go back. Then I tried Quickshell, which lets you build your whole shell (bars, panels, launchers, lock screens) in QML, and boom. This was what I'd been looking for my whole life without knowing it. Omarchy had just come out around then, and after poking at it for a bit I had the same thought I think DHH must've had. I can build my own desktop environment, exactly how I want it. So I did. What CLOUDWERX OS actually is It's a keyboard first desktop on CachyOS, niri and Quickshell. I used the best models I could get to help me write the code, and I brought my own design and UX instincts, and it came together faster than I believed it could. I've shipped countless projects over the years and none of them has been as much fun as this one. It's smart, it's sexy, it's capable, and most of all it's free. Here's the tour. The CLI is the heart There's a Rust binary called cloudwerx and it's the stable API for the whole machine. Everything goes through it. Themes, wallpapers, volume, snapshots, tailscale, tasks, the project manager, the editor, the radio. Fifty something commands and every one of them has --json , so scripts and agents can drive the desktop the same way I do. cloudwerx theme set tokyo-night cloudwerx wallpaper next cloudwerx fx set koi-pond cloudwerx doctor That last one checks the entire install and tells you how to fix whatever it finds. I built it because I knew I'd break things at 1am. I was right. The settings app covers everything Holy shit, does this cover everything. It's a native GTK4 app with a left rail that groups every page into ten categories, and there's a page for basically every part of the machine. Lock screen, login screen, boot logo, desktop FX, keyboard shortcuts, app rules, startup apps, Tailscale, firewall, SSH and file sharing, disks, power, updates, and on and on. Search works with normal words, so typing "wifi" or "dark mode" lands you on the right page. All of my servers sit behind Tailscale and get managed from here. My security camera, Noteism, the snipping tool, TaskPass, Hangar, a Herdr app that's been customized into something freakish. They all have a home in this one window. Here's a few more pages, because I'm proud of them. Themes, and the part that still makes me grin I have 69 themes. They don't just change the colors of my windows. One command re-renders dozens of apps at the same time: niri's focus ring, the terminal, GTK, Qt, the editor, the browsers, btop, fzf, the shell, all of it. Then the shell cross fades and a transition shader plays over the whole screen while it happens. You can pick Ink bloom, Melt, Shatter, Scanline, Prism, whatever, or let it roll the dice. It can even start the effect from wherever you clicked. Here's the theme switcher running through a few of them. This is a real recording of my real desktop, with a terminal and the settings app open so you can watch everything change at once. Most of the GIFs in this post are a lot slower then reality, just a warning. And it can build a theme out of a wallpaper. It grabs the prominent colors from the image, makes a full palette, and applies it everywhere right after the transition. It works on video wallpapers too. It takes the first frame, pulls the colors from that, and builds the whole theme around it. I thought that was genius when I came up with it and I still do. Wallpapers get the same treatment Same shader engine, same transitions, a switcher panel along the bottom of the screen. Wave, drop, curtain, bloom and a lot more. Here it is cycling through a few. Desktop FX, aka the part I should've been doing something productive instead of building I have shaders playing on my desktop, between the wallpaper and my windows. There are 34 of them. Aurora, koi pond, meteor showers, rain on glass, a synthwave horizon. They stop drawing completely when a window covers the screen, so they don't cook the battery. Some of them react to music. Oh yeah and they double as screensavers too. And then there's Littlewick. I made an entire pixel art village simulation that runs on my desktop. It's a little town called Applebrook with a clock tower, a bakery, a school, a clinic, an inn, 36 folks wandering around, and a Christmas tree in the middle of the square (it is Nov 27th afterall!). It's synced to my computer's time and date and to my weather widget, so when it rains here, it rains there. Today was Thanksgiving and the whole town was celebrating with a feast. I realize I built a tiny town to live behind my terminal. I'm fine with it. Don't @ me. There are also audio reactive effects. Spectrograms and skylines that dance to whatever's playing, and what's playing is usually the Radio panel, my own internet radio player. It searches hundreds of thousands of stations, and you can sort them, search them and like them. The boot logo Even the boot screen is mine. It's a Plymouth theme, built from a page in Settings, with a comet of light that runs around the ring, goes behind the cloud and comes out the other side, plus a breathing halo and a shimmer. When startup finishes there's a finale flare. These are the actual frames the system plays on boot. The login screen and the lock screen are customized too. And if you type a wrong password, my camera takes a picture of whoever did it so I can look at their face later. It's off by default, because I'm not a monster, but I turned it on. I keep the photos. For science. Bar plugins are one of my favorite things I took what Omarchy did and ran with it. The bar is built out of plugins, and so is basically everything else. Each island, each panel, each picker, each background service. I've made dozens of my own now, and they connect everything together. There's a launcher that searches apps, files, the words inside files and even files by meaning. There's a clipboard history, a time panel, a planner with a Pomodoro, a tray, a sysmon, and a couple of islands I'm not totally sure I'll ever explain to anyone. Omarchy plugins run on it too, unmodified. Sixteen bar styles The bar isn't one look. It has sixteen styles and you flip between them live with Super+Alt+Shift+B or cloudwerx bar style next . Floating islands, one floating panel, a full width edge, a molded edge where the screen corners curve in under it, corner pods, hanging tabs, a liquid band that swells into each group of islands, a screen frame, powerline segments, minimal, capsules, a hanging bar, scrim, zone pills, a compact pill like a dynamic island, and an outline. Here's the whole lineup, and the recording cycles through them. Panels that earn their spot Every island on the bar can open a panel, and I went a little overboard on a few of them. The clock is a good example. Click it and you get a big readout, a month calendar with your events and reminders, timers with presets and progress rings, alarms with repeat days and a stopwatch with laps. The rings keep running and still go off with Snooze and Stop buttons even when the panel is closed. Tasks from the planner show up in there too, so the calendar is the one place I look to see what the rest of my week wants from me. The control center holds the volume, mic and brightness sliders, the toggles (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, focus, night light, power profile, caffeine, tablet mode, recording, Tailscale and exit nodes), the weather card with an hourly strip, and the notifications at the bottom. Notifications are my own daemon, so there's no second one fighting it, and there's a Do Not Disturb you can flip from the bell with a right click. I blurred my face, my Wi-Fi name, my Tailscale IP and my city in this one. The notifications are test ones I fired off with notify-send , because I'm not putting my real messages in a blog post. Thirty five ways to open a panel Panels don't just appear. Every panel in the shell (clock, control center, launcher, agents, radio, all of it) opens with the same animation engine, and there are 35 presets to choose from. Smooth glide is the original and my default. Then there's spring, liquid pour where the panel stretches out of the island you clicked, flap, drop and bounce, jelly, cinematic, a bunch of Material 3 ones, and some I borrowed ideas for from other Quickshell shells I was reading through. Super+Alt+Shift+M cycles them live, and Settings › Panels & Motion has a gallery where every card plays on hover so you can see the real motion before you pick it. There's an editor for your own too, with curve plots (expo, cubic, back, elastic, bounce). Here are ten of them opening the clock panel, one after another. Window shaders in niri This one makes me laugh every time. niri lets you write a GLSL shader for how a window opens and closes, so I bundled a whole shelf of them. There's the niri shader collection (fades, slides, scales, ribbons, masks, noise, burn, honeycomb) and 13 Window FX shaders: ember, dissolve, pixel, shatter, melt, glitch, tube off, snow, scan, code rain, swirl, squares and blinds. Pick them in Settings › Niri Compositor › Individual animations, separately for open and close. If a shader fails to compile, niri falls back to the default and tells you in the journal, so you can't brick your windows. Mine is code rain. Here are a few of the others opening and closing a terminal. Search, and why I'm a little obsessed with it This is the feature I'd miss most if you took it away. You hit Super+Space , start typing, and it finds a file anywhere on the computer in a few milliseconds. By name, by the words inside it, or by what it's about even if you can't remember a single word from it. Right now my machine has 13,973,978 items in the name index, 40,762 documents with their text indexed, and 477,799 passages from 36,818 files turned into vectors for meaning search. The screenshot below shows it answering a name search for /changelog in 11 ms. You switch modes with a prefix, or with the tabs under the search box. Type this You get invoice apps and commands first, then the best file matches /invoice every file and folder named like it, ranked /~/Code/ browse a folder, or complete names inside it #tax deduction documents, notes, PDFs and code containing those words ~notes about moving house documents about it, even with totally different words There's a filter syntax too, and it stacks with everything. ext:pdf size:>10mb mod:week in:~/Documents does exactly what you think it does. Name matching is fuzzy, so rtrn finds return-2025.pdf . How it actually works There's a Rust daemon called cloudwerx-searchd running as a user service. No root, no background cron job. It keeps three separate indexes, and the launcher, the CLI and the settings page all talk to it over a unix socket with JSON lines. launcher / cloudwerx search / settings page | cloudwerx-search.sock (0600) | cloudwerx-searchd (Rust) / | \ names (RAM) text (tantivy) meaning (vectors) \ | / inotify watches Names live in a compact in-memory table, 24 bytes plus the name for every file and folder on the machine. It's the same idea as Everything on Windows. A full walk of the disk runs in parallel at idle priority. Each search scores every entry with nucleo (the fuzzy matcher from the Helix editor) across all cores, after a 64 bit character set test throws out most names in a single instruction. That's how you get single digit milliseconds across millions of entries. My home folder updates live through inotify, and the rest rescans on a schedule. I deliberately didn't use fanotify, because it would watch the whole disk but needs root, and I'm not putting a root daemon on my search box. Words inside files go through tantivy, which is Lucene style BM25. It reads text, Markdown, HTML, CSV, source code, PDFs (through pdftotext ) and Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OpenDocument and EPUB files by cracking open their zipped XML. I build the queries by hand so typing feels instant. Every word also matches the common indexed words it starts, so keybind finds keybinds , phrases match exactly, a hit in the file name counts double, and the snippets highlight what matched. Meaning is my favorite. Documents get split into passages of about 700 characters, and each passage is embedded with Model2Vec static embeddings ( potion-retrieval-32M , the best static retrieval model I could find). A static model turns each token into a vector with a table lookup and averages them. That's hundreds of times faster than running a transformer, with no GPU and no model server, so a whole home folder gets embedded in about a minute. The vectors are stored as 8 bit integers and searched exhaustively in parallel, which is exact and takes around 5 ms. Junk like hashes, base64 and minified code gets skipped before it ever gets embedded. The # search mixes the text and meaning rankings with reciprocal rank fusion. A document that matches your words and your intent floats to the top, and a meaning match can surface a file that uses none of your words at all. Meaning matches only join in when they're strong (similarity of at least 0.45 and close to the best hit), because static embeddings will always hand you some nearest neighbor, even when the honest answer is "nothing". That second one is me typing "how do I make the desktop look different", and getting results from files that don't contain those words. The footer says it found it by meaning. (The first word search in the screenshot above it shows 447 ms because it was cold. Warm it's usually somewhere between 3 and 15 ms.) Indexing never gets in the way of work. The threads run at nice 15 with the idle I/O class, the first content index does the newest files first and commits every 20 seconds, and a manifest of modification times means a restart only re-reads what changed. Everything stays local. Nothing leaves the machine. And once you find the file, it's not a dead end. Enter opens it, Ctrl+Enter shows it in the file manager, Alt+Enter opens it in Noteism, Ctrl+T drops you into a terminal in its folder, and Ctrl+K opens every other action. Files you open from here rank higher next time. My apps all grow up here This is the part that's changed how I work. CLOUDWERX OS is now my breeding ground. Every new project, app or idea I have gets grown inside it, with its own plugin on the bar and its own page in settings, hooked up to everything else. Noteism is the code and text editor I've been building for a year and a half. Picture VS Code and Obsidian having a very good time together. It's fast, it's pretty, it's agentic, and it renders markdown in a way where you can type straight into code blocks, like Typora does. That screenshot is Noteism with nothing open, so you can see the default screen. It's version 1.8.3 right now, and we've been updating the hell out of it lately. I wrote this whole post in it, by the way. Every word, in live preview, with the images dropped in as I went. The big new thing is a complete AI panel. It's off until you turn it on, and when it's off there's no panel, no menu, no status item and no network calls. When it's on, Ctrl+Shift+A opens a chat beside your notes that can actually do things. It reads and searches your notes and files, looks at the note you're in and your selection, edits and rewrites, creates notes, opens files, checks and draws Mermaid diagrams, looks at pictures and loads skills. Every change it makes shows up as a line diff you accept or reject first ( Ctrl+Enter to accept), and Ctrl+Z undoes it either way. You add context with @ for notes, files, folders and the selection, / for quick prompts and skills, and chats are saved, named, searchable and come back when you restart. Then there's Tab completion, and yes, I mean the Cursor kind. Grey text suggests the rest of what you're writing, and a marked change suggests the next edit nearby, like a rename you started or a typo a few lines down. Tab takes it, Ctrl+Right takes one word, Esc dismisses it. It's all bring your own accounts. Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini keys, any OpenAI compatible server (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, OpenRouter), your Claude Code sign in, and your ChatGPT sign in through Codex. Keys live in the system keyring, encrypted, and never reach the window or a chat. Encrypted notes are never sent to AI at all. A few other things I love: it counts tokens live in the status bar, it can make 18 kinds of Mermaid diagram from a selection, and it has a "changed on disk" bar so a Git pull or a sync tool never silently stomps your text. It also ships as an AppImage now, so it runs on almost any Linux, not just mine. It is coming soon at noteism.app . Herdr is where all my agents live. I run all my agents and sub-agents in there, and with my own handoff skills I can drop a TASK.md on an agent and it'll go assign sub-agents to knock out every task, orchestrating the whole thing, picking the engine, the model and the thinking level either perfectly or exactly how I pre-set it. I've got a library of 125 skills that agents load on demand, so they stop making things up about APIs. Some details, because I'm a nerd about it. Herdr has two halves. hc (herdr-core) is a small server that runs terminals and agents and keeps them alive when the window closes. herdr-app is the desktop window. It's drawn with GPUI, the GPU toolkit from the Zed editor, so there's no web view and no Electron, and mods are JavaScript written against gpui-kit. Agents report whether they're working, blocked, idle or done with an escape sequence (OSC 7501), and the app turns that into badges and toasts in the sidebar. Everything is files in ~/.config/herdr-app . Save one and the window reloads it in about a second. My layout on top of it is called cloudwerx-herdr. It started life as someone else's layout (Bettr, by dissimulate) and I've taken it a long way. It has usage cards for Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity and OpenCode with a meter for each limit window and the time left until it resets, CPU, GPU and RAM, an agent activity panel with running sub-agents, a context and cache breakdown, and a Tasks panel that renders the TASK.md of whatever project you're in and updates live while an agent edits it. The theme gets rewritten from my desktop theme every time I change it, so Herdr follows along. And the bar has an island for it, with jumps straight to a pane. I am a HUGE fan of the new herdr-app, it's kind of genius. Get it at http://herdr.dev Being able to see every agent, what it's doing, and how much of its limit it has left, all in one window, changed how I work. I love this thing. I also wrote TaskPass for it, a small native editor (Rust and GPUI) for one job: writing long careful TASK.md files, where every task gets worked by a brand new agent session with its own engine, model, autonomy and effort. Hangar is where all my projects get managed. It's a CLI, a web UI and a desktop app that all sync together, and I mean deliciously . Projects go in there, tasks get made with a quick capture box, agents can add their own, and it can dump a TASK.md out to hand to an agent. Rust and PostgreSQL underneath. Task Manager is a new one I wrote in Rust with GPUI. Not a port, not a wrapper. It's got per core CPU graphs, GPU, disks, services, startup items and a flight recorder. Snip is my screenshot and annotation tool, and it's easily one of the most useful things on the machine. Hit Print and the screen freezes. The freeze happens before the overlay opens, so menus, tooltips and hover states end up in the picture, and the overlay itself can never be in the shot. Drag a rectangle, or click a window to snap to it. There's a magnifier with the pixel colors while you aim, a size label in real pixels, and an action bar with Copy, Save, Edit, Pin and Text. It has a mode for everything. Region, window, this screen, all screens in one wide picture, repeat the last region, a timer (3, 5 or 10 seconds with a countdown ring, so you can open a menu first), a color picker that copies #rrggbb , and a "copy text from the screen" mode that runs OCR with tesseract over whatever you drag across. It also refuses to capture anything while the session is locked, which is the kind of thing you only think about once. Then there's the editor, and this is where it gets ridiculous. Pen, highlighter, lines, arrows (filled, open, double, dashed), rectangles, ellipses, text, numbered step badges with a Renumber button, blur, pixelate, spotlight, crop with aspect locks, an eraser and a color picker. The highlighter multiplies on light pages and screens on dark ones so text stays readable. Blur and pixelate actually redact what's under the box, which is handy when you're about to post a screenshot of the control center and your Wi-Fi name is sitting right there. Here's one I made in about ten seconds. That arrow, the label, the two step numbers and the box are all separate objects. A few more things I like. Beautify wraps the picture in a frame with padding, rounded corners and a soft shadow, using your theme colors. Pin floats a screenshot over everything in a borderless window, and you can scroll to resize it. When you save a picture that has annotations, it also stores the untouched original and every annotation as an object, so you can open the file later and move an arrow that you got wrong. The whole thing is scriptable too: cloudwerx snip region --action edit cloudwerx snip window --focused cloudwerx snip ocr-file receipt.png --copy Every mode has a hotkey, a bar island, a menu and a page in Settings. Voice dictation is the one that makes people stop and stare. I hit Super+Alt+Space , talk, hit it again, and the words get typed wherever my cursor is. It runs on Voxtype, which is Whisper running on my own machine. No cloud, no account, nothing leaves the laptop. The part I'm proud of is the bar. While it's recording, an island shows up in the middle of the bottom bar with a mic that breathes with your voice, a live waveform of what the microphone is actually hearing, and a timer. The waveform is drawn from Voxtype's own audio stream, colored with my theme's accents, and it goes red if you clip. When you stop, it turns amber and ripples while the words get transcribed. There's a bars style and a ribbon style, and everything about it is configurable. Here's a real take. I'm talking into the mic, the waveform is moving on the bar, and the text shows up in a terminal when I'm done. That's 10 seconds of talking, and you can watch the words get typed out right after the mic stops. It transcribes on the CPU with the small base.en model, so it takes a few seconds to finish. It's more than a toggle, too. It supports Whisper, Parakeet, Moonshine, SenseVoice and a few other engines, with model downloads from Settings. There's spoken punctuation, filler word removal, word replacements for the stuff it always gets wrong, and a "submit" command that presses Enter for you. It pauses my music while I talk, and it has a meeting mode with speakers and past meetings. I even had to fix the volume OSD, because a Bluetooth headset flips into headset mode when you record and the volume jumped around like a toddler on a trampoline. cloudwerx voice toggle cloudwerx voice replace set "cloud works" "CLOUDWERX" cloudwerx voice meeting start The updater and the rest work the same way. Tiny focused things that all talk to each other. The tools I built so agents can work on my machine A funny thing happened while I was building all of this. I kept running into the same three problems whenever an agent worked on the desktop, so I fixed each one properly and put them out in the open. They're all CLOUDWERX LAB projects, they're all small Rust binaries, and all three are public. Ghosthand: a real hand on a real pointer github.com/CLOUDWERX-DEV/Ghosthand I got tired of agents that could write an entire UI but couldn't right click a menu on it. A screenshot tells you what's there. It can't tell you what happens when you hover or drag. So Ghosthand gives an agent my actual mouse and keyboard. Click, double click, right click, drag, scroll, hover, type text, press shortcuts, then take a screenshot and see what happened. How it works is simple. It creates a virtual absolute pointer through /dev/uinput , so the display server just sees a normal mouse. That means it isn't tied to one compositor. No portals, no plugins. It reads my real keyboard layout so it types what it should, and focus tells the agent which window will get the keys before it types. The part I care about most is the gate. Before anything moves or types, a card shows up on my screen saying who's asking, why, and exactly what it's about to type. Nothing happens until I click Allow. No answer counts as a no. While an agent is driving, a little "Agent Control" tag and a ring follow the cursor, so I always know it isn't me. One key takes the pointer back at any time, and it refuses to run while the session is locked. For a long testing job I approve one session instead of a card per click. It's one small Rust binary, with a background daemon keeping the virtual devices alive so a run starts in milliseconds. I've tested it daily on niri. The README is honest that Hyprland, sway, X11, KDE and GNOME are parser tested but not driven live by me, so bug reports are welcome. Here's the prompt. This is what I see before an agent touches anything. It says who's asking, why, how long I've got to answer, and exactly what it's about to type, word for word. Then Deny, Allow for 10 minutes, or Allow. If I don't answer, it counts as a no. And this is a real recording of it working. The card pops up, I click Allow for 10 minutes, and from there every click, scroll and keystroke is the agent. It jumps around Settings pages, types into the search box, and opens the launcher to search for a file. I didn't touch anything after clicking Allow. While an agent is driving, you can't mistake it for yourself. There's a ring around the pointer and an Agent Control tag that follow the cursor everywhere. Here's a close up, with it gliding across the desktop and clicking. agent-sudo: root without a password, with a seatbelt github.com/CLOUDWERX-DEV/agent-sudo Regular sudo wants a password from a terminal. A script or an agent can't type one, so it hangs forever, or you do the dangerous thing and put NOPASSWD: ALL in your sudoers file and now one bad command takes the whole machine with it. An empty variable in rm -rf "$DIR/"* is all it takes. agent-sudo (or asudo for short) sits in the middle. It runs the command as root with no prompt, but first it reads the command against ten named guardrails that refuse the catastrophic stuff: rm -rf / , mkfs on a disk, dd onto /dev/sda , editing /etc/shadow , fork bombs. It reads the command, it doesn't just regex a string, so env , nice , timeout , sh -c "..." , $(...) , redirections, .. and symlinks don't hide anything. Every run goes into an audit log at /var/log/agent-sudo.log with when, who, where and how it ended, and I get a desktop notification each time. agent-sudo pacman -S --noconfirm ripgrep agent-sudo --explain dd if = x of = /dev/sda # which rule fires, and why agent-sudo --logs 10 # what ran lately I want to be straight about what it is. It's a seatbelt, not a security boundary. It stops mistakes and careless commands. It can't stop something that's actively trying to get around it, because anything running as root can do anything, and the README says so in a big warning box. The installer checks the sudoers rule with visudo before it touches anything, and it's only two dependencies. skills-cli: stop paying for skills you aren't using github.com/CLOUDWERX-DEV/skills-cli Skills are great, but the usual way of using them doesn't scale. Put a hundred of them where your agent looks and every single conversation starts by paying for the name and description of all hundred, whether you need them or not. The agent also gets worse at picking the right one, and one careless read of a big skill can dump a couple hundred thousand tokens of docs into the context. So I flipped it around. The library lives on disk, and the agent gets one tiny instruction. From there it searches, loads and fetches only what it needs. skills search "pdf merge" skills load pdf-tools skills ref get pdf-tools merge # one reference page, not the whole folder skills run pdf-tools split.py in.pdf # only the output comes back My own library is 130 skills in 3,377 files, about 14.8 million tokens. The instructions alone are around 400 thousand. Listing every one of them takes about 4 ms. And the agent only ever sees what it asked for, with a 30,000 token guard so a slip can't flood the context. It also makes new skills ( skills new ), installs them from git, validates them, and can pin one as a slash command. skills skill prints a guide built into the binary, so an agent can learn the whole tool with one command. My laptop is also a security camera I can watch my laptop's camera and listen to its microphone from my phone, from anywhere, and nothing is exposed to the internet. It works over Tailscale only.
