Constraints: four weeks, a 1991 survey with hand notes, an uninspected screen tower, and a client family in the room. The rule I used If it appears on a tax map, GenAnywhere. If it has a serial number, Tripo3D. Everything else is judgment. Step 1: land I drew a box on the map around the site plus a margin, about 600 by 600 feet, and let GenAnywhere generate it. • Input: one rectangle on a map. • Output: lot surface, neighboring houses, strip mall, tree line, road edge, roof shapes. • Time: under fifteen minutes. • Fidelity: right for massing, light, and sightlines. Wrong for boundaries and anything you would measure. It also invented a building in the east field and flattened the screen tower into a wall panel. Both were deleted. That is normal for a context model, and why the survey stayed open the whole time. Step 2: assets Tripo3D took three kinds of input and I used all three. • Sketch: the ticket booth, from a page of the owner's graph paper. Best result of the batch. • Photo: a speaker post from a phone picture of one still standing in row 3. • Text: picnic tables, bins, bollards, the screen tower, the playground slide. Each simple object took ten to twenty minutes. The tower took a morning, because bracing is geometry Tripo3D has to guess, and it guessed a different pattern on each side. Segmentation split the tower into screen, frame, and legs so the frame could serve a second camera. Topology optimization cut it enough that a browser viewer loads the scene without a stall. Exports mattered more than expected: GLB for the web preview, FBX for the renderer, STL for the model, OBJ for the civil engineer checking queue geometry. Step 3: merge and verify Everything went into one scene, with a person-height block and a car-sized block for scale. Then the checks. • Tower legs against the base plate from the survey: off by about eight inches. Fixed. • Lot width: three feet narrow against the survey. The site model lost that argument. • Door height on the ticket booth: right after I reset it, wrong out of the box. The lot fix is the one worth remembering. The error was invisible in the drone view and obvious to the client's son, who has parked there for years. Two triangles of mismatch cost us a day. Where the handoff broke • Units. One export arrived in centimeters and made the booth knee-high on the first merge. • Pivots. Assets land at the center of the world, centered on their bounding box, so "on the ground" is always a manual step. • Texture repetition. The speaker post texture tiled visibly once it was placed forty times, so I baked a variant. None of these are dealbreakers. All of them are invisible in a tool's marketing. Where the time went Roughly a day on the land, three days on assets, two days on merge, render, and print. The rest was meetings. Hand-modeling, the land alone would have been two days and forty speaker posts an afternoon of array and cleanup. The saving is real, but it is not in the generation. It is in not modeling context nobody will look at. What I would automate next A scale gate that compares every asset bounding box to a target dimension before it enters the scene. A naming convention that survives export, so row numbers stay attached. And a flat-material render pass, which would have caught the tower-leg mismatch a day early. The scorecard Land: GenAnywhere. Fast, plausible, good for light and massing, useless for exact boundaries. Objects: Tripo3D. Sketch input is the sleeper feature, segmentation saves hours, and the export list covers whatever comes next. The seam is still manual and still where the errors live. That is not a knock on either product, just the shape of the work.

title: It's Not the Model: Five Checks That Catch Agent Workflows Before Production
summary: # Why Most AI Agent Workflows Break in Production — and the Five Checks That Catch It Early Everyone has a demo that works. Very few have a workflow that survives Tuesday. I've read through a lot of agent pipelines — internal ones, open-source ones, the ones people post asking "why does this randomly do X". The failure patterns repeat with almost boring regularity. What's more interesting: almost none of them are model capability problems. They're contract problems. Swapping in a stronger model fixes exactly none of them. Here are the five I see most often, and the check that catches each one before it reaches production. ## 1. Context drift A long-running task accumulates its own history. By step 30, the agent is reasoning from a summary of a summary of step 4, and the original constraint — "don't touch the billing schema" — has quietly evaporated. Nothing errors. The agent just starts solving a slightly different problem than the one you gave it. The usual fix is "better prompting", which is the wrong layer. Prompts don't survive compression. The check: does any step re-assert the hard constraints from the original request, independently of the conversation history? If a constraint only exists inside the message log, it is already gone. ## 2. Unverified self-assessment The agent writes the code, then writes the test, then reports that the test passes. This is not verification; it's a closed loop with one participant. It will report success with total confidence, and it will be wrong at a rate that stays invisible to you because you only ever see the successes that happened to be real. The check: can you name the independent verifier? It has to be something the generator cannot influence — a deterministic assertion, a different model with no access to the reasoning trace, or a human gate. If the answer is "the agent checks its work", you have no verifier. ## 3. Silent tool failure A tool returns empty. An API returns 200 with an error body. A search returns zero results because the query was malformed. The agent treats all three as "completed, nothing to report" and keeps building on the void. Ten steps later you get a fluent, well-structured, entirely fictional answer. This one is brutal because there is no exception to catch. The check: does every tool have a success/failure contract that is distinct from "returned something"? Empty is not success. 200 is not success if the body says otherwise. If you can't state a tool's failure condition in one sentence, you don't know when it's lying to you. ## 4. Retry amplification Non-idempotent side effects plus automatic retries equals duplicate orders, duplicate emails, duplicate charges. The agent sees a timeout, retries, and the first attempt was actually fine. Now you have two. The check: classify every side effect as reversible / compensable / irreversible, and put the irreversible ones behind an idempotency key or a human confirmation. "It usually works" is not a classification. ## 5. Over-broad agency The agent has write access to everything, because scoping permissions is tedious. Then one plausible-sounding misinterpretation reaches production data. The damage isn't proportional to the bug — it's proportional to the permissions. The check: for each credential the agent holds, can you name the task that requires it? If not, remove it. Least privilege is cheap; incident response isn't. ## The pattern Notice what these have in common. Every one is a missing boundary: a missing constraint re-assertion, a missing independent verifier, a missing failure contract, a missing idempotency key, a missing permission scope. Boundaries are unglamorous. They don't demo. They don't make it into the launch thread. But they are the entire difference between a workflow that runs and a workflow that mostly runs. The temptation, when an agent misbehaves, is to upgrade the model. Notice that a stronger model fails these five checks in exactly the same way — faster, and with more convincing prose. ## The 15-minute audit Before shipping any agent workflow, answer these five in writing. If you can't, you've just found your next task. Where do the original hard constraints get re-asserted, independent of the message history? Who is the independent verifier, and what can it not see? For each tool: what does failure look like, and how is it distinguished from empty success? Which side effects are irreversible, and what stops a retry from duplicating them? For each credential the agent holds: which task requires it? Five questions. Most workflows fail two or three of them. Next in this series: how to actually measure the failure rate instead of guessing at it — the harness, the metrics, and what "reliable enough" means for a task that has no test suite.

title: I Build Tools to Solve My Own Problems. How Do You Find Yours?
summary: It usually starts with something small. I run into a problem while working. I solve it manually, move on, and then run into it again. After a while, I start wondering: could I build a tool to make this easier? That’s where many of my ideas come from. I don’t start with a market or a list of startup opportunities. I start with something that gets in my way. With AI coding tools, it’s easier to turn that kind of idea into a working prototype. What used to take days of setup and experimentation can sometimes be tested much faster. But building the first version leaves me with a harder question: Am I solving a problem other people have, or am I just making my own workflow more comfortable? Building for yourself is a useful starting point The obvious advantage is that I understand the problem. I know when it appears, what I currently do about it, and which parts of the process are annoying. I can try a solution in my own work instead of guessing whether it makes sense. I also get feedback quickly. If I build a tool for myself and stop using it after two days, that tells me something. Maybe the problem wasn’t painful enough. Maybe the tool added more steps than it removed. Either way, I’ve learned something without asking anyone else to spend time on it. But my experience is still only one data point A problem can be real for me and rare for everyone else. Maybe it depends on my operating system, my setup, or the way I work. Maybe other people encounter the same issue but already have a solution they’re happy with. And even if they don’t, that doesn’t automatically mean they want a new tool. Some problems are annoying enough to complain about but not annoying enough to install an app, change a workflow, or pay for a solution. That’s the part I find difficult to judge from my own experience. How do you tell if a problem is worth solving? I’ve been thinking about a few questions: Who else runs into this? Can I find people describing the same problem in their own words? How often does it happen? Is it a daily interruption or a one-time inconvenience? What do people do now? Do they use another tool, keep a spreadsheet, write scripts, or simply tolerate it? What would make them switch? Is the current solution genuinely frustrating, or just imperfect? Can I reach those people? Even a useful tool needs a way to find its users. I don’t think every personal tool needs to become a business. Sometimes saving yourself time is enough reason to build something. An open-source project can be worth sharing even if it never makes money. But if the goal is to create a product for other people, I think it helps to look beyond the excitement of getting a prototype working. The code can answer, “Can I make this?” It can’t answer, “Does anyone else need it?” How do you find problems? I’m curious how other developers and founders approach this. Do you start with problems you face yourself? Talk to people in a particular industry? Read forums and support requests? Look at existing products and their reviews? And when you find a problem, how do you decide whether it’s worth building a solution for? I’d be interested to hear about ideas that turned out to be useful to others, and ones that seemed promising but didn’t.

title: Why 5.5GHz+ CPUs and DDR5 Matter for Low-Latency Game Servers
summary: Modern multiplayer engines—from competitive shooters to survival and roleplay servers with heavy entity counts—put intense pressure on a small number of execution threads. When a server stutters during a raid or large firefight, average tick rates often look healthy while players feel rubber-banding and delayed hit registration. Here is a look at why clock speed, cache/memory behavior, and network routing play such a big role in keeping competitive game servers responsive. 1. Single-Thread Speed Still Drives the Main Simulation Loop Many game servers rely on a sequential simulation tick: reading player inputs, stepping physics, running AI pathfinding, resolving combat state, and broadcasting updates. While extra CPU cores help with background tasks like networking, I/O, or plugins, a single-threaded main loop cannot be arbitrarily split across dozens of cores without synchronization overhead. In practice, a processor with high single-core boost clocks (such as 5.5GHz+ desktop/workstation architectures) can finish each tick faster than a higher-core-count, lower-clock chip—giving the server more headroom before tick times slip. 2. Why 1% Lows Matter More Than Average TPS Looking only at average Ticks Per Second (TPS) hides worst-case behavior. A server can maintain a solid hourly average and still feel choppy if heavy events—explosions, boss spawns, or crowded engagements—push individual ticks past their frame budget. High-frequency cores help shorten those worst-case ticks, and large L3 caches (such as 3D V-Cache designs) keep frequently accessed entity and world data closer to the compute cores, reducing trips to main memory during crowded scenes. 3. What DDR5 Changes Under Load Even fast cores can stall if memory bandwidth or capacity becomes a bottleneck during chunk generation, world saves, or heavy mod loading: Higher bandwidth: Helps smooth out data movement during map updates and asset loads. On-die ECC: Corrects single-bit errors inside the DRAM chip itself for continuous operation (though if you need full end-to-end memory bus error correction, verify full platform/DIMM ECC support separately). Higher per-DIMM density: Allows more memory capacity per node without sacrificing clock speed. 4. Latency Tuning and Network Transit Low-latency infrastructure engineering shares common ground with other real-time workloads (such as algorithmic trading): determinism and jitter reduction matter more than peak theoretical throughput. OS & firmware tuning: Disabling deep C-states avoids wake-up latency on active cores, and CPU pinning keeps latency-critical processes from bouncing across cores via scheduler migrations. Network path: Total player latency combines server tick time and network transit time (ping) . Fast hardware cannot fix congested routing or unmitigated DDoS traffic that adds jitter. Checklist When Evaluating Game Server Hosts Before deploying a latency-sensitive server, verify: Dedicated / bare-metal allocation rather than heavily contended shared resources. Sustained clock speeds under load, not just peak boost ratings. DDR5 specs (MT/s and whether full ECC is supported if required). Fast NVMe storage for map loads, backups, and database writes. Low-latency DDoS mitigation and clean network peering near your player base. If you want to read the full comparison table and breakdown, you can check out the original write-up here: 5.5GHz+ CPUs and DDR5 for Competitive Game Hosting . How do you approach server tuning for high-entity or high-tick workloads—do you prioritize higher clock speeds, larger L3 cache, or network peering first?

title: CVE-2026-136716: Drupal corrige falha que mantém expostos sites com a correção anterior
summary: CVE-2026-136716: Drupal corrige falha que mantém expostos sites com a correção anterior O Drupal publicou em 25 de novembro de 2026 o aviso SA-CORE-2026-019 para a CVE-2026-136716, uma falha altamente crítica de contorno de controles de acesso. Sites em estado de instalação incompleto ou incomum podem continuar vulneráveis à tomada do site, inclusive em produção. O aviso chegou oito dias depois da correção SA-CORE-2026-017 (CVE-2026-132165), que tratava uma falha no mesmo arquivo, core/install.php, capaz de levar à tomada do site ou à execução de código. A correção anterior não protege contra a nova falha: sites que a instalaram também precisam atualizar novamente. Exploração e urgência O Drupal classifica as duas vulnerabilidades como altamente críticas: a anterior recebeu 20 de 25, e a nova, 21 de 25. O projeto informa que ambas estão sendo exploradas. Ataques contra sites em produção foram registrados a partir de 19 de novembro de 2026, às 19h UTC, pouco depois da divulgação da primeira correção. A CISA incluiu a CVE-2026-132165 em seu catálogo de vulnerabilidades exploradas em 24 de novembro e fixou 27 de novembro como prazo. A CVE-2026-136716 ainda não constava na edição de 25 de novembro, mas o Drupal já relata exploração ativa, então a ausência no catálogo não reduz a urgência. Versões afetadas e corrigidas Nas linhas com suporte, a versão indicada na última coluna corrige os dois avisos. Uma instalação abaixo desse número permanece exposta, mesmo que já tenha recebido a correção anterior. LinhaCorreção anteriorNova correçãoAtualizar para11.4.xAbaixo de 11.4.13Abaixo de 11.4.1411.4.1411.3.xAbaixo de 11.3.22Abaixo de 11.3.2311.3.2310.6.xAbaixo de 10.6.22Abaixo de 10.6.2310.6.23 As linhas 11.2, 11.1 e 11.0, assim como 10.5 e anteriores, Drupal 9 e Drupal 8, também são afetadas e estão fora de suporte. A orientação é migrar para 11.3 ou 11.4, ou para 10.6, conforme a instalação. Os números estavam corretos em 26 de novembro de 2026. Como o Drupal publicou duas atualizações de segurança para esse código em uma semana, confira o aviso SA-CORE-2026-019 e a página de segurança no dia da atualização, para identificar uma versão pontual mais recente, se houver. Confira a versão e as dependências Confira a versão instalada pela linha de comando, a partir da raiz do projeto, onde fica o arquivo composer.json. O Composer consulta o arquivo de lock, que registra as dependências implantadas, enquanto o Drush confirma a versão do site inicializado. cd /var/www/drupal composer show drupal/core | head -12 vendor/bin/drush status --fields=drupal-version,php-version,db-driver,db-status,bootstrap,root,site O comando composer outdated também compara as versões instaladas às releases permitidas pelas restrições do projeto e mostra atualizações pendentes para pacotes Drupal. composer outdated 'drupal/*' Na versão de laboratório, o Drupal 11.4.13 já corrigia o aviso anterior, mas ainda estava exposto à CVE-2026-136716. A interface administrativa não indicava essa diferença, por isso a conferência manual da versão é importante. O comando antigo drush pm:security foi removido das versões atuais do Drush. Tarefas agendadas ou rotinas de CI que ainda o executem podem falhar sem deixar claro que a consulta não foi feita; use composer audit --locked para verificar os avisos associados ao arquivo de lock. composer audit --locked Na execução de laboratório, a auditoria encontrou 18 avisos em sete pacotes, incluindo drupal/core, Symfony e Twig. As dependências também precisam ser consideradas na atualização; incluir a auditoria no pipeline de implantação permite detectar novos avisos quando forem publicados. Bloqueie o instalador no servidor web Segundo o aviso do Drupal, um instalador já protegido não fica vulnerável a essa falha. Em produção, o arquivo não é necessário depois da instalação; para implantar sites novos, o comando drush site:install evita o instalador pelo navegador. Faça o bloqueio antes de seguir para a investigação e a atualização. No Nginx, localize o bloco de servidor correto com sudo nginx -T e insira a regra antes da configuração de PHP. O prefixo ^~ também cobre caminhos que continuem depois de /core/install.php. location ^~ /core/install.php { return 404; } Teste a configuração e verifique a rota principal, a alternativa e um caminho com sufixo. A regra precisa estar nos blocos que atendem HTTP ou HTTPS, conforme a configuração do site. sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx curl -I http://example.com/core/install.php curl -IL http://example.com/install.php curl -I http://example.com/core/install.php/foo Na configuração de laboratório, as três rotas responderam com 404. Respostas 403 ou 404 indicam bloqueio; um 200 exige revisar o bloco de servidor e a ordem das regras. Repita os testes de fora do servidor para verificar possíveis rotas ou respostas de CDN e balanceadores. No Apache, inclua a restrição no host virtual. A diretiva em .htaccess pode causar erro 500. O exemplo abaixo bloqueia o acesso à rota e também aos caminhos que começam com ela. Require all denied sudo apachectl configtest && sudo systemctl reload apache2 O teste de laboratório retornou 403 para o instalador; a rota /install.php redirecionou para a rota bloqueada. No RHEL, o serviço Apache se chama httpd. Em hospedagem compartilhada sem acesso ao host virtual, o guia do Drupal descreve uma regra em .htaccess. Investigue antes de atualizar o banco Antes de executar drush updb, verifique se houve tomada do site. A atualização do banco reescreve valores que podem ajudar a identificar uma invasão anterior. A ordem recomendada é bloquear o instalador, investigar sinais de comprometimento e só então atualizar o banco. Evite entrar como usuário 1 antes de conferir o horário de login desse usuário: o acesso pode sobrescrever justamente o valor que será auditado. A página de verificação de comprometimento do Drupal orienta essa etapa antes da atualização. Atualize e mantenha o bloqueio Depois das verificações, atualize o Drupal para a versão corrigida de sua linha e execute a atualização de banco. A atualização pelo Composer fecha os dois avisos nas linhas compatíveis, mas a etapa de banco com Drush também é necessária. drush updb O Drupal recomenda remover também web/core/install.php após cada instalação e atualização do Composer, junto do bloqueio no servidor. Os comandos abaixo configuram essa remoção para os dois eventos e executam uma instalação de dependências. composer config scripts.post-install-cmd 'rm -f web/core/install.php' composer config scripts.post-update-cmd 'rm -f web/core/install.php' composer install Antes de usar composer config, confira os scripts existentes: o comando substitui o evento e pode apagar rotinas já configuradas, como as do modelo drupal-composer/drupal-project. Nesse caso, acrescente a remoção à lista existente em composer.json. Ajuste também o caminho se a raiz pública do projeto não for web/; projetos antigos podem usar docroot/ ou a própria raiz. Como composer install --no-scripts pula a remoção, mantenha o bloqueio do servidor web ativo. Consulte o guia de atualização e verificação do Drupal para os procedimentos relacionados. Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/drupal-cve-2026-136716-falha-critica-instalador/

title: Web form consent for AI callbacks: what to check
summary: This is a copy of a guide first published on the Halyard Ops site. The original is the version we keep up to date: halyardops.pages.dev/guides/web-form-consent-wording-for-ai-callbacks . This copy was refreshed from the original on November 26, 2026. The FCC ruled in 2024 that an AI-generated voice is an artificial voice under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, so a callback with that voice needs the person's consent, and written consent if the call is advertising or telemarketing, unless an exemption applies. The rule lists what written consent must contain; whether a quote-request callback counts as telemarketing, and whether a form covers an AI voice, the sources we read do not settle. Status. Published November 16, 2026. Checked against the linked sources on November 15, 2026. Laws change. Not legal advice and not reviewed by counsel. We are a new studio and our voice agent is a demo build. Which kind of consent does an AI voice callback need? It depends on what the call is. The FCC's 2024 ruling says current AI technology that generates human voices produces an artificial voice under the Act. Under 47 CFR § 64.1200(a) , a call that advertises or is telemarketing needs prior express written consent; other calls to a cell phone with an artificial or prerecorded voice need prior express consent. Calls to a residential line follow their own paragraph, § 64.1200(a)(3), which has limited exemptions. Courts are not bound by the FCC's reading. In June 2025 the Supreme Court held that district courts in civil enforcement proceedings must decide a statute's meaning themselves, giving the agency's reading appropriate respect ( McLaughlin Chiropractic v. McKesson ). That a private suit could test the AI-voice ruling is our inference, not something the opinion says. The ruling and the rule sit with the other federal rules on the federal baseline . Whether a callback about the quote the person asked for is telemarketing or an informational call is not answered in the text we read. A cautious approach is to meet the written-consent elements anyway. That is our judgment, not a rule. What must written consent contain? The federal definition is specific. Written consent is a signed agreement, and an electronic signature is allowed. These are the pieces the definition lists. A signed agreement, which can be a web form. The agreement bears the signature of the person called. An electronic or digital signature counts where it is valid under federal law or state contract law. The FCC has said a website form can qualify ( FCC 12-21 , para 34). ( 47 CFR § 64.1200(f)(9); FCC 12-21, para 34 ) Clear authorization for these calls, to a stated number. The agreement must clearly authorize the seller to deliver advertisements or telemarketing messages using an automatic telephone dialing system or an artificial or prerecorded voice, and it must state the telephone number they may be delivered to. ( 47 CFR § 64.1200(f)(9) ) A clear and conspicuous notice that signing is not required. The form must tell the person, clearly and conspicuously, that signing authorizes those calls and that the person is not required to sign the agreement as a condition of purchasing any property, goods or services. ( 47 CFR § 64.1200(f)(9) ) In the text we read we found nothing on type size, on whether a checked box is enough, or on whether a pre-checked box is acceptable. Those are questions for counsel. Does the form have to name one company? The FCC adopted a rule in 2023 that would have required consent to one named seller. In January 2025 the Eleventh Circuit struck that part down, and the FCC then restored the earlier wording of the definition; the current text has no one-to-one wording. The one-to-one rule is gone from the text. The court said the rule conflicts with the ordinary meaning of prior express consent. The FCC reinstated the earlier text of the definition effective August 29, 2025 ( 90 FR 42137 ). That text still speaks of an agreement that “clearly authorizes the seller” to deliver the calls, and “seller” means the business on whose behalf the call is made (47 CFR § 64.1200(f)(9)-(10)). We did not check for a later FCC proposal to bring a revised rule back. ( Insurance Marketing Coalition v. FCC, No. 24-10277 (11th Cir. 2025) ) The Telemarketing Sales Rule still names a seller. For a prerecorded call that induces a purchase, the FTC's rule requires a signed written agreement, with the person's number, that shows willingness to receive prerecorded calls by or on behalf of a specific seller, plus the required disclosures and an automated opt-out. Whether the FTC treats a conversational AI voice as a prerecorded message is not stated in the text we read. ( 16 CFR § 310.4(b)(1)(v) ) The practical point (judgment): a form that names the business that will actually call is easier to defend than one that says "our partners". What must the call itself say? Consent on the form is one half. The other half is the first seconds of the call. Identify the business, give a number, offer an opt-out. An artificial or prerecorded message must state the business's registered name at the start and give a callback number during or after the message. For telemarketing it must offer an automated opt-out within two seconds of the identification. The FCC applied these rules to AI calls ( FCC 24-17 , para 9). ( 47 CFR § 64.1200(b)(1)-(3); FCC 24-17, para 9 ) What happens when someone says stop? A caller that relies on consent also has to honor a request to take it back. Until November 25, 2026, the text of 47 CFR § 64.1200(a)(10) that we read on our check date (eCFR dated 12 Nov 2026) said that a person may revoke consent by any reasonable method, and that a keypress opt-out, a stop-type text word, or a designated website or number counted as reasonable. The request had to be honored within a reasonable time, at most 10 business days. A final rule ( 91 FR 67214 , FCC 26-67 ) took effect on November 25, 2026 and revised that paragraph. A caller may now designate one of three automated methods as the only way to revoke consent: an automated voice or keypress opt-out on a call, a reply text using a standard word such as “stop”, or a website or number the caller designates. It must say so clearly and conspicuously on the call or in the text. A caller that designates none must still honor a request made by any reasonable means, and a request must still be honored within a reasonable time, at most 10 business days. Revoking in response to a call or text that contains advertising or is telemarketing ends consent to all future calls or texts from that caller that contain an advertisement or are telemarketing. We re-read the rule's effective date and revised text in the Federal Register on November 25, 2026; our full check of this page was on November 15, 2026. The FCC has also proposed further changes, including a shorter deadline, that were not adopted when we checked. What can a state add to the form? States can add their own consent and calling rules on top. Florida shows the pattern, and our state guides go through the others we have read ( how these guides are written ). Florida: written consent for automated or recorded sales calls. A person may not make, or knowingly allow, an unsolicited telephonic sales call that uses an automated system to select and dial numbers, or plays a recorded message when answered, without the called party's prior express written consent. A signature may be an electronic signature or a ticked box. ( Fla. Stat. § 501.059(1)(g)-(h), (8)(a) ) Florida does not say a web form is an express request. The statute excludes calls made “in response to an express request of the person called” from “unsolicited”. It does not define an express request or say whether a form submission is one, and it does not mention AI voices. If a form submission were an express request, the call would fall outside the “unsolicited” consent rule in (8)(a); the statute does not say. ( Fla. Stat. § 501.059(1)(k) ) California's do-not-call exemption names a specific party. California's do-not-call exemption for a written agreement speaks of calls “by or on behalf of a specific party” placed to that number, and the solicitor has to prove the agreement. ( Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17592(e)(1) ) What should a form and its records show? Some of these follow from the elements above; the questions about texts, stopping and records come from the revocation rule and from practice. It is a checklist of questions to take to counsel, not approved wording. Is the consent text next to the button, and not only in a linked policy? Does it name the business that will call, and say the calls may use an automated system and an artificial or AI-generated voice? Does it say which number, and are calls and texts both covered if you plan both? Does it say, clearly, that signing is not a condition of buying anything? Does it explain how to stop: a keypress on a call, a stop word in a text? Do you save the exact text the person saw, the number they entered, and the date and time? The FCC has said that if a consumer disputes giving written consent to robocalls, the telemarketer must show the consent was given ( FCC 12-21 , footnote 68). Does the state your lead is in add its own rule, as Florida does? An illustration that follows the wording of the federal definition and nothing else. It is not a template: “By checking this box and submitting this form, I authorize [Company name] to deliver telemarketing calls to the number I entered, including calls that use an automated system or an artificial or AI-generated voice. I am not required to agree to this as a condition of buying anything.” Texting, what the calls may be about, and how to stop are not part of that list and are for your counsel to decide. We have not had this wording reviewed by a lawyer, and it does not cover any state rule. What can we do for a home service company? Our one built agent is a demo for a fictional roofing company: a web form triggers a call that books an inspection (see the roofing page ). We are a new studio with no clients yet. We are not lawyers and do not write consent wording. If your counsel supplies it, we would agree with you where it goes on the form and what is saved with each submission, and say plainly if any part is not built yet. Questions about consent for AI callbacks Is a checked box enough for written consent? The federal definition accepts an electronic signature where it is valid under federal law or state contract law, and Florida's statute counts a ticked box as a signature. Whether a particular box and its wording meet the rule is a question for counsel, and a pre-checked box is not addressed in the texts we read. Did the 2025 court decision mean forms no longer need to name the company? Not necessarily. The court removed the one-to-one wording and the current definition has none. The definition still speaks of an agreement that “clearly authorizes the seller” to deliver the calls, with “seller” meaning the business on whose behalf the call is made (47 CFR § 64.1200(f)(9)-(10)). The FTC's rule for prerecorded sales calls separately requires an agreement covering “a specific seller”; whether it reaches a conversational AI voice is not stated in the text we read. Naming the business that will call is the cautious course (our judgment, not a rule). Does the AI voice have to say it is an AI? We found no federal rule yet that says so; the FCC proposed one in September 2024 (89 FR 73321), and a later final rule cannot be ruled out because our search of the docket was limited. Some states have their own rules. Maine's (10 M.R.S. § 1500-DD) bars using AI in a way that may mislead a reasonable consumer into thinking they are dealing with a human unless clearly told otherwise, and its definition of a chatbot includes aural communication. California's rule for automatic dialing-announcing devices (Pub. Util. Code § 2874) requires telling the person when a message uses an artificial voice; whether it reaches a live AI agent is covered on our California guide. How fast must calls stop after someone opts out? Within a reasonable time and at most 10 business days, both in the text in force on our check date and in the final rule that took effect on November 25, 2026. That rule lets a caller designate an exclusive revocation method. Further changes have been proposed; they had not been adopted when we checked. Originally published at halyardops.pages.dev/guides/web-form-consent-wording-for-ai-callbacks . Halyard Ops is a new AI and software studio. This guide was drafted by an AI model from the linked primary sources and checked by an AI review against them; it was not written by a person. Halyard Ops directs the work and publishes it. This guide is general information, not legal or financial advice.

title: Why I Built a 337 KB Native Swift Port Manager Instead of Another 200 MB Electron App
summary: Every full-stack developer hits the exact same friction multiple times a day: Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000 You stop what you're building, open a new terminal tab, run lsof -nP -iTCP:3000 -sTCP:LISTEN , squint at the PID, run kill -9 <pid> , and lose your flow. And if you look for a macOS menu-bar utility to handle it, half the options are 200–350 MB Electron wrappers eating 300 MB of RAM just to sit in your menu bar — or bundled into $10/month subscriptions. So I started Kilobyte Labs to compile tiny, native Apple Silicon Swift/AppKit menu-bar utilities with zero Electron and one-time pricing. How PortPilot Fits in 337 KB Instead of shipping Chromium + Node.js, PortPilot compiles directly to a stripped native ARM64 Mach-O binary ( swiftc -O -whole-module-optimization -parse-as-library -Xfrontend -disable-reflection-names -Xlinker -dead_strip -Xlinker -x + strip -u -r ): Machine-parseable port scanning: Uses /usr/sbin/lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -F pcnT combined with a single batched ps -ww -o pid=,rss=,args= lookup so process names with spaces never break parsing. Smart runtime tagging: Automatically identifies Next.js ( :3000 ), Vite ( :5173 ), PostgreSQL ( :5432 ), Redis ( :6379 ), FastAPI/Django ( :8000 ), Ollama ( :11434 ), and protects macOS system daemons ( ControlCenter , mDNSResponder , rapportd ) with a shield badge. 1-click actions right from the menu bar: Open http://localhost:<port> , Copy URL, Pin favorites, graceful SIGTERM stop, right-click Force SIGKILL , and Clean All Dev Ports . Offline hardware-bound licensing: Verifies once against the Gumroad License API and caches a CryptoKit HMAC-SHA256 receipt bound to the Mac's native IOKit IOPlatformUUID so it works 100% offline afterward. Tool #2: SnapShrink (Offline ImageIO Compressor + GPS/EXIF Stripper) Right alongside PortPilot, I built SnapShrink — a native macOS menu-bar utility powered by Apple's hardware-accelerated ImageIO & CoreGraphics ( CGImageSource / CGImageDestination ): Shrinks bloated 4–8 MB macOS Retina screenshots and photos up to 80% smaller locally (also super useful for compressing screenshots before pasting into Claude, Cursor, or ChatGPT). Automatically strips hidden GPS coordinates, camera serial/model, TIFF, and IPTC EXIF metadata with zero cloud uploads. Includes an optional Auto-Shrink Desktop Screenshots watcher mode.
