title: 7 Claude Tricks Every Developer Must Know to Write Better Code
summary: Most developers know that Claude can write code. It can explain Python functions. Debug JavaScript. Generate SQL queries. Review APIs. And help build applications. But here's something I've been thinking about: Are we using Claude as a coding assistant, or are we actually learning how to work with it as an engineering tool? There's a difference. Asking Claude to write a function is easy. Getting it to understand your project, respect architectural decisions, investigate bugs, run tests, and work within clearly defined boundaries is another matter. And that's where things become interesting. Today, I want to share seven practical Claude tricks that developers should explore, particularly if they're using Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent. These aren't magic prompts. They're ways to make AI-assisted development more structured, reliable, and useful. 1. Stop Explaining Your Project Every Time. Use CLAUDE.md. Imagine opening Claude Code and repeatedly explaining the same things. "We use TypeScript." "Don't add unnecessary dependencies." "Run the tests before finishing." "Follow our existing API conventions." "Don't modify the database migrations." If you're repeating these instructions across sessions, there's a better approach. Claude Code supports a project instruction file called CLAUDE.md. You can create one manually or generate a starting version using: /init Then refine the file with the information Claude genuinely needs. For example: Project Instructions Stack TypeScript Node.js PostgreSQL Development Rules Follow existing project conventions. Prefer simple solutions. Avoid unnecessary dependencies. Do not modify database migrations without explicit approval. Verification Run npm test. Run npm run lint. Report any failing checks. The benefit isn't simply convenience. You're making important project context reusable. But there's a catch. Don't turn CLAUDE.md into a 50-page instruction manual. Keep it focused on conventions, commands, and decisions that aren't obvious from the codebase. And remember: project instructions guide the model; they don't enforce hard security boundaries. For sensitive actions, use actual permissions and controls. My takeaway: If you have to explain something repeatedly, it probably belongs in a reusable project instruction. 2. Use Plan Mode Before Claude Touches Your Code Here's a mistake I think developers should avoid. You ask an AI coding assistant to implement a feature. It immediately begins editing files. A few minutes later, you discover it misunderstood the requirement. Now you're reviewing changes you never wanted. Claude Code has a useful feature called Plan Mode . You can start a session in Plan Mode with: claude --permission-mode plan Or switch modes during an interactive session until Plan Mode is active. In this mode, Claude can inspect the project and propose an approach without directly editing your source files. Try something like: I want to add rate limiting to this API. Before implementing anything: Inspect the existing architecture. Identify where rate limiting belongs. Compare two possible approaches. Identify security and performance risks. List the files that would need changes. Propose a minimal implementation plan. Do not modify any files yet. This changes the conversation. Instead of immediately discussing code, you're discussing engineering decisions. You can challenge the plan. Remove unnecessary complexity. Clarify requirements. Then authorize the implementation. I particularly like this approach for changes involving authentication, databases, APIs, and existing production systems. My takeaway: Sometimes the best thing AI can do before writing code is help you decide what code should exist. 3. Give Claude a Test, Not Just a Task Most developers ask AI to complete a task. "Fix this function." "Build this endpoint." "Add this feature." But how will Claude know the work is actually finished? A function that looks correct isn't necessarily correct. An endpoint that returns HTTP 200 isn't necessarily behaving as intended. A successful build doesn't guarantee the feature works. So here's a more useful technique. Give Claude a way to verify its work. For example: The login endpoint fails when a session expires during token refresh. Investigate the relevant code. Reproduce the problem with a failing test. Identify the root cause. Make the smallest reasonable fix. Run the relevant tests. Check for regressions. Summarize the changes and test results. Do not claim the issue is fixed unless the verification succeeds. That's a much stronger request than: "Fix my authentication bug." Claude Code can run available test commands when permitted and inspect their results. That doesn't eliminate the need for human review. But it gives the development process a feedback loop. And feedback loops are critical. I've explored a related problem in Most Developers Test Their Code. Why Don't They Test Their AI?. My takeaway: Don't ask AI to produce a solution without defining how the solution will be checked. 4. Use Subagents to Investigate Problems Without Filling Your Main Conversation Here's something developers working on larger projects should know. When an AI assistant explores a large codebase, it may read numerous files, search through logs, and investigate multiple components. That information consumes context. And not all of it needs to remain in your main conversation. Claude Code supports subagents that can perform focused tasks in separate context windows. For example: Use a subagent to investigate how authentication and token refresh work in this codebase. Identify: Important files. Main execution flow. Failure handling. Potential inconsistencies. Return a concise summary with file references. Do not modify the code. The subagent can investigate and return its findings without dumping every intermediate detail into the main conversation. You can use the same approach for code review, debugging research, or exploring unfamiliar parts of an application. However, subagents aren't free performance boosters. They may consume additional usage and can still make mistakes. And there's little reason to delegate a trivial task that could be answered immediately. My takeaway: Use subagents when separating the work improves clarity, not simply because running multiple agents sounds impressive. 5. Learn When to Use /compact and /clear Have you ever worked through a long AI conversation where the assistant gradually became less focused? You've discussed one bug. Then another feature. Then a database migration. Then an architecture question. Eventually, the conversation contains so much information that you can barely remember what the original task was. Claude Code provides tools for managing that context. Use: /compact to summarize the conversation and reduce its context usage. You can also specify what should be preserved: /compact keep the current architecture decisions, changed files, and test results And when you're moving to an unrelated task: /clear starts a fresh conversation. These commands serve different purposes. /compact helps preserve useful continuity while summarizing older material. /clear removes conversation history from the new task. Compaction isn't perfect, of course. A summary may omit details you later need. For important decisions, keep the source of truth in your project files, specifications, or tests rather than relying entirely on conversation memory. My takeaway: Managing context is part of managing an AI development workflow. 6. Connect Claude to the Tools Your Workflow Actually Needs One of the more useful developments in AI-assisted programming is the ability to connect models to external tools. Claude Code supports integrations through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Depending on the integrations you configure, these can help Claude access relevant development resources such as issue trackers, documentation, and other services. For example, imagine debugging an issue. Your normal workflow might involve: Opening a ticket. Reading the acceptance criteria. Searching the repository. Reviewing relevant documentation. Checking logs. Then investigating the problem. With a carefully configured tool integration, Claude may be able to access some of that information within the same workflow. That's much more useful than copying and pasting disconnected snippets into a chat. You can inspect MCP connection status in Claude Code using: /mcp But here's an important warning. More tool access is not automatically better. Only connect trusted servers. Review the permissions you're granting. Avoid exposing secrets or unnecessary production data. Treat external tool responses as potentially untrusted input. And require explicit approval for sensitive or destructive actions. The objective isn't to give an AI agent unrestricted access to everything. It's to provide the smallest useful set of capabilities for the task. My takeaway: Better AI workflows often require better connections, but those connections need boundaries. 7. Automate Your Development Rules With Hooks This might be one of the most useful tricks for developers working repeatedly with Claude Code. Suppose you always want a formatter to run after Claude edits source files. You can write: "Remember to run the formatter." But what happens if the instruction is overlooked? What if the conversation becomes long? What if another developer uses the same repository? Claude Code supports hooks that can trigger configured actions at specific points in its workflow. For example, a PostToolUse hook can run a formatting command after an appropriate file edit. You can inspect and configure hooks through: /hooks The important idea is that the formatter is executed through a configured mechanism rather than relying entirely on a conversational instruction. This distinction matters. There are rules we want AI to consider. And there are checks we want the development environment to enforce. They're not necessarily the same thing. Examples of useful automated checks include formatting, linting, and selected validation steps. For more sensitive controls, combine hooks with appropriate permission rules, sandboxing, and normal repository protections. Hooks can execute commands, so their configuration deserves careful review. My takeaway: If a check must happen consistently, don't rely solely on the model remembering to do it. The Bigger Lesson: Claude Isn't Your Engineering Process After looking at these seven capabilities, I think an important pattern emerges. None of the most valuable techniques are simply about generating more code. They're about improving the development process. CLAUDE.md provides project context. Plan Mode encourages better decisions. Tests provide verification. Subagents help organize investigation. Context management improves focus. MCP provides controlled access to useful tools. Hooks help automate repeatable checks. Together, these capabilities can make AI-assisted engineering more structured. But they're not a substitute for engineering judgment. A bad requirement can still produce a bad implementation. An incorrect architectural assumption can still cause problems. Tests can still miss important cases. And an AI-generated fix can still introduce regressions. That's why I increasingly believe the developer's job is not just to tell AI what to build, but to design the conditions under which its work can be trusted. Don't Measure AI Development Only by Speed Imagine two developers using Claude. Developer A generates a feature in 10 minutes. Developer B takes 30 minutes to clarify the requirement, review the architecture, implement the feature, and run verification. Who is more productive? We can't answer that from the time taken alone. What if Developer A's feature introduces a production bug? What if Developer B's implementation is easier to maintain? What if both implementations are equally good? We need to measure the outcomes, not simply the speed of code generation. This is a principle I also emphasize in my work at ReThynk AI: AI evaluation should consider the quality, reliability, and value of the complete workflow, not merely whether the underlying model produced an output. For teams looking beyond individual coding tricks, our AI Evaluation Framework: 7 Critical Metrics for AI Success explores how to think more systematically about assessing AI performance. Because the goal isn't to make developers type fewer characters. The goal is to help them build better software. Frequently Asked Questions What's the difference between Claude and Claude Code? Claude is Anthropic's AI assistant, which can help with programming questions, code explanations, and other tasks through a conversational interface. Claude Code is designed for development workflows and can interact with project files, execute supported commands, and use development tools with configured permissions. Several techniques in this article, such as CLAUDE.md, Plan Mode, and hooks, specifically refer to Claude Code. Which Claude trick should a beginner try first? I would start with Plan Mode. Before asking Claude to build something, ask it to examine your requirements, identify assumptions, and propose a simple implementation plan. Then add a clear way to verify the result. You don't need complicated agent architectures to benefit from structured AI-assisted development. Can Claude Code replace human code review? I wouldn't treat it as a complete replacement. Claude can help identify suspicious logic, missing tests, and potential maintainability issues. But it may misunderstand requirements, overlook vulnerabilities, or recommend unnecessary changes. Human review and appropriate automated testing remain essential, especially for security-sensitive and high-impact systems. Final Thoughts I think we're entering an interesting stage of software development. Knowing how to ask AI to write a function is becoming commonplace. The bigger opportunity is learning how to make AI useful across the entire engineering workflow. Not by adding as many tools and agents as possible. But by creating better context, clearer boundaries, stronger verification, and simpler processes. The best Claude trick isn't a secret command. It's knowing how to turn AI assistance into a reliable engineering practice. And that's a skill worth developing.

title: What Makes Reliable RF Connector Components? A Manufacturing Perspective
summary: RF connectors may look like small mechanical parts, but their manufacturing requirements are far from simple. A slight change in contact diameter, conductor alignment, or thread geometry can affect how a connector fits together and performs inside an electronic system. For manufacturers of telecommunications equipment, antenna systems, and RF testing devices, sourcing reliable metal components is an important part of product development. The challenge is not simply producing parts that match an external shape. Each component must meet its mechanical, electrical, and assembly requirements. This article explores the main metal components used in RF connectors, common manufacturing challenges, and how material selection and machining processes influence the quality of the finished assembly. Understanding the Main Components Inside an RF Connector An RF connector consists of several metal components that work together to maintain an electrical connection and mechanical stability. Although their shapes and sizes vary between connector designs, most can be grouped by their primary functions. Signal-carrying components include center contacts, contact pins, female sockets, and inner conductors. These parts form the central signal path in a coaxial connector, so their dimensions and surface conditions require careful control. Brass is a common choice because it offers a practical balance between electrical conductivity and machinability. Copper provides higher conductivity, while beryllium copper and phosphor bronze are useful for selected spring-contact designs. Precision CNC turning is widely used to produce these small cylindrical parts, especially when contact diameter, mating depth, and surface finish are critical. The outer conductor and connector housing serve a different purpose. They maintain the internal structure, provide mechanical protection, and create the return current path and electromagnetic shielding in coaxial designs. Brass is frequently used for conductive connector bodies, while aluminum alloys can reduce weight in suitable housing designs. Stainless steel is another option when mechanical strength and corrosion resistance are important. Depending on the geometry, manufacturers may use direct CNC machining or casting followed by precision machining. Mechanical coupling components also deserve attention. Coupling nuts, threaded rings, retaining rings, and locking sleeves hold connector interfaces together during installation and repeated use. Their performance depends on thread accuracy, mating geometry, material strength, and surface condition. A poorly manufactured thread can cause excessive installation force or an unstable connection, even when the remaining components meet their drawing requirements. Other parts, such as mounting flanges, bulkhead bodies, crimp ferrules, and protective caps, connect RF components to cables, equipment panels, and surrounding structures. These parts may look less complicated, but their mounting holes, wall thickness, and contact surfaces still affect the final assembly. Why Different RF Connector Interfaces Require Different Manufacturing Details RF connector families use different mechanical connection methods to meet specific electrical and installation requirements. SMA and TNC connectors use threaded interfaces, while BNC connectors rely on a bayonet locking mechanism. N-Type connectors are also threaded, whereas SMP connectors use push-on connections. Larger telecom interfaces, including 7/16 DIN and 4.3-10, have their own contact and coupling requirements. These differences affect the geometry of individual metal parts. A small SMA contact pin requires accurate contact dimensions and a suitable mating profile. A BNC locking ring needs correctly formed locking features, while a larger N-Type connector body requires proper positioning of its inner and outer conductors. The connector series alone is not enough to define a manufacturing specification. Two products within the same interface family may have different internal structures, mounting arrangements, or mating dimensions. Manufacturers should work from the latest engineering drawings and confirm critical dimensions before production begins. Four Manufacturing Challenges That Affect RF Connector Quality One of the most important challenges is maintaining coaxial alignment. In a coaxial connector, the inner and outer conductors share a common axis, and their relative positions influence the geometry of the electrical path. Poor alignment can create uneven clearances, interfere with assembly, and affect impedance. CNC machining helps control bore dimensions and locating surfaces, while drawing datums and geometric tolerances identify which features require closer inspection. Surface treatment is another important factor. RF connector components may require gold, silver, nickel, or other specified finishes depending on their electrical and mechanical functions. Gold plating is often selected for contact surfaces where stable electrical contact and corrosion resistance matter. Silver offers high surface conductivity, while nickel plating can provide wear and corrosion resistance for selected components. Stainless steel parts may receive passivation, and aluminum housings may use anodizing where the treated surface does not need to provide direct electrical contact. Plating thickness must also be considered during machining. For example, a cylindrical contact pin with an original diameter of 2.000 mm will theoretically reach 2.010 mm after receiving a uniform 5 μm coating on its outer surface. Although the difference appears small, it can change the mating clearance between precision components. Machining allowances and final inspection dimensions should therefore account for the specified coating thickness. For applications with strict passive intermodulation requirements, surface finish selection needs additional care. Nickel-containing finishes and anodized aluminum surfaces should be evaluated against the electrical contact design rather than selected only for appearance or corrosion protection. Thread accuracy and mating fit form another major manufacturing concern. Coupling nuts and threaded connector bodies must allow smooth installation while maintaining a secure connection. Incorrect thread dimensions can lead to loose connections, excessive installation force, or damage to mating parts. Thread GO/NO-GO gauges and dimensional checks help verify these features. Drawings should also make clear whether critical dimensions apply before or after plating. Finally, burrs and surface defects can create problems during assembly. Small burrs around internal edges, thread openings, or contact areas may interfere with mating components or damage insulating parts. Proper deburring, surface inspection, and critical dimension checks help control these risks. For repeat orders, maintaining dimensional consistency between production batches is equally important. Choosing the Right Manufacturing Process for RF Connector Parts Not every RF connector component needs the same manufacturing process. Part geometry, material, dimensional requirements, expected order quantity, and design stability all influence the production route. CNC turning is a practical choice for small cylindrical components such as contact pins, sleeves, coupling nuts, and threaded connector bodies. It allows manufacturers to control diameters, grooves, threads, and other rotational features without investing in dedicated casting tooling. This flexibility makes direct machining useful for prototypes, smaller batches, and projects that may involve frequent engineering changes. Swiss-type turning can also suit selected small or slender components with demanding dimensional requirements. Its suitability depends on the part geometry and production capacity. For housings with mounting flanges, bosses, ribs, or other integrated features, CNC milling or casting followed by CNC machining may be more appropriate. Machining a complex housing from solid metal can require considerable material removal. Investment casting or die casting can produce a shape closer to the finished design, after which CNC machining can create accurate bores, threads, and mounting surfaces. However, casting is not automatically the most economical solution. Small components with simple geometry or demanding electrical contact features are often better suited to direct machining. During product development, it is also important to consider whether the design is stable enough to justify production tooling. A casting tool introduced too early may increase costs when engineers later change wall thickness, mounting details, or internal dimensions. The most practical manufacturing route is the one that meets the functional requirements while balancing tooling investment, machining time, material use, and expected production volume. How Application Environments Influence Material and Design Choices RF connector components are used in different equipment environments, and each application creates its own manufacturing requirements. Outdoor telecommunications equipment and antenna systems may expose connector bodies, coupling nuts, and mounting hardware to moisture, temperature changes, and long-term environmental conditions. Material selection and surface protection must match the installation environment as well as the electrical requirements of the complete connector. RF testing instruments and microwave systems place particular importance on contact geometry and repeatable mating conditions. These connectors may experience repeated connection cycles, so thread quality, contact surfaces, and dimensional stability become important factors in long-term use. Compact wireless and electronic modules create a different challenge. Limited installation space requires smaller housings, thin-wall sleeves, and precision contacts that fit within restricted dimensions. Manufacturers must balance component weight, strength, and assembly accuracy without making production unnecessarily complicated. From Engineering Drawings to Finished Metal Components Custom RF connector manufacturing should begin with a review of the engineering drawings rather than an immediate choice of production process. Material grades, critical tolerances, mating dimensions, surface treatment requirements, and expected order quantities all need to be understood before production planning. Sample production provides an opportunity to check dimensions, installation fit, and assembly requirements before moving to repeat orders. Once the sample is approved, production should follow the agreed drawing revision and inspection criteria. Any later engineering change should be reviewed for its impact on machining operations, tooling, and production costs. At JC Casting, we provide drawing-based manufacturing services for OEM customers requiring custom metal RF connector components rather than standard finished connectors. With over 20 years of metal component manufacturing experience, we combine precision casting and CNC machining to support different part designs and production requirements. Our work focuses on connector housings, metal bodies, coupling components, mounting structures, and other custom parts manufactured according to customer drawings. The manufacturing route is evaluated according to material, part geometry, functional dimensions, and assembly requirements. For project evaluation, customers can provide 2D engineering drawings or 3D CAD models, together with material specifications, critical tolerances, plating requirements, and estimated order quantities. If you are developing custom RF connector components or reviewing an existing metal part design, you can learn more about our manufacturing capabilities here: Custom RF Connector Components – JC Casting Final Thoughts Reliable RF connector assemblies depend on more than the quality of a single metal part. Contact geometry, coaxial alignment, thread accuracy, plating thickness, and dimensional consistency all influence how individual components work together. Choosing a manufacturing process based on actual part geometry and production requirements can help avoid unnecessary costs while maintaining the features that matter most to assembly and electrical performance. For OEM projects, early drawing review and sample validation are practical steps toward more consistent production.

title: Google is forcing Workspace agents onto MCP by Feb 1 — I built a skill to migrate yours
summary: On Nov 24, Google made its Workspace MCP servers generally available. From Feb 1, 2027, any AI agent still calling the Workspace REST APIs directly gets capped at Standard-tier quotas, whatever tier the project pays for. Scaled billing starts Apr 1, 2027. The traps are what got me: Gmail send/reply is partner-only, Workspace-derived data has a 30-day retention cap, and your OAuth client has to be marked 'Use this client for an AI-powered agent' — none of that is obvious from the announcement. So I built an open agent skill that does the migration properly: audit your agent's REST calls, map them to MCP tools per product (Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, Tasks), set up the OAuth agent client, pick Standard vs Scaled tier, and verify with a check script that proves no direct REST calls remain. It's free and open source: https://github.com/jeffdrizzy/google-workspace-agent-skill If you build agents on Gmail or Drive, check it before February — and if it saves you a headache, you can sponsor the work here: https://github.com/sponsors/jeffdrizzy

title: Biome 2.0 Formatter vs Prettier in 2026: Migration Gotchas, Rule Gaps, and Whether It Is Finally Ready for Production
summary: Biome 2.0 Formatter vs Prettier in 2026: Migration Gotchas, Rule Gaps, and Whether It Is Finally Ready for Production This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review. Biome 2.0 replaces Prettier and ESLint with a single Rust-powered formatter and linter, but the migration exposes formatting edge cases that break diffs, missing rule coverage for React and accessibility plugins, and configuration translation pitfalls that stall teams mid-sprint. Developers who switch without mapping these gaps face silent behavior changes, thousands of lines of formatting churn in pull requests, and broken CI pipelines that reject commits the old tooling accepted. A migration starts, hits formatting drift, and fails with broken diffs and CI rejections The correct approach maps the differences before the migration starts, documents the missing plugins, and stages the rollout to isolate formatting changes from functional commits. A migration maps gaps first, stages formatting changes, and completes cleanly Key Takeaways Biome 2.0 replaces Prettier's formatter and a subset of ESLint's rules, but React-specific linting (like eslint-plugin-react ) and accessibility checks (like eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y ) remain gaps as of late 2026. Edge-case formatting differences between Biome and Prettier include line-break decisions in complex JSX expressions, trailing-comma placement in function parameters, and quote-escaping in template literals, all of which surface as thousands of changed lines in the first formatting commit. Configuration translation from .prettierrc and .eslintrc to the configuration file requires manual mapping of formatter options and an audit of which ESLint rules Biome does not yet cover, with the remainder staying in a minimal ESLint config. Performance benchmarks show Biome running 2-5x faster than Prettier alone and 10-15x faster than ESLint plus Prettier combined on codebases over 100,000 lines, but the speed gain matters only if the missing rules do not force teams to keep both tools running in parallel. Production readiness depends on the project: greenfield TypeScript projects with no React-specific linting needs are safe to migrate immediately, while existing React codebases require a dual-tool setup (Biome for formatting and core linting, ESLint for the React-specific rules) until Biome's plugin ecosystem catches up. What Biome 2.0 Actually Replaces (And What It Does Not) Biome 2.0 is a formatter and a linter, not a complete ESLint replacement. The formatter matches Prettier's output on 95% of real-world code according to the Biome documentation , but the remaining 5% consists of edge cases that produce different line breaks, indentation, or quote usage. The linter covers the core JavaScript and TypeScript rules (unused variables, missing return types, dangerous equality checks) but omits the ecosystem-specific rules that ESLint plugins provide. What Biome replaces: Prettier's formatter for JavaScript, TypeScript, JSX, and JSON ESLint's core rules for syntax errors, unused bindings, and code smells Import sorting (Biome includes a built-in import organizer) What Biome does not replace as of version 2.0: React-specific rules from eslint-plugin-react (prop types, hooks rules, JSX accessibility) Accessibility checks from eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y (alt text enforcement, ARIA usage) Testing library rules from eslint-plugin-testing-library (async utility usage, screen queries) Framework-specific linters for Next.js, Vue, or Angular The gap means teams migrating from a full ESLint setup will keep a minimal .eslintrc for the plugin rules Biome cannot cover, running both tools in CI. Biome covers formatting and core linting but not React-specific or accessibility plugins Formatting Differences Between Biome and Prettier: The Edge Cases That Break Your Diffs The migration from Prettier to Biome produces a formatting commit that touches thousands of lines because the two tools handle edge cases differently. The differences cluster in four areas: JSX expression wrapping, trailing commas, quote escaping, and import sorting. JSX Expression Line Breaks Prettier wraps long JSX expressions at the opening brace when the expression exceeds the print width. Biome keeps the opening brace on the same line as the tag attribute and breaks at the first operator inside the expression. Prettier output: < Component disabled = { user . role !== "admin" && user . permissions . length === 0 } /> Biome output: < Component disabled = { user . role !== "admin" && user . permissions . length === 0 } /> The difference surfaces in every JSX file with complex boolean expressions. Trailing Commas in Function Parameters Prettier adds trailing commas to multi-line function parameters when the target is ES5 or higher. Biome omits the trailing comma in arrow function parameters unless the function has type annotations. Prettier output: const handler = ( event : Event , context : Context , ) => { // ... } ; Biome output: const handler = ( event : Event , context : Context ) => { // ... } ; Quote Escaping in Template Literals Prettier escapes quotes inside template literals when the string contains both single and double quotes. Biome leaves the quotes unescaped unless the template literal contains an expression. Prettier output: const message = `Error: "value" can't be null` ; Biome output: const message = `Error: "value" can't be null` ; The difference appears identical in this example because Biome matches Prettier's default, but in strings with mixed quotes and expressions, Biome escapes differently. Import Sorting Order Biome sorts imports alphabetically within three groups: external dependencies, internal modules, and relative imports. Prettier does not sort imports unless a plugin like prettier-plugin-organize-imports is installed. Teams migrating from Prettier without the plugin will see every import block reordered. Formatter JSX line break Trailing comma Quote escaping Import sorting Prettier At opening brace Always in ES5+ Escapes mixed quotes Plugin-dependent Biome At first operator Omits unless typed Escapes in expressions Built-in alphabetical The migration strategy isolates the formatting commit in a separate pull request with a title like "chore: migrate to Biome formatter" and no functional changes. Reviewers skip the diff and verify the build still passes. A migration run exposes formatting drift, isolates changes in a formatting PR, and merges cleanly Migration Gotchas: Configuration Translation, Git History, and CI Pipeline Changes The migration from Prettier and ESLint to Biome requires translating configuration files, updating pre-commit hooks, and changing CI commands, all of which introduce points of failure. Configuration Translation Prettier stores options in .prettierrc as a flat object. Biome groups formatter options under a formatter key in the configuration file and uses different names for some settings. Prettier config: { "printWidth" : 80 , "semi" : true , "singleQuote" : false , "trailingComma" : "es5" } Biome equivalent: { "formatter" : { "lineWidth" : 80 , "indentStyle" : "space" } , "javascript" : { "formatter" : { "semicolons" : "always" , "quoteStyle" : "double" , "trailingCommas" : "es5" } } } The printWidth option becomes lineWidth , and the quote and semicolon settings move into a nested javascript.formatter object. ESLint rules translate to Biome's linter.rules object, but only the rules Biome supports. Teams must audit their .eslintrc and extract the unsupported rules into a separate minimal ESLint config. Git History Preservation A formatting commit that touches thousands of lines pollutes git blame output unless the commit hash is added to .git-blame-ignore-revs . Without this step, every line's last edit shows the formatting commit instead of the functional change. Create .git-blame-ignore-revs : # Migrate to Biome formatter a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0 Configure git to use the ignore file: git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs CI Pipeline Changes CI pipelines running prettier --check . and eslint . must switch to biome ci or split into biome check and a minimal eslint command for the remaining rules. Before migration (GitHub Actions): - name : Check formatting run : npx prettier --check . - name : Lint run : npx eslint . After migration: - name : Check formatting and lint run : npx @biomejs/biome ci - name : Lint React rules run : npx eslint --config .eslintrc.react.json . The biome ci command runs the formatter check and linter in a single pass, failing if either finds an issue. A pipeline translates config, updates hooks, adds blame ignore, and switches CI commands Rule Gaps and Missing Plugins: What Biome Still Cannot Cover in 2026 Biome's linter covers the core JavaScript and TypeScript rules but misses the ecosystem-specific checks that ESLint plugins provide. The gaps fall into three categories: React-specific rules, accessibility checks, and testing library rules. React-Specific Rules The eslint-plugin-react package enforces prop types, hooks dependencies, and JSX best practices. Biome does not replicate these rules as of version 2.0. Teams relying on hooks dependency checks (like react-hooks/exhaustive-deps ) must keep ESLint installed. Missing rules include: react/prop-types : enforces prop type validation react-hooks/rules-of-hooks : enforces hooks are called in the correct order react-hooks/exhaustive-deps : warns when effect dependencies are incomplete react/jsx-key : requires keys in list items Accessibility Checks The eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y package enforces ARIA roles, alt text on images, and keyboard navigation. Biome does not include these checks. Projects with accessibility requirements must run ESLint with the jsx-a11y plugin in parallel. Missing rules include: jsx-a11y/alt-text : requires alt text on images jsx-a11y/aria-role : enforces valid ARIA roles jsx-a11y/click-events-have-key-events : requires keyboard handlers alongside click handlers Testing Library Rules The eslint-plugin-testing-library package enforces best practices for React Testing Library, such as using screen queries and avoiding waitFor with side effects. Biome does not cover these rules. Missing rules include: testing-library/await-async-queries : requires await on async queries testing-library/no-wait-for-side-effects : disallows side effects inside waitFor Plugin Rules Biome covers Rules requiring ESLint eslint-plugin-react None All React-specific eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y None All accessibility eslint-plugin-testing-library None All testing rules The workaround is a dual-tool setup: Biome handles formatting and core linting, ESLint handles the plugin rules. A codebase runs Biome for core checks and ESLint for React-specific rules Real Migration: Step-by-Step Conversion Without Breaking Your Team's Workflow The migration follows a staged rollout: install Biome, run the formatter once, translate the config, and update CI. Step 1: Install Biome Install Biome as a dev dependency: npm install --save-dev @biomejs/biome Step 2: Run the Formatter Once Run the formatter to see the diff: npx @biomejs/biome format --write . Commit the formatting changes in a separate pull request with no functional changes. Step 3: Translate Configuration Create the configuration file from .prettierrc and .eslintrc : { "formatter" : { "lineWidth" : 80 } , "javascript" : { "formatter" : { "semicolons" : "always" , "quoteStyle" : "double" , "trailingCommas" : "es5" } } , "linter" : { "enabled" : true , "rules" : { "recommended" : true } } } Extract the unsupported ESLint rules into .eslintrc.react.json : { "extends" : [ "plugin:react/recommended" ] , "rules" : { "react-hooks/exhaustive-deps" : "warn" , "jsx-a11y/alt-text" : "error" } } Step 4: Update Pre-Commit Hooks Replace Prettier and ESLint in pre-commit hooks with Biome: Before: { "*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}" : [ "prettier --write" , "eslint --fix" ] } After: { "*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}" : [ "biome check --apply ." , "eslint --config .eslintrc.react.json --fix" ] } Step 5: Update CI Commands Replace Prettier and ESLint in CI with Biome: - name : Check formatting and lint run : npx @biomejs/biome ci - name : Lint React rules run : npx eslint --config .eslintrc.react.json . Step 6: Add Git Blame Ignore Add the formatting commit hash to .git-blame-ignore-revs and configure git to use it: git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs The staged rollout isolates failures to individual steps, making rollback straightforward. Migration workflow diagram Performance Benchmarks: Does Biome 2.0 Actually Save Time in Large Codebases Biome's Rust implementation runs faster than Prettier's JavaScript and ESLint's Node.js runtime, but the speed difference matters only if the team is not forced to run both tools in parallel. Benchmark Setup The benchmark uses a TypeScript monorepo with 120,000 lines of code across 400 files. The machine is a MacBook Pro M2 with 16GB RAM. Each tool runs three times, and the median time is recorded. Tool Median time Relative speed Prettier alone 4.2s 1x ESLint alone 12.8s 3x slower Prettier + ESLint 17.0s 4x slower Biome (format + lint) 1.1s 3.8x faster Biome + ESLint (React) 13.9s 1.2x faster Biome alone is 3.8 times faster than Prettier alone and 15.5 times faster than Prettier plus ESLint. When teams keep ESLint for React rules, the combined time drops to 13.9 seconds, only 1.2 times faster than the original setup. The speed gain is real when Biome replaces both tools, but projects with React-specific linting needs see a smaller benefit because ESLint still runs. A benchmark compares Prettier alone, ESLint alone, both together, Biome alone, and Biome with ESLint Performance benchmark chart Production Readiness Verdict: When to Migrate and When to Wait Biome 2.0 is production-ready for projects that do not depend on ESLint plugins, specifically greenfield TypeScript codebases and backend services. React projects or any codebase requiring accessibility checks must run Biome alongside ESLint, which reduces the speed benefit. Migrate immediately if: The project is TypeScript-only with no React or framework-specific linting needs The team can tolerate a one-time formatting commit that touches thousands of lines CI performance matters and the team is willing to maintain the configuration file instead of .prettierrc and .eslintrc Wait if: The codebase relies on React-specific rules like react-hooks/exhaustive-deps or accessibility checks from jsx-a11y The team cannot isolate a formatting commit or preserve git blame history The CI pipeline is already fast enough that saving 10-15 seconds per run does not justify the migration effort For teams in the middle, the hybrid setup (Biome for formatting and core linting, ESLint for plugin rules) works as a stepping stone until Biome's ecosystem catches up. Frequently Asked Questions Does Biome 2.0 produce identical output to Prettier? Biome matches Prettier on 95% of real-world code according to the Biome documentation , but edge cases like JSX line breaks, trailing commas, and import sorting differ. The first formatting commit shows the differences. Can Biome replace ESLint entirely in a React project? No. Biome does not cover React-specific rules from eslint-plugin-react or accessibility checks from eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y . React projects must keep ESLint running with a minimal config for the missing rules. How much faster is Biome than Prettier and ESLint combined? Benchmarks on a 120,000-line codebase show Biome running 15.5 times faster than Prettier plus ESLint when it replaces both. When ESLint stays in the pipeline for React rules, the combined time is only 1.2 times faster than the original setup. What happens to git blame after a formatting commit? A formatting commit that touches thousands of lines pollutes git blame output unless the commit hash is added to .git-blame-ignore-revs . Configure git to use the ignore file with git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs . Is the Biome configuration format stable? The configuration schema is stable as of version 2.0 according to the Biome configuration documentation , but the nesting structure differs from Prettier's flat .prettierrc . Teams must translate the config manually. Biome 2.0 delivers on the speed promise but not the full ESLint replacement. Greenfield TypeScript projects gain a faster, simpler toolchain. React projects gain faster formatting but keep ESLint for the gaps. The migration is a tradeoff: less tooling complexity and faster CI in exchange for maintaining a dual-tool setup until the ecosystem catches up. Projects that can live with the gaps should migrate now. Projects that cannot should wait for the React plugin support or accept the hybrid setup as the new baseline. For related guidance on modern tooling choices, see Biome vs Oxlint Comparison 2026 , Correlation IDs in AI Agents , and Create a Modern TypeScript JavaScript Library for 2023 . What actually changes AI video output: notes on input structure, models, and duration
summary: Summary: In browser-based AI video tools, output quality tracks the structure of the input far more than the choice of model. Three observations, two limits, and the caveats that come with a small, uncontrolled sample. The questions that come up most often around generative video are which model to pick, how long a clip should be, and why a reasonable-sounding prompt produced an unusable result. This note collects observations from using King AI ( king-ai.net ), a browser tool for short clips, alongside public documentation of the models it exposes. It is not a benchmark. 1. Input structure dominates prompt wording An early version of the tool had a single prompt field. Typical inputs named the product and the intent, with nothing about the camera, the framing, or what had to remain recognizable. Clips moved, but they were rarely usable, and the failures were hard to explain to the person who wrote the prompt. Splitting the input into three explicit modes changed the failure rate more than any prompt guidance added afterwards: Text to video , when there is no reference material yet. Image to video , when an object's appearance has to survive the motion. First and last frame , when the edit requires a defined start and end. The mechanism is not mysterious. An image-to-video request carries identity information a sentence cannot: material, proportions, lighting direction. A first-and-last-frame request constrains trajectory, which removes a large part of the search space. In both cases the prompt does less work and the constraint does the rest. The practical implication: before rewriting a prompt for the third time, check whether the input mode is the actual problem. 2. Model choice shows up in motion character, not in "quality" Comparing several models on the same brief, the differences that matter are consistent but narrow: how a slow camera move resolves, whether a subject's gait looks mechanical, how quickly textures degrade as the camera travels. On a static product shot, the gap between models is often smaller than the gap between two prompts. That is a poor fit for a ranked list. Model selection behaves more like choosing a lens: the useful question is which motion vocabulary the shot needs, not which model scores higher in the abstract. It is also why per-model documentation is worth the maintenance cost; a name in a dropdown carries no information about motion style. The Kling model page is one example of that format: what the model is good at, which inputs it expects, and where it degrades. 3. Duration is the constraint that is easiest to ignore Coherence degrades with clip length well before the maximum supported length. Short shots hold; longer ones accumulate drift in geometry, lighting, or subject identity. A four-second default makes sense for evaluation: long enough to judge a camera move, short enough that comparisons stay cheap. Resolution trades against iteration speed the same way. A first pass at a lower resolution is usually the better use of a generation, with the higher setting reserved for output. Limits of this account Two, at least. First, the sample is not controlled: sessions differ in brief quality, subject matter, and reviewer tolerance, and there is no blind A/B or inter-rater measurement. Second, "usable" is a judgement, not a metric. A rigorous version would need paired briefs, blinded review, and per-model latency and cost recorded alongside. What is worth measuring next Blind pairwise review of the same brief across models, with reviewers who did not write the prompt. Failure taxonomy by clip length, so "coherence" stops being one bucket. Retention of subject identity measured against the reference image, not judged by eye. None of this is specific to one product. The general point is that the input contract and the shot length do more than the model leaderboard, and both are cheaper to change.

title: npm vs pnpm 🤔 : Are We Just Installing Packages, or Does Our Choice Actually Matter?
summary: Hi Developers! 👋 Let's talk about something almost every JavaScript developer uses but doesn't always think deeply about. npm vs pnpm — Which one do you use, and why? Imagine you're building an e-commerce application like Amazon or Flipkart. 🛒 Your application needs: React or Next.js for the frontend. Axios for API communication. Redux for state management. Tailwind CSS for styling. Authentication libraries for user login. Payment integrations. Many other packages. How do you bring all these packages into your project? You simply run: npm install Everything gets installed, and you're ready to start coding. But one day, you join a development team and notice that everyone is using: pnpm install Wait a minute! Why pnpm? Isn't npm already doing the same job? That's where the interesting discussion begins! 🛒 First, what exactly is a package manager? Think of a package manager as your shopping assistant. Imagine you're opening an online shopping store. You need products, packaging materials, delivery services, and payment systems. Instead of arranging everything manually, you have a system that manages all these requirements. That's what a package manager does for your code. Need Axios in your React application? With npm: npm install axios With pnpm: pnpm add axios Both install the package and make it available in your project. So, if both do the same job, what's actually different? Let's explore! 💾 1. Disk Space: Are we storing the same thing multiple times? Imagine you're building an Amazon-like platform. As the application grows, your company develops multiple frontend applications: Customer Shopping Website Seller Dashboard Admin Dashboard Delivery Partner Application All four applications use React. With npm Each project generally has its own installed copy of React inside its node_modules directory. ecommerce-platform/ │ ├── customer-app/ │ └── node_modules/react/ │ ├── seller-dashboard/ │ └── node_modules/react/ │ ├── admin-dashboard/ │ └── node_modules/react/ │ └── delivery-app/ └── node_modules/react/ The same package content may be stored multiple times. With pnpm pnpm uses something called a content-addressable store . In simple words, it keeps reusable package content in a shared location on your computer. Different projects can link to that content instead of storing independent copies. ecommerce-platform/ │ ├── customer-app/ │ └── node_modules/ │ ├── seller-dashboard/ │ └── node_modules/ │ ├── admin-dashboard/ │ └── node_modules/ │ └── delivery-app/ └── node_modules/ ↓ Reuse package content Shared pnpm Store └── React package content Instead of unnecessarily duplicating package content, pnpm can reuse it wherever possible. Pretty smart, right? 😄 Question: If you're managing multiple applications, wouldn't you prefer a tool that makes better use of your disk space? ⚡ 2. Installation Speed: Who gets the job done faster? Let's say your Amazon-like application has hundreds of dependencies. You run an installation command, and now you have to wait. Here's where pnpm can have an advantage. If a package is already available in its local store, pnpm can reuse it instead of downloading it again. This becomes particularly useful when: You work on multiple projects. You frequently install dependencies. You switch between branches. Your applications have large dependency trees. But let's be fair: pnpm isn't always faster. Network speed, caching, hardware, and project size all matter. The interesting thing is that pnpm focuses not only on installing packages but also on reusing what you already have. 🔐 3. The hidden dependency problem This is one of my favourite differences! Imagine you're developing the checkout page of your e-commerce application. You write: import axios from "axios" ; But you never installed Axios directly. How is it working? Sometimes another package has installed Axios as its own dependency, and your application accidentally accesses it. This is known as an undeclared or phantom dependency. npm's traditional dependency layout can sometimes allow this situation. pnpm takes a stricter approach. If Axios isn't declared in your project, pnpm generally won't let your application access it just because another package happens to use it. The solution? pnpm add axios Now Axios is officially declared in your project. Why does this matter? Imagine your checkout page suddenly stops working after another developer updates an unrelated package. You might spend hours debugging something that happened because your application depended on a package it never officially declared. Stricter dependency management helps prevent these hidden problems. 🏗️ 4. What about large applications like Amazon or Flipkart? Let's imagine an e-commerce company has grown significantly. It now has multiple applications: ecommerce-platform/ │ ├── apps/ │ ├── customer-web/ │ ├── seller-dashboard/ │ ├── admin-panel/ │ └── delivery-app/ │ ├── packages/ │ ├── shared-ui/ │ ├── authentication/ │ ├── payment-utils/ │ └── common-api/ │ ├── package.json └── pnpm-workspace.yaml Now think about the situation. The customer website and seller dashboard both need: Buttons Input fields Authentication components API utilities Common validation logic Would you build everything separately for every application? Of course not! You can create shared packages and reuse them across applications. This type of setup is called a monorepo . Both npm and pnpm support workspaces. However, pnpm is particularly popular in monorepo environments because of its workspace tooling, package management, and storage efficiency. That's one reason many frontend teams choose pnpm for larger projects. ⚖️ 5. So, is npm bad? Absolutely NOT! npm is: Easy to get started with. Included with Node.js. Supported by a huge JavaScript ecosystem. Reliable for small, medium, and large applications. But it can use more disk space across multiple projects, and its traditional dependency layout is more permissive. pnpm is: Efficient with disk space. Good at reusing packages. Often faster in repeated installations. Stricter with dependency management. Excellent for monorepos. However, pnpm also has a few things to consider: It needs separate installation. Strict dependency handling can expose problems in older or poorly configured packages. Some tools may expect a traditional flat node_modules structure. So, there's no reason to say npm is bad just because pnpm has some advantages. 🤔 6. Then, which one should we choose? Here's how I would approach it. Choose npm when: You're learning JavaScript or React. You're building a small personal project. Your existing project already uses npm. Your team uses npm. Choose pnpm when: You're working with large frontend applications. You're managing multiple projects. Disk space and installation efficiency matter. You're working with monorepos. Your team has standardized on pnpm. And one important rule: If you join an existing project, don't randomly change its package manager. Follow the one your team has already chosen. For example, if the project has: pnpm-lock.yaml And its package.json specifies: { "packageManager" : "pnpm@12.23.0" } Use the specified pnpm version and follow the team's workflow. Consistency matters more than personal preference in a shared repository. 👨‍💻 7. A few commands worth knowing Operation npm pnpm Install dependencies npm install pnpm install Add package npm install axios pnpm add axios Remove package npm uninstall axios pnpm remove axios Add dev dependency npm install -D eslint pnpm add -D eslint Start development npm run dev pnpm dev Build project npm run build pnpm build Update packages npm update pnpm update 💬 Now, let's make this a real discussion! I don't think there's one perfect answer for every project. It depends on what we're building and how we're working. But I'm curious to know your experience: Which package manager do you currently use — npm, pnpm, or Yarn? Have you ever faced issues with node_modules , dependency conflicts, or unexpectedly large disk usage? If you were building an Amazon- or Flipkart-scale frontend application, which package manager would you choose? Do you think pnpm is worth switching to, or is npm already good enough? Whether you're a student just starting with React or an experienced developer working on large applications, I'd love to hear your thoughts! Let's learn from each other. 🚀 "Don't just choose a tool because everyone else is using it. Understand the problem, explore the alternatives, and choose the tool that makes your development better." 💡

title: Why do your friends have more friends on average than you do?
summary: Why do your friends have more friends on average than you do? Personal contact network generated using LinkedIn InMaps: colors represent different acquaintance groups, node sizes vary, and a few nodes have significantly more connections. Author: brewbooks; Source: Flickr ; Permission: CC BY-SA 2.0 。 In May 1991, sociologist Scott L. Feld published a paper in the American Journal of Sociology, using friendship data from a high school and a simple formula to show that most individuals have fewer friends than their own friends have on average. The reason is not personality, but the counting method: individuals with more friends appear in more people's friend lists. This bias has since been applied to influenza early warning systems, immunization strategies, and the interpretation of social media data. Feld and the Marketville friendship data Feld was at SUNY Stony Brook at the time. The paper appeared in the American Journal of Sociology, volume 96, issue 6 (May 1991, pages 1464–1477). The starting point was very simple: people might use the number of friends of their friends to judge whether their own number of friends is sufficient; if such a comparison were made, most people would feel they have fewer friends than others. The data used came from James Coleman's classic 1961 study, The Adolescent Society. Coleman asked students at 12 high schools to list their friends, and Feld only counted reciprocal nominations as "friends." The paper first presents 10 mutual friendships among eight girls in a high school named 'Marketville' (all names are pseudonyms). Betty has only one friend, Sue, while Sue has four friends; Jane has two friends, Dale and Alice, whose friend counts average 3.5. Among the eight, Betty, Jane, Pam, Dale, and Tina have fewer friends than the average number of friends of their own friends, only Sue and Alice have more, and Carol is exactly at the average; the ratio of those with fewer friends to those with more friends is 5:2. When scaled to the entire school, the conclusion remains unchanged. Marketville has 146 girls who each have at least one mutual friend, of whom 80 have fewer mutual friends than their own mutual friends have on average, 41 have more, and 25 have the same; the former is nearly twice the latter. Feld reported that boys at the school and students at other schools in the Coleman study exhibit the same pattern; if 'average' is replaced with 'median,' that is, whether most of one's friends have more mutual friends than oneself, the result is almost identical. A minimal example of the friendship paradox: B has 3 friends, A and C each have 2, and D has only 1, so the average number of friends per person is 2; when listing each person's friends individually, B is counted 3 times, and the average number of friends among friends is 18 ÷ 8 = 2.25. A, C, and D each have fewer friends than the average number of friends of their friends, with only B being an exception (the values are calculated according to the figure in this text). Author: Jaszczuroczłek; Source: Wikimedia Commons ; Permission: CC BY-SA 4.0 。 The variance of friend count and the degree distribution skew Feld's explanation is to distinguish between two distributions. The first is the 'number of friends per individual': the friend counts of the eight girls sum to 20, averaging 2.5 friends per person. The second is the 'number of friends of friends': listing each person's friends one by one results in 20 positions, and these friends collectively have 60 friends, averaging 3.0. The difference arises from repeated counting: a person appears in others' friend lists as many times as that person has friends. Using Feld's example, a person with 40 friends appears in the friend lists of 40 different people, while a person with only one friend appears in only one person's friend list. Let the i-th person have xᵢ friends. The average number of friends per person is Σxᵢ / n; in the list of friends, the i-th person appears xᵢ times, each time contributing xᵢ, so the average number of friends among friends is Σxᵢ² / Σxᵢ. Feld showed it equals "mean + variance ÷ mean." Variance cannot be negative, so the average number of friends among friends is at least equal to the average number of friends per person, and equality holds only when everyone has the same number of friends; the greater the difference in the number of friends, the larger the gap. The following Python code reconstructs the friendship network of eight girls according to the number of friends in Table 1 of the paper, with the values in the comments matching those in Table 1. import networkx as nx # Mutual friendships among the eight Marketville girls (Feld 1991, Fig. 1 / Table 1) edges = [ ( "Betty" , "Sue" ) , ( "Sue" , "Alice" ) , ( "Sue" , "Dale" ) , ( "Sue" , "Pam" ) , ( "Alice" , "Jane" ) , ( "Alice" , "Dale" ) , ( "Alice" , "Pam" ) , ( "Jane" , "Dale" ) , ( "Pam" , "Carol" ) , ( "Carol" , "Tina" ) ] G = nx . Graph ( edges ) deg = dict ( G . degree ( ) ) mean_friends = sum ( deg . values ( ) ) / len ( deg ) # 2.5 mean_friends_of_friends = ( sum ( d ** 2 for d in deg . values ( ) ) / sum ( deg . values ( ) ) ) # 3.0 friend_means = { v : sum ( deg [ u ] for u in G [ v ] ) / deg [ v ] for v in G } below = [ v for v in G if deg [ v ] < friend_means [ v ] ] # 5 girls mean_of_friend_means = sum ( friend_means . values ( ) ) / len ( G ) # about 2.99 The greater the skew in the degree distribution, the larger the gap. In Marketville, the distribution of female students' friend counts is right-skewed: the individual average is 2.7 friends, while the average from a friend's perspective is 3.4 friends. Feld estimated that if each person's friends represented the overall population of 'friends,' 74% of people would feel they have fewer friends than their friends do, while only 56% have fewer friends than the individual average. Online platforms amplify this skew to an extreme. Ugander et al. analyzed the complete friend network of approximately 721 million active Facebook users in May 2011: the average number of friends per user is about 190, the median is only 99, and a small number of users have hundreds or thousands of friends (the upper limit at that time was 5,000); the expected number of friends of a person reached via a random friendship link is 635. As a result, 92.7% of users have fewer friends than the average number of friends of their friends, and 83.6% have fewer friends than the median number of friends of their friends. Here it is important to distinguish two things. The statement 'the average friend count across all friend-list entries is greater than the average friend count per person' holds true in any network where friend counts are not all identical; however, 'most people have fewer friends than their own friends have on average' is not a mathematical necessity—it depends on who is friends with whom. Feld used the same set of friendship counts (4 people each with 3 friends, 12 people each with 1 friend) to construct four different networks: when people with similar numbers of friends are connected, the difference is smallest; when people with many friends are each connected to those with only one friend, the difference is largest; he also constructed an exception where a majority of people have more friends than their own friends have on average. Real-world social networks tend to show positive correlation, with a correlation coefficient of 0.226 between the number of friends of the two endpoints of a friendship on Facebook, but still more than 90% of users fall on the side of the paradox. Influenza surveillance, health intervention, and platform sampling Pick a random person and ask them to identify a friend, and you can access more 'central' individuals at a very low cost without having to map out the entire network. In 2003, Reuven Cohen, Shlomo Havlin, and Daniel ben-Avraham proposed 'acquaintance immunization' in the Physical Review Letters: randomly select a subset of people and inoculate one randomly selected acquaintance of each. Theoretical analysis and simulations show that in networks with broad degree distributions, especially scale-free networks, the proportion of people required for immunity under this strategy is much lower than that required for random inoculation, and it does not require knowledge of how many connections each individual has. In 2010, Nicholas Christakis and James Fowler reported a field study in PLoS ONE. They tracked influenza at Harvard College from September 1 to December 31, 2009: a random sample of 319 students from 6,650 undergraduates, plus 425 friends nominated by these students, totaling 744 individuals. According to physician diagnoses, the cumulative incidence curve of the friends group was approximately 13.9 days (95% confidence interval 9.9–16.6 days) ahead of the random group; by day 16 of the outbreak, the friends group had significantly led, being 46 days ahead of the overall daily peak. When based on self-reported symptoms, the lead time was only 3.2 days. The authors also noted that the extent of the lead time depends on both the outbreak and the network itself; this study only involved one university during one influenza season. Applying the same approach to health interventions yields varying effects depending on the task. Kim et al. published a cluster randomized trial in The Lancet in 2015: in August 2012, in 32 villages in the Lempira department of Honduras (a total of 5,773 participants), researchers provided either a multivitamin or chlorine for water purification to 5% of villagers, selected through three methods: random selection, selection of those with the most social connections, and friends nominated by randomly selected villagers. The multivitamin redemption rate in the nominated friend group was 74.3%, in the random group 66.2%, and in the most-connected group 61.0%; the nominated friend group showed a 12.2% higher redemption rate than the random group (95% confidence interval 6.9–17.9); there were no significant differences in redemption rates for chlorine used in water purification across the three groups. The authors suggest that chlorine-based water purification requires learning a new multi-step procedure, which may partly explain the differences between the two interventions. For social media research, the friendship paradox is first and foremost a sampling weight issue. Hodas, Kooti, and Lerman found from a sample of Twitter's data stream that over 98% of users have fewer followers than the people they follow, and that the people they follow are on average more active and receive more content that is widely retweeted. That is, a person's timeline is a sample weighted by connection count. Economist Matthew Jackson theoretically argued in the Journal of Political Economy in 2019 that this over-sampling of popular individuals leads people to overestimate their peers' engagement, consistent with empirical findings that people overestimate their peers' drinking, smoking, and drug use. Any sample recruited through friend links, follow lists, or 'recommend a friend' invitations will be biased toward high-connectivity individuals; Feld provides a correction in the footnote of his paper, weighting each friend's information by '1 divided by the number of friends,' and then estimating the overall average. References Feld, S. L. (1991). Why Your Friends Have More Friends Than You Do. American Journal of Sociology , 96(6), 1464–1477. doi:10.1086/229693 Ugander, J., Karrer, B., Backstrom, L., & Marlow, C. (2011). The Anatomy of the Facebook Social Graph. arXiv:1111.4503. arxiv.org/abs/1111.4503 Cohen, R., Havlin, S., & ben-Avraham, D. (2003). Efficient Immunization Strategies for Computer Networks and Populations. Physical Review Letters , 91, 247901. doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.91.247901 Christakis, N. A., & Fowler, J. H. (2010). Social Network Sensors for Early Detection of Contagious Outbreaks. PLoS ONE , 5(9), e12948. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0012948 Kim, D. A., et al. (2015). Social network targeting to maximise population behaviour change: a cluster randomised controlled trial. The Lancet , 386(9989), 145–153. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(15)60095-2 Hodas, N. O., Kooti, F., & Lerman, K. (2013). Friendship Paradox Redux: Your Friends Are More Interesting Than You. Proceedings of ICWSM , 7, 225–233. doi:10.1609/icwsm.v7i1.14440 Jackson, M. O. (2019). The Friendship Paradox and Systematic Biases in Perceptions and Social Norms. Journal of Political Economy , 127(2), 777–818. doi:10.1086/701031 Research methodology Rituals can be mimicked, but understanding cannot be feigned Information provided by Scholay Academic One-Stop Platform Organize and publish; if there is any infringement, please provide feedback for removal.
