title: Comparing 1911 Brushless Shaft Resistance vs 2002 Clutch Holding on 900 mm Indoor Swing Lanes
summary: Full disclosure up front: I am referencing BMT Smart's published Chinese product sheets for the 1911 and 2002 swing mechanisms here (checked 2026-11-23), not claiming independent third-party lab testing. I am putting together an enclosure RFQ for a 900 mm indoor office lane and ran into a classic spec-sheet trap that I wanted to share and sanity-check with integrators who have fielded both drive styles. On paper, BMT 1911 and BMT 2002 look almost identical for a 900 mm lane: Both support 600–1200 mm lanes. Both use aluminum alloy and 45# steel with a standard 1:102 gear ratio. Both use a DC 24 V 50 W brushless motor and list 50–70 persons/min throughput (1911 throughput and torque come from technical drawing material) and −20 to 55 °C on the Chinese pages. Here are the three checks that changed how we separated them in our bid sheet: Holding physics are not comparable on one scale: 1911 relies on brushless motor output-shaft resistance rated at 30 N·m in technical drawing material, with no electromagnetic clutch. 2002 adds a DC 24 V 15 W electromagnetic clutch rated at 100 N·m clutch locking torque. Treating 30 N·m vs. 100 N·m as a simple 3x multiplier ignores how each hardware reacts when someone leans against a 900 mm wing. Catalogue endurance and electrical sub-loads shift: On the Chinese sheets, 1911 lists 8 million manufacturer-rated cycles (50 W motor), while 2002 lists 5 million cycles plus the extra 15 W clutch load. Cross-language page trap on 1911: The historical English page ( pd.jsp?id=16 ) still shows different endurance and ambient temperature numbers than the Chinese page, so we locked our RFQ strictly to the Chinese sheet plus written factory confirmation. We also checked whether 2507 (100 W servo + 100 N·m clutch) was relevant, and ruled it out for this specific lane because 2507 is listed for 600 mm lanes and its Chinese sheet has a gear-ratio discrepancy (1:1 table excluding motor vs. 1:2 gear detail) that requires confirmation. For those running 900 mm indoor office swing lanes with standard reader controllers: in real daily traffic, where have you found brushless shaft resistance (like 1911) sufficient vs. where has an electromagnetic clutch (like 2002) genuinely prevented forced-push maintenance headaches?

title: AI Isn't Transforming Work, Because the System Hasn't Changed
summary: The speed is real. The change is not. A draft that took an hour now takes ten minutes. A summary arrives in seconds. A first version of anything is one prompt away. And yet the week feels the same. The same meetings. The same rework. That gap is the subject of this piece. AI is doing real work at the level of the single task. It is not, on its own, changing how work moves through a team. Those are two different things, and most teams have only touched the first one. A New Shape for Work opens with a plain diagnosis. AI is helpful, but it has not transformed the way most teams operate. The difference feels marginal. The reason, the guidebook says, is leverage. Used without a clear strategy, AI gives surprisingly little of it. The image the guidebook uses is a bicycle with one gear. "It's like adding a power boost to a bicycle with only one gear," the Introduction says, "the pedals move frenetically, but nothing has fundamentally changed." The pedals spin faster. The bike goes no faster. The rider works harder and arrives at the same place. Leverage is what lets you move up a level. The guidebook puts it this way: "Increased leverage allows you to move up to a higher level, and work on the system rather than in the system." That sentence is the whole argument in one line. Working in the system means doing the tasks faster. Working on the system means changing how the tasks flow and what survives them. Before and after The guidebook draws the contrast as a before and after list. Before: information scattered everywhere; everyone reinventing their own wheel; agents confused by outdated docs; one-off chats; isolated achievements. After: everything automatically organized; rationalized, shared systems; clean context for agents; automated processes; compounding flywheel. Read that list slowly. Nothing on the before side is a complaint about AI being weak. The AI works. The system around it does not. Outdated docs confuse agents. Scattered information means every task starts from zero. One-off chats mean nothing learned on Monday helps on Tuesday. Isolated achievements mean one person's win stays one person's win. The after side is not about a smarter model. It is about a shared system that holds what the team knows, so the model has something solid to work with. Organization comes first, automation second. That order matters. Automating a mess gives you a faster mess. Think about your own week. How much of it goes to finding things, re-explaining things, and redoing things? That is the tax of a system that has not changed. AI can cut the time each task takes, but it cannot cut the tax. Only a change to the system can do that. A faster draft does not fix a slow approval. A faster summary does not fix a meeting that should not exist. This is why the guidebook refuses to sell AI as a tool upgrade. A tool upgrade makes the same work faster. A system change makes different work possible. The first feels like progress for a month and then stalls. The second is slower to start and keeps paying. The core philosophy The guidebook states its core philosophy in plain terms: "Humans thrive when we do the creative work that we love, and that only we can do. Everything else can, should, and eventually will be automated." The question is how. The path has two parts. First, create a shared context system that your whole team and their agents can work in together. Second, create shared AI systems, sometimes called factories, that a handful of people can be responsible for, and that everyone else can benefit from. That sounds large. The guidebook insists it is not. The simplest version, it says, is nothing more than a shared to-do list with an agent and your team. That takes a few minutes to set up, and it can grow to handle tasks of near-infinite complexity. You do not need to change everything overnight. Start with one workflow, or one team. See if it works. Then go from there. That is the practical test hidden inside the philosophy. If the only place AI touches your work is inside private chats, the system has not changed. If one shared list exists, and an agent works from it, and the whole team can see the result, the system has started to change. When one part of a team adopts this way of working, the guidebook says, the rest quickly follow, without need for persuasion or change management. That claim is easy to test. It either happens or it does not. But it points to the real measure of success: not whether individuals use AI, but whether the team works differently because of it. What to do with this Pick one repeated piece of work. A weekly update. A status report. A triage step that happens every day. Give it a shared home instead of a private chat. Put the instructions and the expected output in one place the team can see. Let an agent run it from there. Watch what breaks, fix that one thing, and run it again. Do that, and you will learn more about your system in a week than a year of faster drafts will teach you. The drafts were never the problem. The system was. AI is not failing at work. It is waiting for the system to change. The bicycle needs another gear. The Matrix framed the same choice years ago. The blue pill is the faster draft in the same system. The red pill is changing the system itself. Transformation is a choice, not a tool swap.

title: Read Your Own Writes on Async Replicas: PostgreSQL 19's WAIT FOR LSN
summary: PostgreSQL 19's WAIT FOR LSN lets a read on an asynchronous replica wait until that replica has replayed your write. You get read-your-writes consistency without sending every read to the primary. The problem: the write succeeded, the read missed it Read-write splitting is a common way to scale: writes go to the primary, reads spread across asynchronous replicas. It breaks a simple expectation: A user renames their profile from Alex to Sam. The primary commits. Success. The user refreshes, and the read lands on a replica. The replica hasn't replayed the change yet, so it returns Alex. Nothing failed. Replication lag let the user miss their own write. The guarantee that this never happens is called read-your-writes (RYW) consistency . Why not just read from the primary? You can, and it's a valid fix. Route reads that must see the latest write to the primary. The cost is load: the more traffic does this, the more you lose the reason you added replicas. A common variation is sticky primary routing : after a write, read from the primary for a fixed window, say 5 seconds. But replication lag is unpredictable: The replica catches up in 20 ms. The primary served almost 5 seconds of reads it didn't need to. The replica lags 8 seconds. The window closes at 5 seconds, and reads hit a stale replica anyway. We're using time to guess replication progress . What if we waited for actual progress instead? PostgreSQL 19: WAIT FOR LSN PostgreSQL replicates by streaming its Write-Ahead Log (WAL). A Log Sequence Number (LSN) is a position in that stream. If you know the LSN of your commit, you know exactly how far a replica must get before it can show your write. The pattern takes five steps: Commit the write on the primary. Capture the WAL position right after the commit. Send that LSN along with the next read, to a replica. On the replica, wait until it has replayed up to that LSN. Run the read on the same replica. Its fresh snapshot includes your write. On the primary, after committing: SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn ( ) ; -- 0/0306EE20 On the replica, before the read: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH ( TIMEOUT '200ms' , NO_THROW ) ; If the replica has already caught up, the command returns immediately. Otherwise it waits until the LSN is replayed or the timeout expires. With NO_THROW , a timeout returns a status ( success or timeout ) instead of raising an error, so check the status before running the read. Run the wait before your transaction takes a snapshot: outside a transaction block, or as its first statement. Earlier versions could do this with application-side polling. PostgreSQL 19 makes it a native command. Don't make every write wait. Make only the reads that need consistency wait. Is this a new idea? Not really. Other databases have tackled the same problem. MySQL can wait on transactions instead of log positions, using Global Transaction Identifiers (GTIDs): SELECT WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET ( 'required-gtid-set' , 0.2 ) ; The read waits until the replica has executed those transactions, with a 0.2-second timeout. SQL Server (Always On Availability Groups) has LSNs too, and its sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states view reports last_hardened_lsn and last_redone_lsn per replica. Synchronous commit guarantees the log is hardened on the secondary. Queries only see a change after redo replays it into the data pages, and redo can lag. There's no directly equivalent built-in wait command, so you would poll that view yourself. Replication durability and read consistency are different guarantees. Data can be safe on a replica before a query there can see it. Where it fits in production Every approach pays somewhere: Approach Trade-off Primary routing More load on the primary Sticky primary routing Assumes replication progress Synchronous replay Higher write latency Replication-aware reads ( WAIT FOR LSN ) Read latency and token management Replica waits don't replace primary routing. Waiting requests hold database connections, raise tail latency, and need careful timeout and failover handling. A practical setup combines all three: Regular reads go straight to replicas, with no waiting. Reads right after a write run WAIT FOR LSN on a replica first. If the replica can't catch up in time ( timeout ), fall back to the primary. Takeaway WAIT FOR LSN doesn't remove replication lag or add a new consistency model. It lets you keep asynchronous replication and make only the reads that need consistency wait, instead of making every write wait. Read-your-writes is a consistency requirement, not a routing strategy. Sometimes reading from the primary is the right answer. Sometimes waiting on a replica is the better trade-off. Let the architecture decide. References PostgreSQL 19: WAIT FOR LSN MySQL: GTID functions SQL Server: readable secondary replicas SQL Server: sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states

title: GitHub Actions runner pricing per minute in 2026: the rate table, larger runners, self-hosted costs and nine billing traps
summary: How much does a GitHub Actions runner cost per minute? In November 2026, GitHub’s hosted Linux x64 runners cost $0.006 a minute at 2 vCPU, $0.012 at 4 vCPU and $0.022 at 8 vCPU, per GitHub’s Actions runner pricing reference; the 4 and 8 vCPU larger runners need GitHub Team or Enterprise Cloud. Sengi Basic runs the same Linux x64 jobs for $0.001, $0.002 and $0.004 a minute, one-sixth of GitHub’s rate at 2 vCPU, with 3,000 free Basic minutes a month; Sengi Premium costs $0.003, $0.006 and $0.012. The rate is only part of the bill: nine traps below, from dollar allowances and per-job rounding to plan fees, cache fees and runs nobody cancelled, change what you pay. Last checked November 11, 2026 : GitHub’s runner pricing reference and Actions billing documentation re-read that day with no change, and Sengi’s rates against its published pricing. Other providers’ rates and terms as read on November 7, 2026 from each provider’s own pricing page and docs. We list only what a provider states; where a page is silent, we say so. GitHub Actions runner pricing per minute: the November 2026 table GitHub’s hosted Linux x64 rates next to both Sengi runner classes at matched vCPU counts, in US dollars per minute at list price. Linux x64 size GitHub hosted Sengi Premium Sengi Basic Sengi Basic label 2 vCPU $0.006 $0.003 $0.001 sengi-basic-2-ubuntu-2404 4 vCPU $0.012 $0.006 $0.002 sengi-basic-4-ubuntu-2404 8 vCPU $0.022 $0.012 $0.004 sengi-basic-8-ubuntu-2404 At every size Sengi Basic is the lowest rate per minute and Sengi Premium is about half of GitHub’s. To price your own month, put your minutes into the GitHub Actions cost calculator; the cheapest runners table adds every other hosted runner. What does a GitHub Actions Linux 2-core runner cost per minute? GitHub’s standard Linux 2-core x64 runner, the machine behind ubuntu-latest in a private repository, costs $0.006 a minute with 8 GB of memory: $6 per 1,000 minutes once the plan’s included usage is spent. Sengi Basic at 2 vCPU costs $0.001 a minute with 8 GB, $1 per 1,000 minutes; Sengi Premium costs $0.003, $3 per 1,000. The 2-core runner is where most minutes go: lint, unit tests, type checks, small builds and the checks AI coding agents trigger on every pull request. That makes the 2 vCPU rate the one number that moves a CI bill most. GitHub larger runners pricing per minute: 4-core and 8-core GitHub calls anything above the standard runner a larger runner, and offers them only to organizations on GitHub Team or Enterprise Cloud. On Linux x64 it lists 4-core at $0.012 a minute and 8-core at $0.022: the 8-core rate is 3.7 times the 2-core rate. Each step up on Sengi doubles the price: Sengi Basic: $0.002 a minute at 4 vCPU and $0.004 at 8 vCPU, 18% of GitHub’s 8-core rate. Sengi Premium: $0.006 at 4 vCPU and $0.012 at 8 vCPU, 55% of GitHub’s 8-core rate. Both run on personal and organization repositories. GitHub larger runners vs third-party runners works out when a bigger runner pays for itself, and runner sizes lists every Sengi label. What a month of GitHub Actions minutes costs Per-minute rates hide how fast a bill grows. Each cell is the list rate times the minutes, before any included or free usage. Minutes a month GitHub hosted Sengi Premium Sengi Basic 1,000 at 2 vCPU $6 $3 $1 10,000 at 2 vCPU $60 $30 $10 10,000 at 4 vCPU $120 $60 $20 10,000 at 8 vCPU $220 $120 $40 100,000 at 2 vCPU $600 $300 $100 Sengi’s 3,000 free Basic minutes take $3 off a Basic month, and GitHub’s included usage, $12 to $300 by plan, comes off a GitHub month; trap 1 shows how far it goes. What 100,000 GitHub Actions minutes cost runs the sum on every hosted runner. Trap 1: included usage is dollars, and bigger runners spend it faster GitHub now states each plan’s included compute as a dollar amount, not minutes, and deducts each runner’s own rate from it. On GitHub Team and Enterprise Cloud, larger runners draw on it too: GitHub plan Included a month 2 vCPU minutes 4 vCPU minutes 8 vCPU minutes Free $12 2,000 Not available Not available Pro $18 3,000 Not available Not available Team $18 3,000 1,500 818 Enterprise Cloud $300 50,000 25,000 13,636 Allowances that count in 2 vCPU units shrink the same way elsewhere: Sengi’s 3,000 free Basic credits are 3,000 minutes at 2 vCPU, 1,500 at 4 and 750 at 8; Avrea’s 3,000 free minutes are used proportionally at larger sizes; Depot counts included minutes at 2× and 4× for 4 and 8 vCPU; Latchkey counts a 4 vCPU minute as two and an 8 vCPU minute as four. Compare allowances in dollars: Sengi’s is worth $3 a month, Avrea’s $12, GitHub Team’s $18. Trap 2: per-job rounding to the whole minute GitHub rounds the minutes and partial minutes each job uses up to the next whole minute. A matrix of 20 jobs that each run 61 seconds bills as 40 minutes, not 20.3. Latchkey also rounds up per job, and so does Sengi. Namespace bills a minimum of one minute and rounds the next 15 seconds down, so 70 seconds is one minute and 150 seconds is three. CRACI and tempus.build bill per second. Rounding matters most for many short jobs. Merge small jobs into fewer steps, or cut a matrix you do not need; GitHub Actions billing explained shows how. Sengi never bills boot or teardown, only the minutes the job runs. Trap 3: plan fees before the first minute Provider What you pay before any minutes Sengi Basic Nothing : no plan, no subscription, no base fee Depot Developer $20 a month (2,000 included minutes, one user) or Startup $200 (20,000) Namespace None pay as you go; $100 (Team) or $250 (Business) a month for its in-plan rate Latchkey $5, $19 or $49 a month, with 2,000, 4,000 or 6,000 included minutes Bitrise Build Hub From $13.50 a month billed yearly, $15 billed monthly, as a compute budget RunsOn A licence of €300, €900 or €1,800 a year by jobs per month, plus about $7 a month of AWS control plane Actuated $150 a month for the first server, $125 for each additional one, plus the servers Cirrus Runners $150 a month per runner A plan fee is cheap at volume and expensive in a quiet month. At 3,000 minutes on 2 vCPU, Depot’s Developer plan comes to $26 against $0 on Sengi Basic. Trap 4: the in-plan rate is not the rate you pay past the plan Namespace: 2 vCPU and 8 GB is $0.004 a minute inside a plan and $0.006 pay as you go or past the plan’s unit minutes. Bitrise Build Hub: Linux Medium (4 vCPU, 16 GB) at $0.0125 a minute from a monthly budget, plans from $13.50 a month billed yearly; pay-as-you-go past the budget is twice the rate and off by default. With pay-as-you-go off, jobs stop running on Build Hub when the budget is spent. Depot: past the plan’s included minutes, $0.006, $0.012 and $0.024 a minute at 2, 4 and 8 vCPU. Sengi Basic has one rate per size from the first minute to the last. Trap 5: memory is priced with the vCPU Namespace bills units of 1 vCPU and 2 GB, counting the larger of vCPU and GB ÷ 2, so 2 vCPU with 8 GB costs the same as 4 vCPU with 8 GB: $0.006 a minute pay as you go. Avrea lists 4 vCPU at $0.006 with 8 GB and $0.008 with 16 GB, and 8 vCPU at $0.012 with 16 GB and $0.016 with 32 GB. CRACI ’s default 2 vCPU runner has 6 GB of memory, against 8 GB on GitHub’s private-repository runner. Compare at matched memory. Sengi Basic gives 4 GB per vCPU at every size, 8, 16 and 32 GB, at one price per size. Trap 6: cache, storage and add-ons are billed separately Provider Cache and storage Other add-ons Sengi Included : actions/cache, setup-action caches and Docker layer caching None GitHub 10 GB of cache per repository; more is billed hourly once the limit is raised Artifact storage from 500 MB to 50 GB by plan Blacksmith Docker layer caching and sticky disks, $0.50 per GB a month each Static IPs, $100 per IP a month WarpBuild $0.20 per GB-month, plus $0.0001 per cache write or restore Snapshot restore $0.04 a job; SAML SSO $250 and audit logs $400 a month Depot 25 GB or 250 GB included by plan, then $0.20 per GB a month Container builds $0.04 a minute past the plan Namespace Cache volumes $0.0048 per GB-day past the plan’s free amount Registry and artifacts $0.20 per GB-month Avrea 25 GB of cache storage included Static IPs, $100 a month each A Docker-heavy repository with a 20 GB layer cache pays $10 a month for it on Blacksmith before a single minute runs. On Sengi the same cache is included. Trap 7: some sizes need a particular plan or account GitHub offers larger runners only to organizations on GitHub Team or Enterprise Cloud; a personal account stays on 2 vCPU. Latchkey on GH and tempus.build need a GitHub organization, and Blacksmith requires one. Namespace caps concurrency by plan: 32 Linux vCPU at once on Developer, 64 on Team and 160 on Business. Sengi runs personal and organization repositories at 2, 4 and 8 vCPU on every account. Trap 8: the wrong size for the job Many jobs sit on a 4 or 8 vCPU runner out of habit. Lint and unit tests rarely use the extra cores, so every minute costs double or quadruple for no gain. Size each job: put light jobs on sengi-basic-2-ubuntu-2404 and keep the larger sizes for compiles and Docker builds that keep every core busy. Trap 9: superseded runs keep billing A new push to a pull request leaves the previous run going unless the workflow cancels it. A concurrency group with cancel-in-progress: true stops superseded runs and their minutes. It matters most when AI coding agents push many commits to one pull request. GitHub Actions self-hosted runner pricing in 2026 On December 16, 2025 GitHub announced a $0.002-a-minute platform charge on self-hosted runner usage in private repositories, to start on March 1, 2026. It then postponed the charge to re-evaluate its approach, and has announced no new date; its Actions billing documentation, read November 11, 2026, still lists self-hosted runners as free. GitHub Actions pricing changes in 2026 keeps the dated timeline. Free to GitHub is not free. A self-hosted minute still costs: The machines , servers or cloud instances, including the hours they wait between jobs. The operations : building and patching images, autoscaling, cleaning up between jobs, and someone on call when a runner wedges at night. The isolation work : making sure one job cannot see what the last one left behind. The charge, if it returns : $0.002 a minute on private-repository usage, as announced. Sengi folds all of that into one per-minute rate: every job runs in a fresh VM, there is no fleet to patch, and Sengi Basic costs $0.001 a minute at 2 vCPU. Hold that against your server bill plus your team’s time; what a self-hosted runner really costs and the self-hosted runner alternative work the comparison through. A simple way to compare runner prices Put every provider on the same three lines: the plan you pay before any minutes, the rate at the size you use, and how a minute is counted. At 4 vCPU: Runner Plan fee 4 vCPU, per minute How minutes are counted Sengi Basic None $0.002 Rounded up per job; boot and teardown not billed compiler.dev None, prepaid credit $0.004 Not stated Latchkey $5 to $49 $0.005 Rounded up per job Blacksmith None $0.008 Not stated WarpBuild None $0.008 Per minute tempus.build None, prepaid balance $0.008 Per second GitHub None for Actions; larger runners need Team or Enterprise Cloud $0.012 Rounded up per job Depot $20 or $200 $0.012 Billed minutes = minutes × 2 at 4 vCPU Namespace None, or $100 or $250 $0.012 pay as you go One-minute minimum, next 15 seconds rounded down Bitrise Build Hub From $13.50 $0.0125 From the monthly budget, then twice the rate Then price a real month. What 100,000 GitHub Actions minutes cost does it for every hosted runner, and the runner alternatives do it at 3,000, 20,000 and 100,000 minutes. Sengi Basic or Sengi Premium: which per-minute rate to pick Sengi Basic is the lowest price for every Linux x64 job, $0.001, $0.002 and $0.004 a minute at 2, 4 and 8 vCPU, and the right default for tests, lint, packaging and agent-triggered checks. Sengi Premium , $0.003, $0.006 and $0.012 a minute, is the faster class for CPU-bound builds that must finish sooner. In Sengi’s Docker build benchmark, measured October 27, 2026 (median of 3 runs), sengi-premium-2-ubuntu-2404 built the Atuin server, a Rust project, in 6m13s with no layer cache, $0.019, and in 1m44s with the type=gha layer cache, $0.005. Fast Docker builds in GitHub Actions has the method and all three projects, and choose your Sengi runner helps you pick job by job. Moving to Sengi: a one-line runs-on change jobs : test : runs-on : sengi-basic-2-ubuntu-2404 Use sengi-basic-4-ubuntu-2404 or sengi-basic-8-ubuntu-2404 for larger jobs, and sengi-premium-2-ubuntu-2404 , sengi-premium-4-ubuntu-2404 or sengi-premium-8-ubuntu-2404 for CPU-bound builds. Workflows, required checks and logs stay in GitHub, every job runs in a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 x64 VM, actions/cache and Docker layer caching are included, and you start with 3,000 free Basic minutes a month. If a coding agent such as Claude Code or Codex works in your repository, give it one prompt and it opens the pull request; the guide covers the rest. When is Sengi the wrong fit? macOS, Windows, arm64 or GPU jobs. Sengi runs Ubuntu 24.04 on Linux x64 at 2, 4 and 8 vCPU; keep those jobs where they are and move the Linux x64 ones. Jobs that must run inside your own cloud account. RunsOn or a bring-your-own-cloud runner keeps the machines yours. Move the rest with the one-line change above. Frequently asked questions What is the GitHub Actions hosted runner price per minute in 2026? GitHub’s hosted Linux x64 runners cost $0.006, $0.012 and $0.022 a minute at 2, 4 and 8 vCPU, per GitHub’s Actions runner pricing reference, checked November 11, 2026. Sengi Basic runs the same sizes at $0.001, $0.002 and $0.004 a minute, and Sengi Premium at $0.003, $0.006 and $0.012. How much does a GitHub Actions Linux 2-core runner cost per minute? GitHub charges $0.006 a minute for its standard Linux 2-core runner, $6 per 1,000 minutes, once a plan’s included usage is spent. Sengi Basic at 2 vCPU is $0.001 a minute, $1 per 1,000 minutes, one-sixth of GitHub’s rate. What do GitHub larger runners cost per minute at 4-core and 8-core? GitHub lists Linux x64 larger runners at $0.012 a minute for 4-core and $0.022 for 8-core, for organizations on GitHub Team or Enterprise Cloud. Sengi Basic is $0.002 and $0.004 at those sizes, and Sengi Premium $0.006 and $0.012, on personal and organization repositories. Is there a GitHub Actions self-hosted runner platform fee in 2026? Not today. On December 16, 2025 GitHub announced a $0.002-a-minute charge on self-hosted runner usage in private repositories from March 1, 2026, then postponed it with no new date. Its billing documentation, read November 11, 2026, still lists self-hosted runners as free. Are self-hosted GitHub Actions runners cheaper in 2026? The minutes are free to GitHub, but you pay for the machines, including the hours they wait between jobs, and the time to patch, scale and isolate them. Sengi Basic runs each job in a fresh VM for $0.001 a minute at 2 vCPU, with nothing to operate. What are the hidden costs of GitHub Actions runners? Five things move the bill more than the headline rate: included usage that is a dollar amount and runs out faster on bigger runners, per-job minute rounding, plan fees before the first minute, memory tied to vCPU count, and per-GB cache and storage fees. Sengi Basic has one per-minute rate at each size, $0.001, $0.002 and $0.004, no plan, and the cache included. Do GitHub's included minutes cover larger runners? On GitHub Team and Enterprise Cloud, yes, at the larger runner's own rate: GitHub Team's $18 a month covers 3,000 minutes at 2 vCPU, 1,500 at 4 vCPU or about 818 at 8 vCPU. Larger runners are not available on Free or Pro, and they are billed on public repositories. Read November 7, 2026. Does GitHub round Actions minutes up? Yes. GitHub rounds the minutes and partial minutes each job uses up to the nearest whole minute, so a 61-second job bills as two minutes. Sengi, Latchkey and GitHub round per job; CRACI and tempus.build bill per second. Which GitHub Actions runners charge a monthly plan? Depot from $20 a month, Namespace $100 or $250 for its lower in-plan rate, Latchkey from $5, Bitrise Build Hub from $13.50 billed yearly, and RunsOn a licence from €300 a year. Sengi Basic, GitHub, Blacksmith, WarpBuild, Avrea and CRACI list no runner plan fee. Why does memory change a runner's price? Some providers price memory and vCPU together. Namespace bills units of 1 vCPU and 2 GB, so 2 vCPU with 8 GB costs the same as 4 vCPU with 8 GB. Sengi Basic gives 4 GB per vCPU at every size, 8, 16 and 32 GB, at one price per size. Does Sengi charge for cache storage? No. actions/cache, the setup actions' caches and Docker layer caching are included on Sengi with no per-GB fee. Blacksmith bills Docker layer caching at $0.50 per GB a month and WarpBuild bills cache storage at $0.20 per GB-month plus $0.0001 per operation. How do I move a GitHub Actions job to Sengi? Change one line: set runs-on to a Sengi label such as sengi-basic-2-ubuntu-2404. Workflows, required checks and logs stay in GitHub, and every job runs in a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 x64 VM. Originally published at sengi.run .

title: The Expensive Convenience of Someone Else's Intelligence
summary: There's something fascinating about how little you need to know about artificial intelligence to build a product powered by it today. A few lines of code. An API key. A reasonably well-structured prompt. And suddenly, your application can understand language, reason through problems, write code, analyse documents, or hold a conversation. You don't need to understand how a transformer works. You don't need to train a model. You certainly don't need a warehouse full of GPUs. Someone else has already done the difficult part. You simply rent the intelligence. And for a while, it feels like one of the greatest bargains in software engineering. Until you begin to realise that the intelligence is not the only thing you're renting. You're also renting someone else's infrastructure decisions. Their availability. Their performance characteristics. Their pricing structure. Their model lifecycle. And, to an extent, their priorities. None of this is necessarily a problem when you're getting started. In fact, I'd argue that renting intelligence is one of the smartest decisions most AI startups can make. But there's an interesting point in the life of an AI product when the convenience that helped you build it begins to influence what the product can become. And I think we're only beginning to appreciate how important that transition is. We Have Become Very Good at Borrowing Complexity Software engineering has always been a story of abstractions. We rarely write our own database engines. We don't build an operating system every time we want to deploy an application. We use cloud providers instead of constructing data centres. And we generally consider this progress. Good abstractions allow engineers to spend less time solving problems that have already been solved and more time building things that matter to their users. LLM APIs are an extraordinary extension of that idea. Consider what an application developer had to do just a few years ago to build something resembling a capable conversational assistant. The amount of specialised research, training data, compute infrastructure, and machine learning expertise required would have made the project unrealistic for most small teams. Today, an experienced software engineer can build a useful prototype over a weekend. That's remarkable. But abstractions have an interesting property. They remove the need to manage certain kinds of complexity. They don't necessarily remove the consequences of that complexity. When you use a managed database, you may not need to worry about replication internals, but you still care about availability, query latency, and data consistency. When you deploy to a cloud platform, you may not manage the physical servers, but your application still experiences the consequences of network failures, resource contention, and infrastructure costs. And when you integrate an LLM through an API, you may never see the inference engine. But your users certainly experience its behaviour. The abstraction is convenient. The consequences remain yours. The Invoice Is Only the Beginning Most conversations about the cost of AI eventually arrive at tokens. Input tokens. Output tokens. Cached tokens. Reasoning tokens. Price per million tokens. These are useful numbers, but I think they can create a misleading sense of precision. A model that costs less per token isn't necessarily cheaper for your application. Suppose Model A costs twice as much per token as Model B. At first glance, Model B seems like the obvious economic choice. But what if Model B requires longer prompts to achieve acceptable results? What if it generates more tokens before arriving at an answer? What if it needs two attempts to complete a task that Model A handles correctly the first time? What if its tool-calling reliability is slightly worse, causing more failed workflows and human interventions? Suddenly, the price comparison becomes much less straightforward. The real cost isn't simply what you pay to generate a token. It's what you pay to achieve a useful outcome. And that difference becomes particularly important when AI is responsible for completing work rather than merely producing text. Imagine an AI agent responsible for confirming customer orders. It receives an order, contacts the customer, verifies the details, and updates the merchant's system. The business doesn't care how many tokens the agent generated. It cares whether the order was successfully confirmed. If a cheaper model reduces inference costs by 40% but introduces enough failures to increase human intervention and unsuccessful confirmations, the apparent savings may disappear. Conversely, an expensive frontier model might be unnecessary for a workflow that a smaller, specialised model can handle reliably. The right question isn't necessarily: Which model is cheapest? It's: What is the least expensive reliable way to complete this particular job? That question changes how you think about model selection. It also changes how you think about the business you're building. The Strange Economics of Intelligence There's another aspect of this that I find interesting. Traditional software has relatively predictable execution costs. A database query consumes resources. An HTTP request takes time. A background job uses compute. There are variations, of course, but engineers have developed mature techniques for estimating, monitoring, and optimising these systems. LLM workloads introduce a different kind of variability. Two requests that look similar at the application layer can have very different computational characteristics. One may contain a short prompt and produce a concise answer. Another may require extensive context, multiple reasoning steps, several tool calls, and a much longer response. If you're building an agentic system, a single user request might trigger an entire sequence of model interactions. And those interactions can multiply costs in ways that aren't immediately obvious from the initial API integration. This creates an interesting commercial problem. You might charge your customers a fixed monthly subscription while your underlying intelligence costs vary with their behaviour. Your most active customers may also be your most expensive customers. That's not inherently bad. Heavy usage can indicate that customers are receiving real value. But it becomes dangerous when the value you capture doesn't grow alongside the cost of delivering it. A product can become more popular while its unit economics become worse. And unlike an infrastructure problem that only affects performance, this one can threaten the sustainability of the business itself. It's possible to build an AI product that customers genuinely love and still struggle to make money from it. Which is why I think inference engineering is becoming as much a product and business discipline as a technical one. Your Users Don't Know What Time-to-First-Token Means One of the most interesting things about working with conversational AI is how quickly infrastructure performance becomes a user-experience problem. Consider a voice conversation. When someone asks a question, they expect a response. Not eventually. Not when the GPU becomes available. Not after the inference provider finishes scheduling requests. They expect a response within the rhythm of a normal conversation. A delay that might be tolerable in a document-analysis application can feel awkward during a phone call. A longer delay can make the interaction feel unnatural. And a sufficiently long pause may cause the user to repeat themselves, interrupt the system, or assume the call has failed. This is where metrics like time-to-first-token become interesting. Time-to-first-token, or TTFT, measures how long it takes for a model to begin producing output after receiving a request. But even that doesn't tell the entire story. For a voice agent, the user experiences a sequence of operations. Their speech must be captured and recognised, unless the system uses an end-to-end speech model. The application may need to retrieve context or perform other processing. The language model must generate a response. The response must be converted into speech. And the audio must reach the user. Every stage introduces latency. Some of these operations can overlap, and a well-designed streaming pipeline can reduce the perceived delay substantially. But the important point remains: The user experiences the system, not the individual components. You can have a fast language model and a slow voice agent. You can have excellent average inference latency and still deliver a poor experience when the slowest requests occur at the wrong moment. This is why I find averages increasingly uninteresting when evaluating interactive systems. Suppose your median response time looks excellent. But one in twenty requests takes substantially longer. For an application handling occasional document summaries, that might be acceptable. For a conversational system, it can become a recurring interruption. And when a workflow requires multiple sequential model calls, the impact of slow requests can compound. The experience is shaped not only by how fast the system usually is, but by how it behaves when things don't go as expected. The Model Isn't Always the Problem There's a temptation to blame the model whenever an AI application feels slow. Sometimes that's justified. But a great deal can happen between your application sending a request and the model producing its first token. There is network transport. There may be connection setup. There may be request queuing. The inference provider may be operating a shared environment where multiple customers compete for available capacity. A request may land on a worker that needs to load a model or rebuild useful cached context. And the provider may be scaling its infrastructure to accommodate changing demand. These are familiar distributed-systems problems, expressed through a new computational workload. One particularly interesting example is the KV cache. During transformer inference, the system maintains representations of previously processed tokens so it doesn't have to recompute the entire sequence for every generated token. This cache can significantly influence inference performance. But efficiently managing it across multiple workers and requests is not trivial. An application may send a large system prompt repeatedly. From the application developer's perspective, the request is straightforward. But depending on the provider's caching implementation, the same prompt may be processed again, partially reused, or served from an existing cache. That affects both latency and cost. And because many LLM APIs expose stateless request interfaces, the application often has limited visibility into how the underlying infrastructure manages these optimisations. The abstraction is simple. The machinery behind it is anything but. The Illusion of an Interchangeable Model One of the attractive features of modern AI infrastructure is how easy it appears to switch providers. Many inference services expose APIs compatible with popular frontier-model interfaces. Change an endpoint. Update a model identifier. Adjust a few configuration values. And your application is talking to a different model. Technically, that can be surprisingly easy. Operationally, it's a different story. Two models may support similar interfaces while behaving differently in ways that matter to your product. Their tool-calling behaviour may differ. Their adherence to structured output may differ. Their ability to follow complex instructions may differ. They may handle long contexts differently. And the same open-weight model can behave differently depending on how a provider configures or serves it. Quantisation, context limits, inference settings, and serving optimisations can all influence the outcome. So an API-compatible replacement is not necessarily a behaviourally equivalent replacement. This is where evaluation becomes essential. Not generic benchmark scores alone. Not the model leaderboard everyone is discussing this week. Your own evaluations. Built around the actual work your product performs. If your application confirms orders, evaluate order confirmation. If it schedules appointments, evaluate appointment scheduling. If it executes financial workflows, evaluate correctness, authorisation boundaries, and failure handling. Measure the things that would matter if a real customer depended on the system. And measure them repeatedly. Because model quality isn't a permanent property you can assume after one successful test. Models change. Providers change. Your workflows evolve. And user behaviour rarely stays within the boundaries of your original test cases. I increasingly think a company's private evaluation data may become one of its most valuable technical assets. Not because the evaluation framework itself is particularly difficult to build. But because the examples, edge cases, failure patterns, and success criteria represent accumulated knowledge about the problem the company is solving. That knowledge is harder to rent. When Does Renting Stop Making Sense? At some point, an engineering team may begin considering alternatives to frontier-model APIs. Perhaps inference costs are growing faster than revenue. Perhaps latency is too unpredictable. Perhaps the application requires a specialised model. Or perhaps the team needs more control over model versions, capacity, and deployment behaviour. There are several possible responses. One is to route simpler workloads to less expensive models. Another is to use an inference provider hosting open-weight models. Another is to reserve dedicated GPU capacity. And at sufficiently large scale, some organisations may operate substantial inference infrastructure themselves. But I don't think these choices should be treated as a mandatory progression. There's a popular assumption in engineering that maturity means eventually owning more of your infrastructure. Sometimes it does. But owning infrastructure also means owning its problems. Dedicated GPUs don't automatically make inference cheap. They introduce capacity planning, utilisation concerns, operational commitments, model-serving complexity, monitoring, and failure recovery. A GPU sitting idle is still costing money. A GPU operating near its limits may introduce performance problems. And a team that spends months optimising inference infrastructure may be diverting engineering resources away from the actual product. For some companies, that investment will be justified. For others, it may be an expensive distraction. The correct decision depends on workload characteristics, scale, performance requirements, engineering capability, and economics. Not prestige. Not what the largest AI companies are doing. And certainly not the assumption that running your own models automatically makes your company more sophisticated. Sometimes the most mature engineering decision is to continue paying someone else to manage the complexity. The important thing is knowing why. The Infrastructure You Don't Own Can Still Shape Your Product There's a deeper strategic question underneath all of this. When you build on someone else's intelligence, how much control do you really have over the future of your product? Suppose a provider changes its pricing. Or retires a model your application depends on. Or introduces new usage restrictions. Or experiences repeated service degradation. Or changes behaviour in a way that affects a critical workflow. Your product may be functioning exactly as you designed it. And yet its reliability, economics, or user experience can change because of decisions made outside your organisation. This isn't unique to AI. Software companies have always depended on external platforms. Payment processors. Cloud providers. App stores. Communication networks. Identity services. But AI introduces an unusually consequential dependency because the model often sits close to the product's core functionality. If the intelligence layer changes, the behaviour of the product itself may change. That's a different kind of dependency from replacing a logging provider. And it deserves architectural attention. This doesn't mean every startup should immediately become model-agnostic or build elaborate multi-provider routing systems. Premature abstraction can be just as expensive as vendor lock-in. But it does mean teams should understand where their dependencies are concentrated. Which capabilities are difficult to replace? Which workflows are sensitive to model behaviour? Which providers represent single points of failure? And which parts of the system could be redesigned if the economics changed? The goal isn't complete independence. That's rarely realistic. The goal is to preserve enough optionality that your business can adapt. Perhaps the Intelligence Was Never the Product Here's the part I find most interesting. As increasingly capable models become available through APIs, access to intelligence becomes less distinctive. Not irrelevant. Not worthless. But less exclusive. If two companies can access the same model, what makes one product meaningfully better than the other? It probably isn't the API key. It may be the quality of the workflows built around the model. The proprietary context the system can access. The integrations it can execute. The reliability of its actions. The quality of its evaluations. The distribution channels through which it reaches customers. Or the depth of its understanding of a particular industry. Consider two AI agents that can both hold convincing conversations. One answers questions impressively. The other understands the business process, checks relevant information, executes authorised actions, recovers from failures, and knows when to involve a human. They may use the same underlying language model. But they're not delivering the same product. The difference lies in the system around the intelligence. And that system is where a substantial part of the engineering work begins. It's also where much of the commercial value may ultimately reside. A customer doesn't necessarily want access to an intelligent model. They want a problem solved. And the ability to consistently solve that problem is not something you acquire merely by choosing the most capable model. You have to engineer it. The Cost of Convenience Is Not Always Money I started this reflection thinking about inference costs. But the more I examine the subject, the more I think the expensive part of renting intelligence isn't always the invoice. Sometimes it's uncertainty. Sometimes it's limited control. Sometimes it's the engineering compromises required to work around a provider's constraints. Sometimes it's the opportunity cost of building your product around capabilities that may change without your permission. And sometimes it's the distraction of trying to own infrastructure before your business has earned the complexity. None of this makes managed AI APIs a bad idea. Quite the opposite. They've made an extraordinary amount of innovation possible. A small team can now build applications that would have been financially or technically unrealistic not long ago. That's a remarkable shift in what software engineers can accomplish. But the convenience of an abstraction should never be confused with the absence of trade-offs. At the beginning, the question is often whether a model can do what you need. Later, the questions become more difficult. Can it do it reliably? Can it do it quickly enough? Can it do it at a cost your business can sustain? Can you measure when it fails? Can you change providers without rebuilding everything? And can the product continue delivering value as the underlying technology evolves? Those are engineering questions. But they're also business questions. And I suspect the companies that build enduring AI products will be the ones that learn to answer both. Because there is nothing inherently wrong with building on someone else's intelligence. We've built much of the modern software industry on infrastructure we don't own. The mistake would be assuming that because the intelligence is rented, the responsibility for what we build with it is rented too. It isn't. The model may belong to someone else. The infrastructure may belong to someone else. Even the most impressive capabilities may originate somewhere outside our control. But the product is still ours. And so are its consequences.
